timezone_note: Armenia has a single time zone and does not observe daylight saving time; the WMO's country record for Armenia, supplied by the national Hydrometeorology and Monitoring Center SNCO, lists Yerevan at UTC+04:00 with DST flagged 'N'. This agrees with the IANA zone Asia/Yerevan.
passport_validity_rule: Armenia's embassy in India (india.mfa.am, updated 30 June 2026) says the passport must cover the entire stay in Armenia, and the UK FCDO says it 'must be valid for the duration of your stay'; neither names a minimum number of months of remaining validity. Global Affairs Canada instead states the passport 'must be valid for at least 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Armenia' and Smartraveller gives only the generic note that many countries want six months. Armenia's own mission and FCDO are the best-supported, so the rule is recorded as validity for the duration of the stay; an airline following the Canadian reading could still ask for six months at check-in, so carry a passport with that margin if you can. Armenia's foreign ministry site (mfa.am) refused connections when checked, so the destination's own main page was not read.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa depends on nationality. The UK FCDO and Australia's Smartraveller both state that their citizens can enter without a visa for up to 180 days (FCDO: 'in a year'; Smartraveller: 'per year'). Global Affairs Canada states that a tourist visa is required for Canadians and points to Armenia's e-visa; Armenia's own pages listing visa-free nationalities could not be opened, so treat Canada, and any nationality not named here, as unconfirmed and check with the Armenian embassy. Armenia's embassy in India states a visa is required for Indian ordinary passports, to be obtained as an e-visa (processing time 'three working days'), at the border for holders of a qualifying residence permit or visa, or at an embassy. Separately, nationals of 111 listed countries who hold a residence permit issued by the USA, an EU/Schengen state, the UAE, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait or Oman, valid at least six months from entry, are visa-exempt from 1 July 2026 to 1 July 2027 for up to 180 days in a one-year period; the permit must be shown as a card or a sticker in the passport. The country list is in a PDF that could not be opened, and the page does not name India, so whether this exemption covers Indian citizens is not confirmed. E-visa applicants from India must supply travel insurance and, without a qualifying residence permit or visa, a return air ticket reservation, a local invitation and proof of financial means. No official source consulted states an onward-ticket, proof-of-funds or arrival-card requirement for visa-free visitors, so whether an onward ticket is required is unconfirmed (carry a return booking anyway). The FCDO notes strict customs rules and that entry is refused with an invalid travel document or a passport reported lost or stolen; Smartraveller states cash of USD 10,000 or more (or equivalent) is subject to import and export rules. The FCDO notes the land border with Iran is open but can change at short notice. No health declaration is required (armenia.travel: PCR tests and proof of vaccination are no longer required).

recommended_vaccinations: Mpox (for travellers with specific risk activities)
health.malaria_risk: None
health.notes: The US CDC's Armenia page (last reviewed 25 August 2026) states yellow fever vaccine is 'not required' for country entry and 'not recommended'; Global Affairs Canada likewise says proof of yellow fever vaccination is not required. Everything else is advisory: CDC recommends hepatitis A, hepatitis B (under 60), MMR, COVID-19 and routine vaccines, mpox vaccine for travellers with certain risk activities, and says rabies-infected dogs are commonly found in Armenia, so pre-exposure rabies vaccination depends on activities and access to treatment. Global Affairs Canada recommends hepatitis B for all travellers. The CDC Armenia page carries no malaria section, and the FCDO and Global Affairs Canada pages do not mention malaria; no official source consulted advises malaria prevention. Smartraveller notes public hospital standards are basic outside Yerevan, serious cases may need medical evacuation, and some medicines (some sleeping tablets, codeine-containing products) are illegal. Armenia's own health ministry was not used as a source here.

money.card_acceptance: Armenia's official tourism board says credit cards are widely accepted in Yerevan, but the country remains largely cash-dependent outside the capital.
money.cash_culture: Carry cash for markets, restaurants and rural areas; the Yerevan metro runs on a 100 AMD coin/token system and is cash only, and taxis are best paid in cash (armenia.travel).
money.tipping: Armenia's official tourism board says it is customary to leave a 10% tip when dining out.
money.atm_notes: ATMs are plentiful in Yerevan, and currency-exchange offices plus kiosks in some major supermarkets are widely available (armenia.travel). No official source was found on ATM fees or dynamic-currency-conversion practice, so none is stated.

power.adapter_note: Armenia's official tourism board describes sockets as primarily Type C (European standard) at 220-240V, and says a device labelled 'INPUT: 100-240V, 50/60 Hz' needs only a Type C adaptor. Travellers from a 230V country therefore need a plug adaptor but no voltage converter. Supply frequency is not stated by any official source consulted, so it is left null.

emergency.notes: Armenia's tourism board (armenia.travel) lists 911 as the Emergency Situations Crisis Management Center line alongside the direct services (fire 101, police 102, ambulance 103, gas emergency 104, Yerevan municipality 105, airport hotline 187). The UK FCDO says to call 911 for an ambulance and ask for an English speaker, and its 'Getting help' page lists 911 as the emergency services number. Global Affairs Canada lists police 102, medical assistance 103, firefighters 101 and 'emergency services: 112'; Australia's Smartraveller says 'Call 112 or 911 for the emergency hotline' (fire 101, medical 103, police 102). So 112 is named as an emergency number by two foreign governments but not by Armenia's tourism board; the general emergency number shown is 911 (named by the tourism board and FCDO), and 112 is worth trying if 911 does not connect. Smartraveller warns emergency services may take a long time to reach remote regions. No official source states which languages are answered beyond the FCDO's English-speaker request.

getting_around.summary: Yerevan has a metro that runs on a 100 AMD coin/token system (cash only) plus buses and minibuses, and taxis and ride-hailing are cheap and widely used — the official tourism board names GG and Yandex Taxi as the main apps. For timetables the tourism board points visitors at the T-armenia.com app, which covers both Yerevan and national transport services, and at the A2B Yerevan public-transport listing; Yandex Maps is recommended for navigation and Yerevan Ride for bike sharing. Outside Yerevan, carry cash.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Armenia's official tourism board says SIM cards are very accessible and affordable and can be bought at the airport or from providers in the city, with widespread coverage in both cities and rural areas. It does not state what identification is required to register a SIM, and no official source was found that does.
connectivity.typical_cost: The official tourism board states plans can be bought for up to about USD 12 per month including unlimited data, SMS and domestic and international calls (checked 2026-09-28). No official per-10GB or two-week price is published.

timezone_note: Australia is not on one clock. Tourism Australia lists three standard time zones: Australian Eastern (AEST, UTC+10: Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, ACT), Central (ACST, UTC+9:30: South Australia and the Northern Territory) and Western (AWST, UTC+8: Western Australia). Tourism Australia states that New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania and the ACT move their clocks forward an hour in summer, while Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia do not. That matters because the gaps change twice a year: on 17 October 2026 (checked against the IANA tz database) Sydney, Melbourne and Hobart are on AEDT (UTC+11), Brisbane stays on AEST (UTC+10, one hour behind Sydney), Adelaide and Broken Hill are on ACDT (UTC+10:30), Darwin is on ACST (UTC+9:30) and Perth is on AWST (UTC+8, three hours behind Sydney). Per the IANA tz database (not an official page opened for this guide), daylight saving started at 2:00 a.m. on Sunday 4 October 2026 (first Sunday of October) and ends at 3:00 a.m. on Sunday 4 April 2027 (first Sunday of April), when Sydney returns to AEST (UTC+10). Two small zones appear in IANA only: Lord Howe Island (Australia/Lord_Howe, UTC+10:30 standard and UTC+11 in summer) and the Eucla area of Western Australia (Australia/Eucla, UTC+8:45); neither is described on a source opened here. The Bureau of Meteorology and Home Affairs time-zone pages blocked automated retrieval. Book domestic connections against local time at each end. Because Queensland does not move its clocks, the Sydney-Brisbane gap is one hour in summer and zero in winter.
passport_validity_rule: Australia has no six-month rule on the official pages opened. The ABF states all passengers other than Australian and New Zealand citizens must present 'a valid passport or other acceptable travel document' plus a valid visa or authority and a completed Incoming Passenger Card, without giving a minimum number of months. The UK FCDO states: 'To enter Australia, your passport must be valid for the length of your planned stay.' Global Affairs Canada words it as 'Your passport must be valid on the day of entry into the country' and warns that airline or transport rules may be stricter. Home Affairs: an ETA is valid for 12 months or the period the passport is valid, whichever is shorter, is linked to the passport used to apply, and ceases if that passport expires or is replaced, so apply with the passport you will travel on. If you transit a country that wants six months of validity, or your airline applies its own rule at check-in, the stricter rule governs your trip.
entry_requirement_notes: Everyone except Australian citizens needs a visa or electronic authority before travelling. New Zealand citizens are normally granted an electronic Special Category Visa (subclass 444) on arrival, subject to health and character requirements (ABF travel-documents page). Home Affairs: the Electronic Travel Authority (ETA, subclass 601) must be applied for through the Australian ETA app by holders of an ETA-eligible passport, from outside Australia; stay is up to 3 months each entry, valid for 12 months or the life of the passport, whichever is shorter; 'There is a service charge of AUD20 to use the Australian ETA app. There is no other charge payable for an ETA.' The ETA is electronically linked to the passport used to apply and ceases if that passport expires or is replaced. The eVisitor (subclass 651) is free, up to 3 months at a time, for passports from particular (European) countries; the Visitor visa (subclass 600, tourist stream) costs from AUD250 and can be granted for 3, 6 or 12 months. The list of ETA/eVisitor-eligible passports is in an expandable panel on the Home Affairs pages and was not captured here: check it before you book. Arrival card: the ABF states that all arriving passengers must complete an Incoming Passenger Card (IPC), in English, covering identity, address in Australia, customs and quarantine declarations and, for non-citizens, health and character declarations; false information can affect your visa. A digital alternative, the Australia Travel Declaration, is a pilot only (Qantas flights into Brisbane and select flights into Sydney and Melbourne, by invitation through the Qantas app); 'Anyone not invited to apply will continue using the IPC as normal.' So carry/complete the paper IPC unless invited. Cash: AUSTRAC states it is a legal requirement under the AML/CTF Act 2006 to declare currency of AUD 10,000 or more (or foreign-currency equivalent) entering or leaving Australia; failure to report is an offence (AUSTRAC release dated 1 July 2017, the threshold being the figure stated there). Biosecurity (Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry): you must complete a declaration and either declare any risk goods, including food, animal products and plant material (including wooden articles) and footwear, clothing and equipment used in rural areas or near animals, or dispose of them in the bins at the airport or cruise terminal. False or misleading information can bring an infringement notice of up to $7,280, civil penalty proceedings or prosecution, and your visa may be cancelled, with refusal of entry and possibly up to three years before you can return. Yellow fever: see health; Australia does not refuse entry without a certificate. Arrival levy: the ABF lists a Passenger Movement Charge page, but its amount was not read, so it is not stated here. Onward ticket, blank passport pages and proof-of-funds figures were not stated on any official page opened, so none is stated here.

health.notes: Australian Immunisation Handbook (Department of Health): 'Australia strongly recommends that travellers >1 year of age have a valid ICVP with proof of valid yellow fever vaccination if they: are entering Australia within 6 days of leaving a country that is on Australia's list of yellow fever-declared places [and] stayed in the at-risk area overnight or longer.' Travellers arriving without a valid ICVP 'receive information about yellow fever' and are advised to seek medical assessment if symptoms develop within 6 days. This replaces the CDC wording about layovers over 12 hours, which does not appear on the Australian page. CDC (page reviewed 25 August 2026) also lists dengue, Ross River virus, hantavirus, leptospirosis, ciguatera fish poisoning and melioidosis, and a Level 1 global measles notice. The FCDO health page says essential and urgent hospital treatment is free for UK residents under the UK-Australia Reciprocal Healthcare Agreement but that GP visits, prescriptions, ambulances and medical evacuation are not covered, so travel insurance is advised. Malaria is not addressed on the CDC Australia page and no Australian official page on it was opened, so the entry is unchanged. The recommended list is medical advice, not an entry condition.

money.card_acceptance: Tourism Australia states that cards are widely accepted, that merchants may impose credit card surcharges in some places, and that fees may be charged on transactions, particularly when withdrawing from an international account. It also advises checking with your card company about foreign transaction fees.
money.tipping: Tourism Australia states that hotels and restaurants do not add service charges to your bill, that tipping is always your choice, and that in upmarket restaurants it is common to tip waiters 10 per cent for good service.
money.atm_notes: Tourism Australia notes that fees may be charged on international withdrawals. Declare cash of AUD 10,000 or more (Australian or foreign equivalent) on arrival (Tourism Australia). GST is 10 per cent; Tourism Australia says a refund is possible under the Tourist Refund Scheme if you spent AUD 300 or more with a single business no more than 60 days before departing, claimed in the international departure area.

power.adapter_note: Tourism Australia states Australia uses the Type I plug (two flat pins in an inverted V, sometimes with a third centre pin), with a supply of 220-240 volts AC at 50Hz; its packing page says 230V 50Hz and advises a voltage transformer if your home voltage differs. The IEC's World Plugs was not opened to cross-check.

emergency.notes: Australian Government Department of Infrastructure (triplezero.gov.au, opened 18 Oct 2026): 'Triple Zero (000) is Australia's main emergency number for life threatening or time critical situations. You can call 000 from any fixed or mobile phone, satellite phone and certain Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) services.' You say which service you need: police, fire or ambulance. 'In Australia, you can also dial the international standard emergency number (112) from a mobile phone, which will direct you to the same Triple Zero (000) service. This number (112) cannot be called from a fixed landline or satellite phone.' Triple Zero calls are free; with no mobile coverage on any network you cannot reach Triple Zero from a mobile; you cannot contact it by SMS. Deaf or speech-impaired callers can use the National Relay Service via 106 with a TTY. Non-emergency: police assistance line 131 444; State Emergency Service (flood, storm) 132 500. Tourism Australia, Global Affairs Canada and the FCDO also give 000. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page, so none is listed here.

getting_around.summary: No single national transport pass or intercity rail pass was found on an official page opened for this record, so none is listed. Tourism Australia's budget guide (page last modified 30 April 2025; it says costs are a guide only) says public transport trips cost around AUD 2 compared with AUD 20-30 for a taxi or rideshare for a comparable journey, and that daily fare caps apply in most major cities, with a weekday cap of around AUD 17 in Sydney and around AUD 9 in Melbourne. Distances are continental: no source opened here gives flight or rail times, so none are stated. Fare-cap and per-trip figures vary by city and change, so check the local transport operator before you rely on them.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Tourism Australia states mobile phone network coverage is available across Australia, but coverage may be limited in some remote areas. No official page opened states eSIM support, SIM prices or registration rules.

timezone_note: America/Toronto (Eastern) is a representative zone, not the whole country: Canada has six time zones. From east to west the standard offsets are Newfoundland (UTC-3:30), Atlantic (UTC-4), Eastern (UTC-5), Central (UTC-6), Mountain (UTC-7) and Pacific (UTC-8), each one hour later in daylight time (Newfoundland 3:30 behind UTC standard, 2:30 in daylight time). Those numeric offsets are the standard IANA/legal offsets, not read off a page I opened: the National Research Council page lists the zone abbreviations (NST/NDT, AST/ADT, EST/EDT, CST/CDT, MST/MDT) but gives numbers only for Yukon. The NRC states daylight saving time runs from 02:00 on the second Sunday in March to 02:00 on the first Sunday in November (so clocks in Toronto go back on 1 November 2026), is set by provincial legislation, and has exceptions: most of Saskatchewan stays on Central Standard Time all year (Lloydminster-area communities follow Mountain Time with Alberta), Yukon has been on UTC-7 all year since 2020, some areas of Quebec east of 63 degrees W use Atlantic Time, Ontario west of 90 degrees W is on Central Time, and Nunavut covers three zones. British Columbia is changing: the B.C. government states that after clocks moved ahead on 8 March 2026 that was the province's final time change, the 1 November 2026 turn-back will not happen, and B.C.'s new 'Pacific time' is set permanently at UTC-7 (aligned with Yukon). Communities in the northeast (for example Dawson Creek, Fort St. John) stay on UTC-7 year-round and southeastern communities such as Golden, Cranbrook and Fernie keep following Alberta. The practical effect after 1 November is that Vancouver stays on UTC-7 while Toronto drops to UTC-5, a 2-hour gap instead of 3. The NRC page itself warns that from 1 November 2026 some of its content will no longer be accurate and points to provincial and territorial governments. The IANA tz database entry for America/Vancouver was not checked against this change, so do not rely on a device clock alone for B.C. after 1 November 2026. Destination Canada notes that New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island are one hour ahead of Eastern Time and Newfoundland is one hour thirty minutes ahead. Book flights and trains against local times at each end.
passport_validity_rule: Canada's official pages state that you must travel with a valid passport (IRCC: 'When you come to Canada, you must travel with a valid passport or travel document') but none that I opened sets a minimum remaining validity or a six-month rule for visitors, so none is stated here. What the rules do tie to the passport is the length of your stay: IRCC says that if you get no stamp or visitor record, your stay runs six months from entry or until your passport (or biometrics) expires, whichever comes first, and IRCC cannot issue a visitor record valid past passport expiry. An eTA is linked to the passport used to apply, so the same passport must be presented at check-in. Practical advice: carry a passport that is valid for your whole stay plus a buffer; airlines may apply their own stricter rules.
entry_requirement_notes: Canada's eTA (Electronic Travel Authorization) is in force today (17 October 2026). IRCC states it is required for visa-exempt foreign nationals who fly to or transit through a Canadian airport; travellers arriving by land, bus, train or boat (including cruise ships) do not need one, though they still need a valid passport. The fee is CAN$7, non-refundable, paid by credit or debit card online for one person at a time, and you need a valid passport, a card and an email address. IRCC says the eTA is valid for up to five years or until the passport expires, whichever comes first, and a new passport needs a new eTA; it allows repeat short stays, normally up to six months at a time. IRCC advises applying before you book your flight; most approvals arrive by email within minutes but some take several days if documents are requested. Apply only on the official canada.ca site. Who is exempt: US citizens do not need an eTA or a visa but IRCC advises carrying a valid US passport (other identity documents showing name, date of birth and citizenship can be shown by those not flying and without a passport); lawful permanent residents of the US with valid status are exempt but must carry proof of status plus a passport from their country of nationality when flying. Canadian citizens (including dual citizens) and permanent residents cannot apply for an eTA and must travel with a Canadian passport or PR documents. Visa-required nationals need a visitor visa (some may use an eTA instead of a visa for air travel only, if they qualify). An eTA or visa does not guarantee entry: a border services officer decides on arrival. IRCC's visitor page says the officer must be satisfied that you will leave Canada at the end of your authorised stay, have enough money for your stay and have ties (job, home, assets, family) taking you home; most visitors can stay up to six months, and the officer may shorten or lengthen that. That IRCC page sits under the visitor-visa section and does not mention a return ticket, so whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed; carry proof of onward travel and funds anyway. Cash: the CBSA states there is no limit on money you bring in, but amounts of CAN$10,000 or more (cash or monetary instruments, any currency, combined) must be declared; failing to declare can lead to seizure and penalties of 5% to 50% of the seized funds. Blank pages: IRCC says only travellers from visa-required countries need at least one free page; no requirement is stated for visa-exempt travellers, so none applies. Health insurance: IRCC says Canada does not pay for hospital or medical services for visitors.

health.notes: Sourced from the US CDC because the Public Health Agency of Canada's travel-health pages are written for Canadians leaving the country, not visitors arriving, so there is no PHAC arrival page to cite. CDC's Canada page (yellow fever section updated 23 April 2025) states yellow fever vaccine is neither recommended nor required for entry, and I found no vaccination that is a condition of entry. CDC also notes rabies in some wild animals and bats (avoid contact; seek care after any bite, scratch or bat exposure), recommends repellent with 20% or more DEET against ticks and mosquitoes, and, at the time of reading, listed a Level 1 notice for a hepatitis A outbreak in Manitoba (dated 4 June 2026) plus a global measles notice; check CDC for the current list. Medical costs: IRCC states 'Canada does not pay for hospital or medical services for visitors' and advises getting health insurance before you come.

money.cash_culture: No Canadian government source I opened describes cash-versus-card habits, so that is left unstated. What is official: Destination Canada says the currency is the Canadian dollar, with a $1 coin (the 'loonie') and a $2 coin (the 'toonie'), and points visitors to the Bank of Canada for live exchange rates. The CBSA requires a declaration of currency or monetary instruments worth CAN$10,000 or more on entering or leaving (no cap on the amount; seizure and 5%-50% penalties if not declared).

emergency.notes: 911 is confirmed as the emergency number for police, fire and ambulance by three official pages: Parks Canada (national parks), the Government of Canada's IRCC driving page (Canada.ca: 'call the emergency number (911) for police and an ambulance') and the Province of British Columbia (gov.bc.ca: 'If you require immediate assistance from the police, fire or ambulance, pull over and call: 911'). The BC page also says 911 is the number for 'most B.C. communities' and advises adding local emergency numbers when travelling in an area without 911 coverage, so some remote communities still use local numbers. I found no official page saying whether 112 works, so it is not listed. Parks Canada warns that cell coverage is not always reliable in the backcountry or in remote areas, so check the park's own page for local contacts. No national tourist-police line was found, so none is listed here.

getting_around.summary: Canada is very large, so most long hops between regions are by air, and the country has no national rail pass I could verify. VIA Rail is the national passenger operator: its Toronto-Montreal page lists an average travel time of 5 hours 13 minutes over 538 km with 40 departures a week (fares are one-way, per person, excluding taxes, and vary by day and departure time); its Vancouver-to-Toronto page for The Canadian lists 3 days 20 hours 29 minutes over 4,406 km with 2 departures per week. In the Toronto-Montreal-Ottawa-Quebec City corridor rail is competitive with flying, outside it service is infrequent. Domestic flight times, airline fares and bus services were not researched from official sources. City transit is local: Toronto's TTC takes PRESTO, tap-to-pay debit/credit and cash, and some other cities run their own systems. Practical framing (not from a cited source): in most of the country outside big cities a rental car is the usual way to reach national parks.

passes.covers: The TTC fares page lists an adult fare of $3.30 with PRESTO or tap with an Interac debit/credit card (including mobile wallet), $3.35 in cash (exact fare only, no change), with a two-hour transfer on tap payments (not cash), and a PRESTO Day Pass at $13.50. passes.worth_it: The day pass at $13.50 equals roughly four single fares at $3.30, so it pays off only if you take about five or more separate trips that each fall outside a two-hour transfer window; with tap payment and the two-hour transfer, many visitors will do better paying per trip. TTC also states fares are capped at 47 per month for PRESTO and card payers, a benefit for longer stays. Fares as published on the page at the time of reading; confirm at ttc.ca. Other cities (Montreal, Vancouver, Ottawa) were not researched.

timezone_note: Colombia uses a single time zone across the mainland and the island department of San Andres, Providencia and Santa Catalina, and does not observe daylight saving time.
passport_validity_rule: Colombia sets no fixed minimum validity beyond the stay. UK FCDO: the passport must be valid on entry. Global Affairs Canada: valid for the duration of your stay. Germany's Auswaertiges Amt: valid on entry for at least the intended length of stay. Colombian immigration authorities recommend an expiry date at least 6 months after your planned departure (FCDO), and the German page reports travellers refused entry on passports with no more than six months left beyond planned departure. Airlines may also apply their own margin at check-in.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa-exempt visitors (Resolucion 5488 of 2022, Article 3, on cancilleria.gov.co) may enter for short-stay activities that involve no paid work; the resolution defines a short stay as under 90 days, extendable to 180 days in the cases the rules set. Official sources describe the extension differently: Global Affairs Canada says a tourist may be granted up to 90 days at entry and can extend to a maximum of 180 days per calendar year; the UK FCDO says up to 90 days, extendable by up to 120 days through Migracion Colombia, capped at 180 days in any 12-month period; Germany's Auswaertiges Amt says 90 days, usually extendable once by a further 90 days with no entitlement to it. The officer sets the length granted at entry. Onward ticket: the FCDO says you must be able to show an onward or return ticket valid within the 90-day period; Global Affairs Canada and Germany say customs or immigration may ask for a return or onward ticket (and Canada adds proof of sufficient funds); CHECK-MIG: the free online pre-registration form (https://apps.migracioncolombia.gov.co/pre-registro/), completed between 72 hours and 1 hour before travel, for entering and leaving. Official sources disagree on whether it is mandatory. Global Affairs Canada says you must complete it within 72 hours to 1 hour before boarding a flight to or from Colombia or crossing by land, maritime or river routes. Germany's Auswaertiges Amt says travellers must register within 72 hours before entry and before departure, and that the confirmation must be shown to the airline before departure from Germany. The UK FCDO says it can speed up entry but is not mandatory. Migracion Colombia's own pre-registration page describes it as a way to preload trip details and speed up the immigration interview and does not state that it is compulsory. Safest course: complete it before every flight to or from Colombia, since airlines can ask for it. CURRENCY: the FCDO and Germany's Auswaertiges Amt state you may bring in up to US$10,000 (or equivalent) in any currency, and the FCDO says amounts above that must be declared to DIAN (the tax and customs authority). Other formalities (FCDO): make sure your passport is stamped on arrival by land, sea or river or you could be fined on leaving; visas valid for more than 90 days must be registered within 15 days of arrival; travellers flying to San Andres, Providencia or Santa Catalina buy a tourist card at the boarding gate on the day of the flight unless staying under 24 hours.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever certificate only if arriving from, or transiting an airport in, a country with yellow fever transmission risk (Global Affairs Canada names Angola, Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda); not required for direct arrival from Germany (Auswaertiges Amt). See notes - official sources differ.
recommended_vaccinations: Typhoid (rural travel or stays of a month or more)
Yellow fever (for travel to at-risk departments and municipalities, given at least 10 days before arrival there)
health.malaria_risk: Present below 1,700 m (5,600 ft) elevation; CDC records no malaria risk in Bogota, Medellin or Cartagena. CDC lists atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine or tafenoquine as prophylaxis options for at-risk areas.
health.notes: Official sources state the yellow fever entry rule differently and this guide does not pick silently between them. Colombia's Ministry of Health (Minsalud) says that under the International Health Regulations (2005) Colombia takes a non-restrictive recommendation on yellow fever vaccination for people entering the country - not a blanket entry requirement - but travellers going to Very High and High risk municipalities should be vaccinated 10 days in advance. Colombia's tourism board says there are no mandatory vaccinations and recommends the vaccine for certain areas. The UK FCDO says a certificate is needed if arriving from certain countries with transmission risk and you may be asked for it when travelling to high-risk areas in Colombia. Global Affairs Canada says proof is required only for travellers arriving from or transiting Angola, Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo or Uganda. Germany's Auswaertiges Amt says no vaccinations are compulsory for direct entry from Germany, only for arrival from or transit through certain countries, including Brazil, and still recommends the vaccine. The US CDC's country page is the outlier: it states the vaccine is required for all arriving travelers aged 1 year and over (yellow fever notice updated 18 September 2026), while also noting it is generally not recommended for travel limited to Bogota, Barranquilla, Cali, Cartagena, Medellin, San Andres and Providencia, or areas above 2,300 m. The safe course is to carry a yellow fever certificate issued at least 10 days before arrival if you are coming from a risk country or going anywhere outside the high-altitude cities. Colombia's tourism board also notes some domestic routes (for example into the Amazon) ask for a certificate at check-in. Water is described by the tourism board as generally safe to drink in large cities, with bottled water advised in rural areas and small towns.

money.card_acceptance: Colombia's tourism board states that in Bogota, Medellin, Cartagena, Cali and other regional capitals you can pay by card in most hotels, restaurants, shopping centres and tourist services, with Visa and Mastercard the most widely accepted and American Express and Diners Club less frequently taken.
money.cash_culture: Cash remains the most accepted method, especially in markets, small shops, public transport and rural areas. The tourism board advises carrying low-denomination notes (2,000 / 5,000 / 10,000 pesos) because many small businesses cannot break large bills, and recommends changing dollars or euros into pesos rather than trying to spend them - foreign cash is taken at exchange houses, not in shops.
money.atm_notes: Colombia's tourism board notes foreign-withdrawal commissions of roughly USD 3-5 per transaction plus surcharges for paying in another currency, and advises always choosing to be charged in Colombian pesos rather than your home currency when a card terminal offers the choice (dynamic currency conversion gives a worse rate). ATMs run 24 hours in major cities and shopping centres, many with an English-language option; it advises using machines inside banks or shopping centres.

power.adapter_note: Colombia's tourism board describes the common outlets as two flat pins, types A and B, as in the United States, and advises travellers from Europe or other 230V regions to bring a universal adapter and, where needed, a voltage regulator; both are sold in stores, airports and department stores.

emergency.notes: 123 is the single national emergency line and reaches police, ambulance and the fire service; 119 is listed separately for fire. Global Affairs Canada's Colombia page (checked 2026-10-17) says 'For emergency assistance, dial 123', which agrees with the UK FCDO's Colombia travel advice, the source for the 119 fire number. The numbers are taken from these foreign-government pages rather than from a Colombian government page - Migracion Colombia and the National Police sites do not publish a consolidated emergency list that was reachable, and the US Embassy in Bogota's page returned 403 to an automated fetch. Germany's Auswaertiges Amt page carries no emergency number. Bogota's city government describes Linea 123 as operating 24/7 with police and civilian operators dispatching police, the Bogota fire brigade and health-secretariat ambulances. No official source was found stating whether English is answered, and no tourist police number was verified, so none is listed here.

getting_around.summary: Colombia is mountainous and large, so domestic flights (Avianca, LATAM, SATENA and others) are often the fastest way between regions and the only practical way to reach San Andres, Leticia, Nuqui or Cano Cristales; the tourism board advises booking one to two months ahead. An intercity bus network reaches virtually every city and town, with air-conditioned, wi-fi-equipped reclining-seat coaches on main routes - good value for medium distances, but mountain crossings take many hours and road conditions are worth checking in the rainy season. In cities, Bogota runs the TransMilenio articulated-bus trunk network plus the SITP local buses, and Medellin has the country's only metro, linked to the Metrocable gondolas serving the hillside neighbourhoods; Cali's MIO is a similar bus-plus-cable system. Taxis and ride apps are widely available, and in smaller cities like Pereira, Manizales and Bucaramanga transport is simpler and mostly cash.

climate.precipitation_note: READ FIRST - this table is Bogota only, and Bogota is not Colombia. Colombia's official tourism board states there are no seasons in Colombia: climate is set by altitude and region, not by time of year, so temperatures barely move month to month and it is elevation that changes them. Bogota sits at 2,600 m and is cool all year (highs 15-17C); Medellin at about 1,500 m is mild all year; Cartagena on the Caribbean coast is hot and humid all year. Treat every figure below as a Bogota figure only - no verified month-by-month normals for Medellin or Cartagena were obtained, so no offset is given here rather than an invented one; pack for the altitude of each place you are going, not for the month. What does vary is rain: the Andean interior has two wetter periods (roughly March-May and September-November) and two drier ones. January itself is one of Bogota's driest months: 29 mm over about 8 rain days (WMO/IDEAM 1971-2000 normals).
climate.crowd_note: Colombian school holidays run into mid-January, so domestic destinations and coastal flights stay busy in the first half of the month.

timezone_note: One zone nationwide; Costa Rica does not observe daylight saving time, so the offset from North American and European clocks shifts when those countries change.
passport_validity_rule: Costa Rica does not impose a six-month rule. The Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería (DGME) Directrices Generales de Visas de Ingreso y Permanencia para No Residentes (Alcance 148 a La Gaceta 216, 17 November 2025) set the minimum passport validity for First Group nationalities at 'hasta un día' (up to one day), counted from the day of entry; the same text adds that the stay the border officer grants will not exceed the passport's validity. First Group includes the USA, Canada, UK, Australia, Germany, Singapore and Brazil among others. The UK FCDO states the same rule as 'your passport must have an expiry date at least 1 day after the day you plan to leave Costa Rica', so a passport valid at least a day past the planned departure satisfies both. Only machine-readable or biometric ICAO passports are accepted. Second Group nationals (e.g. Belize, Bolivia, El Salvador) need 90 days of validity from entry, and Third and Fourth Group nationals 180 days; check the directive if you hold one of those passports. Sourcing note: the DGME site (migracion.go.cr) returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so the directive was read first-hand from the identical copy of the same Gaceta document hosted on icoder.go.cr (a Costa Rican government domain), and cross-checked against the UK FCDO page.
entry_requirement_notes: Source of the rules below: DGME Directrices Generales de Visas (Alcance 148 a La Gaceta 216, 17 November 2025), read from the copy at icoder.go.cr because the DGME site (migracion.go.cr) blocks automated fetches (HTTP 403). Section 4 of the directive lists the entry requirements for every non-resident: a valid machine-readable or biometric passport; a visa where required; proof of economic means of at least US$100 per month or part-month of legal stay; a return ticket to the country of origin or an onward ticket (or a navigation plan naming the destination port); and no bar to entry. Costa Rica enforces onward travel at the border, not just at airline check-in: the tourism board (ICT) says all travelers must have a ticket for return or onward travel, and accepts a pre-purchased bus or flight ticket or cruise documentation. Stay length: First Group nationalities (which include the USA, Canada, UK, Australia, Germany, Singapore and Brazil) enter visa-free for up to 180 calendar days, non-extendable, with the exact period set by the immigration officer at the border; the directive allows an extension only for someone granted fewer than 90 days, and only up to a total of 90. The UK FCDO also says up to 180 days. The older 90-day figure for Canada and others is not in the current directive. Do not book non-refundable travel past the days actually stamped. Second to Fourth Group nationalities get at most 30 days (Second Group extendable to 90). FCDO additionally notes a currency declaration for amounts of US$10,000 or more, a departure tax of about US$29 (usually included in the airfare), and overstay fines of US$100 per month.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever — required only for travellers aged 9 months and older arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines (MMR, Tdap, polio, varicella, influenza)
Chikungunya (per CDC, tied to an outbreak in the northwest)
health.malaria_risk: Present in the provinces of Alajuela and Limón; rare to no transmission elsewhere (CDC).
health.notes: Yellow fever is checked at the border, not merely advised. Costa Rica's Ministerio de Salud states that foreigners arriving from a risk zone who do not present the Certificado Internacional de Vacunación contra la Fiebre Amarilla to the immigration authority cannot enter the country ('los extranjeros que lleguen a Costa Rica y no presenten el Certificado Internacional de Vacunación contra la Fiebre Amarilla ante la autoridad migratoria, no podrán ingresar al territorio'). The Americas risk list named by the Ministerio de Salud is Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, French Guiana, Paraguay, Peru, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago and Venezuela, plus a set of African countries; CDC states the requirement applies to travellers aged 9 months and older. A separate and easily confused rule runs the other way: since 2026 Costa Rican citizens and residents departing Costa Rica for those same destinations must themselves be vaccinated at least 10 days before travel — that obligation does not apply to foreign visitors arriving. Neither the Ministerio de Salud article read here nor CDC stated a minimum number of days between vaccination and arrival for inbound foreign travellers, so no figure is given. Everything else listed under recommended vaccinations is advice, not a border check.

money.card_acceptance: The official tourism board states that all major credit cards are widely accepted and that US dollars are also widely accepted alongside the colón. No official source was found on where cards stop working, so assume cash for small rural businesses and buses.
money.cash_culture: Intercity buses are privately operated with no central terminal, and the tourism board advises bringing cash for lines that sell tickets only at the station — so carry colones for bus travel and small purchases even though cards are common.
money.tipping: Restaurant and hotel prices already include a 13% value added tax and a 10% service charge, per the official tourism board: an additional tip is optional and only for exceptional service, not expected.
money.atm_notes: The tourism board states ATMs are located throughout the country. No official source was found on fees, bank networks or dynamic currency conversion, so none is asserted.

power.adapter_note: The official tourism board specifies 110V outlets with standard US two-prong plugs (Type A). Grounded three-prong Type B outlets are also in general use but no official source confirmed that, so only Type A is listed. A traveller from a 230V country needs a plug adapter and must check that each device is rated for 110V — many hairdryers and kettles are not. Mains frequency is left null because no official source stated it.

emergency.notes: 911 is the single national emergency number. Costa Rica's Sistema de Emergencias 9-1-1 (operated by ICE) confirms nationwide 9-1-1 coverage, and the UK FCDO lists '911 (ambulance, fire, police)' for Costa Rica. No official source confirmed a separate tourist-police line or whether English is answered, so neither is claimed.

getting_around.summary: There is no national rail network for visitors and no countrywide transit pass. Intercity buses, run by several private companies rather than a government operator, reach nearly every popular destination cheaply, but there is no central terminal in San José — each line has its own terminal, and some sell tickets only at the station, for cash. Over ten domestic airports are served by Sansa and Green Airways, which is how travellers skip long drives between the Pacific coast, the Caribbean and the northern volcanoes. All of the above is as stated by the official tourism board; road-condition and drive-time claims are deliberately omitted because no official source was found for them.

timezone_note: Egypt has a single nationwide time zone (IANA Africa/Cairo). Egypt's State Information Service states that Egypt reintroduced daylight saving time in 2023 after a seven-year hiatus and now runs it annually, clocks going forward on the last Friday of April and back at the end of the last Thursday in October. Daylight saving time is therefore in effect on this guide's verification date (28 September 2026), putting Egypt at UTC+3; clocks return to UTC+2 at the end of October 2026.
passport_validity_rule: The UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office states: "To enter Egypt, your passport must have an 'expiry date' at least 6 months after the date you arrive and have at least one blank page." Global Affairs Canada words the same six-month rule from the other end: valid at least 6 months beyond the date you expect to leave Egypt (it does not mention blank pages). The two differ only on the counting basis; the stricter, safe reading for a long stay is six months beyond departure. Egypt's own e-visa portal (visa2egypt.gov.eg) does not publish the rule on its public pages, so this is sourced from foreign governments' pages about Egypt rather than first-hand from an Egyptian authority.
entry_requirement_notes: Per UK FCDO guidance on Egypt (page checked 2026-10-17): most visitors need a visa, available as an e-visa applied for online through Egypt's official portal visa2egypt.gov.eg (valid up to 3 months; the portal says to apply at least 7 days before departure) or as a visa on arrival at approved airports (30 US dollars, cash only, valid up to 30 days). Since 1 August 2026, travellers arriving at Cairo International Airport can instead buy a digital visa on arrival from self-service machines, card payment only, 36 US dollars including a 6 US dollar digital service fee. Global Affairs Canada, which does not mention the Cairo machines, quotes the cash visa on arrival at roughly 60 to 100 US dollars per person depending on travel plans, so the fee differs between official sources: carry cash or a card for the higher figure and confirm on visa2egypt.gov.eg. Travellers arriving by air at Sharm El-Sheikh and staying under 15 days within the Sharm El-Sheikh, Dahab, Nuweiba and Taba resort area receive a free entry stamp instead of a visa; Canada also describes a 14-day Sinai-only stamp at the Taba land border. Keep the entry stamp: Global Affairs Canada warns exit can be denied without proof of it. A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required if arriving from, or transiting through, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Foreign currency worth more than 10,000 US dollars must be declared on arrival; up to 5,000 Egyptian pounds may be brought in or taken out. Drones are prohibited and satellite phones, radios and large video cameras can be confiscated (Global Affairs Canada). No arrival card, health declaration, proof of funds, hotel booking, travel insurance or onward ticket requirement is stated by FCDO. This is a foreign government's summary, not a first-hand Egyptian citation: confirm against visa2egypt.gov.eg or an Egyptian consulate before travel.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever: certificate required only for travellers arriving from, or with a long layover (CDC: over 12 hours) in, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from the United States
recommended_vaccinations: Rabies (pre-exposure, depending on planned activities and access to medical care)
Routine vaccines (COVID-19, influenza, polio, DTaP, chickenpox, shingles)
health.notes: The only vaccination actually checked at the Egyptian border is the yellow fever certificate, and only for arrivals from a transmission-risk country (UK FCDO, US CDC and Global Affairs Canada agree on this; CDC page reviewed 25 August 2026 and does not recommend the vaccine for Egypt itself). Everything else on the recommended list is advice, not an entry condition. Global Affairs Canada adds that some foreigners staying longer than a month for study, work or training may need an HIV test, and the FCDO says HIV test results are required for work permits, not for tourist entry. No malaria risk level is stated: the CDC and FCDO health pages consulted carry no malaria statement for Egypt and Global Affairs Canada's entry page does not mention it, so no risk level is asserted here.

emergency.notes: The US Embassy in Cairo gives the Egyptian police hotline as 122, the tourist police as 126 and the ambulance service hotline as 123, and lists no fire number. The UK FCDO (gov.uk Egypt 'Getting help' page, checked 2026-10-17) lists the same police 122, tourist police 126 and ambulance 123 together with fire 180, so fire is set to 180 on that single official source. Note a genuine discrepancy in official guidance: Global Affairs Canada's Egypt page lists police 112, medical assistance 113 and firefighters 110, with no separate tourist police number; if 122, 123 or 180 do not connect, those are worth trying. Whether English is answered on any of these lines is not stated by any official source consulted.

getting_around.summary: In Cairo the metro is the practical way to cross the city; its state operator, Cairo Metro Company, runs the first, second and third lines and publishes fares and station lists on its own site. Intercity travel between Cairo, Alexandria and Upper Egypt is by Egyptian National Railways, which sells tickets through its official portal at enr.gov.eg. No nationwide tourist transport pass could be found on any official Egyptian source, so none is listed below.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Egypt's National Telecommunications Regulatory Authority (NTRA) requires every mobile line to be registered against an identified person's data, and enforces it — in August 2026 it referred all four Egyptian mobile operators to the Public Prosecution over lines registered under users' personal data without their consent. NTRA does not state on its site whether a visitor can register a line on a foreign passport, where, or what it costs, so none of that is asserted here.

timezone_note: This guide covers metropolitan France only (mainland France and Corsica), which uses a single time zone, Europe/Paris. France's overseas departments and territories use other zones (France.fr lists Guadeloupe and Martinique at -5, Mayotte and La Reunion at +3, New Caledonia at +11) and are not covered here. Per service-public.gouv.fr, clocks go back one hour on the night of 24 to 25 October 2026 (3 a.m. becomes 2 a.m.), so metropolitan France returns to CET (UTC+1) on 25 October 2026; the label above reflects the state on 17 October 2026, and the same page says the switches follow the last Sundays of March and October.
passport_validity_rule: France is in the Schengen area. The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years; France's service-public.gouv.fr states the same ten-year issue limit and a margin of at least three months beyond planned departure. Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. This applies to metropolitan France.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (17 October 2026). The European Commission's ETIAS page states that ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch; that page is dated 6 October 2025. France's diplomatie.gouv.fr page (April 2026) said it expected ETIAS in the last quarter of 2026, but the EU's official portal (travel-europe.europa.eu, opened 18 October 2026) now gives no launch window and no start date, and Global Affairs Canada says 'Applications are not yet open', so treat no date as fact and check travel-europe.europa.eu before travelling. When it starts it will be a pre-travel authorisation (not a visa) for visa-exempt nationals; the French MFA page gives a fee of EUR 20, validity of three years or until the passport expires, and exemption for people under 18 or over 70. What is already live is the Entry/Exit System (EES): per diplomatie.gouv.fr it was phased in from 12 October 2025 and fully operational from 10 April 2026, replaces passport stamping, and records entry, exit and length of stay with a facial image and (except for under-12s) fingerprints; holders of long-stay visas and residence permits are not registered. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport and france-visas.gouv.fr). The UK FCDO page says border officers may ask you to show a return or onward ticket, proof of enough money for your stay, accommodation and travel insurance, which is a possibility at the border rather than a stated requirement, so whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed. Official pages opened for this guide did not state an onward-ticket requirement, a minimum number of blank passport pages for visa-exempt visitors, or a proof-of-funds figure, so none is stated here. Cash or travellers cheques worth EUR 10,000 or more must be declared to customs when entering or leaving the EU (UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada, both opened 18 October 2026). EES full operation from 10 April 2026 is also stated by the European Commission's Migration and Home Affairs news item.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)

health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's France page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's France page states yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry, and everything in the recommended list is medical advice only. CDC's page, last updated 23 April 2025, has no malaria section; it notes bug bites can spread disease in France (use repellent) and lists a Level 1 notice mainly about rising global measles cases (28 May 2025). Tick-borne encephalitis appears on the page with no France-specific recommendation. CDC is used as a fallback because no French health-ministry page was opened for this guide. Global Affairs Canada's France page (18 October 2026) independently states proof of yellow fever vaccination is not required to enter, and the UK FCDO health page names no required vaccine and no malaria.

money.card_acceptance: France.fr states 'Credit cards are accepted in a large number of shops, hotels, and restaurants' and that shopkeepers often state a minimum charge, and that virtually all ATMs take Visa and MasterCard. The article was last updated on 6 March 2019, so treat contactless and minimum-spend details as unverified.
money.tipping: France.fr states that almost all restaurants include tax and a 15% service charge in their prices (service compris), that a 15% tip is appropriate where service is not included (service non compris), 10-15% of the metered fare for taxi drivers, and about 1.50 EUR each for hotel porters and chambermaids (article last updated 6 March 2019). Tips are customary, not mandatory; the consumer agency DGCCRF's page could not be opened to confirm the legal position.
money.atm_notes: France.fr advises that ATMs often have the best exchange rates, that withdrawing cash on a credit card is treated as a cash advance, that most French ATM keypads have numbers only (convert any letters in a PIN), and to tell your card company you will be abroad. Non-EU residents can claim VAT refunds on purchases over 175 EUR at a single store (per the same 2019 article; check current thresholds).

power.adapter_note: France.fr states electricity runs on a 220-volt, 50-hertz AC current, that France uses a Type E plug (a round pin plus a grounding pin), that visitors bringing appliances need a plug adapter, and that a voltage transformer may also be needed though most major appliances now have one built in. The article is dated 22 March 2012, so the 220V figure is the tourism board's wording; the IEC's World Plugs could not be opened to cross-check.

emergency.notes: service-public.gouv.fr lists 15 as the Samu (emergency medical assistance), 17 as police or gendarmerie, 18 as firefighters and 112 as the European emergency number. The same page lists 114 for deaf and hard-of-hearing callers (France.fr's German-language page says this works by SMS or chat), 196 for maritime rescue, 191 for aeronautical rescue, 115 for social emergencies and 119 for children in danger. France.fr describes 112 as working without an active SIM or credit and routing you to police, ambulance or fire. 0 800 112 112 is a free callback line and does not take emergency calls. 116 117 is for urgent non-life-threatening care outside surgery hours. No dedicated tourist police line was found on an official page, so none is listed here. Cross-checked on 18 October 2026 against the French Gendarmerie nationale's emergency-numbers page (15 medical/SAMU, 17 police-gendarmerie, 18 fire, 112 European number; also 114, 115, 119, 191, 196, 197); Global Affairs Canada confirms 112 and 17 and the UK FCDO says to call 112 for an ambulance.

getting_around.summary: Metropolitan France's long-distance backbone is rail. France.fr describes TGV INOUI as high-speed travel at up to 300 km/h linking Paris with Lyon, Marseille, Strasbourg and Bordeaux in roughly 2 to 3 hours, and Paris to Nice in under 6 hours; slower regional TER trains serve towns, vineyards and coastal villages. SNCF Connect states tickets for TGV INOUI and Intercites open on set dates (12 November 2026 for TGV INOUI travel from 7 January to 2 July 2027, and for Intercites travel through 31 March 2027), and that OUIGO Classique tickets go on sale 60 days before departure. No official fare for any TGV, Intercites or OUIGO journey was found, so none is given here: fares vary by date and booking time, so check SNCF Connect. In Paris and the Ile-de-France, Ile-de-France Mobilites runs the metro, RER, trains, trams and buses on a shared ticket and pass system.

timezone_note: Georgia uses a single time zone year-round and does not observe daylight saving time. The WMO station record for Tbilisi, supplied by Georgia's Department of Hydrometeorology, lists the zone as +0400 with DST = N; this agrees with the IANA zone Asia/Tbilisi (+04 all year). Note that the de facto authorities in Abkhazia and South Ossetia keep Moscow time (UTC+3); those regions are not accessible from the rest of Georgia and Georgian law treats entry to them from Russia as illegal.
passport_validity_rule: Georgia's national tourism board (georgia.travel) states that travellers from most countries need a passport valid for at least 6 months beyond their date of entry into Georgia, and that entry requires an ordinary or biometric national passport unless a treaty provides otherwise. The UK FCDO instead says only that your passport should be valid for the duration of your stay, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs entry page (geoconsul.gov.ge), which was read in full, states no passport-validity rule for visa-free entry; the 6-month figure is kept as the best-supported destination-side statement, so carry a passport with 6 months left. For an e-Visa the passport must be valid 3 months beyond the visa's validity (evisa.gov.ge).
entry_requirement_notes: Visa-free stay is unusually long: the Ministry of Foreign Affairs consular portal (geoconsul.gov.ge, 'Visa free countries' page) lists most eligible nationalities, including the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, Germany, Japan, Singapore, Brazil and the other EU states, at 'Full 1 (one) year' (365 days) without a visa, under Government of Georgia Ordinance No. 255 of 5 June 2015 (Legislative Herald of Georgia; last amended 24 Feb 2026). A few listed nationalities get less (for example Chile 90 days in any 180, Uruguay 90 days, Iran 45 days), and India is not on the list. Holders of valid visas or residence permits of listed countries (including Australia, Canada, the UK, the USA, Japan, South Korea, the Schengen states and Gulf states) may enter and stay 90 days in any 180 without a Georgian visa, if the visa or permit is valid when they cross the border. Nationals not covered may apply for an e-Visa at evisa.gov.ge: fee 20 USD plus a 2% service fee (non-refundable), decision in at least 5 working days, travel document valid at least 3 months beyond the visa's validity, at least two blank pages and issued within the previous 10 years; a short-term single-entry visa is for at most 30 days and the total stay under a short-term visa may not exceed 90 days in any 180. MANDATORY INSURANCE: under the Law on Tourism, since 1 January 2026 every tourist entering Georgia must hold a valid health and accident insurance policy (paper or electronic, in Georgian or English, from a Georgian or foreign insurer) with cover of at least 30,000 GEL for the whole stay including arrival and departure dates, and must present it on entry; exempt are diplomatic/official/special passport and visa holders, accredited diplomatic and international-organisation staff, persons entering under international treaties, and international road freight and passenger drivers (MFA geoconsul.gov.ge; UK FCDO says the same and that proof may be asked at check-in or immigration). The tourism board page (georgia.travel) still calls insurance 'not mandatory'; that page predates or lags the MFA notice, so follow the MFA. The tourism board says proof of sufficient funds may be requested in some cases and that a return or onward ticket is recommended rather than required, so no onward ticket is treated as required; the MFA entry page does not state an onward-ticket rule. Work, including remote work and running a business, needs a work permit under rules changed on 1 March 2026 (MFA, FCDO). No mandatory online arrival form or pre-registration was found.

required_vaccinations: None required for entry — the US CDC's Georgia destination page states that yellow fever vaccine is not required
health.malaria_risk: None — the CDC's Georgia destination page lists no malaria risk or malaria prevention guidance for the country.
health.notes: Nothing is checked at the Georgian border: the list above is travel-health advice, not an entry condition. The CDC page is a US government source used because no Georgian Ministry of Health page stating traveller vaccination advice in English could be located.

emergency.notes: 112 is Georgia's single emergency number for all services. The Public Safety Command Center 112, an entity of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, states that it takes calls 24/7 nationwide from landline or mobile with no prefix, and dispatches police, fire/rescue teams and emergency medical crews. Operators answer in Georgian, English, Azerbaijani, Armenian, Turkish and Russian. A free 112 Georgia app (Android and iOS) and a video-call/SMS channel for deaf and hard-of-hearing callers also exist. No separate legacy service numbers were confirmed by an official source, so none are listed here.

getting_around.summary: Georgian Railway runs the main intercity links, including fast trains between Tbilisi and Batumi on the Black Sea coast (train 802/801, roughly 5.5 hours: 08:00-13:35 westbound, 16:30-21:55 eastbound). Tickets go on sale up to 20 days before departure and can be bought at station ticket offices, at pay boxes, online at ticket.railway.ge or through the operator's mobile app; sales close 10 minutes before departure and a passport or personal ID number is required to book. Georgian Railway also operates international services. Marshrutka minibuses cover routes the railway does not, but no official source for their fares or schedules was found, so none are described here.

timezone_note: Greece uses a single time zone, Europe/Athens. The European Commission's summertime page lists Greece among the Eastern European Time (EET) members and states that Member States switch to summer time on the last Sunday of March and back to standard time on the last Sunday of October; the last Sunday of October 2026 is 25 October, so Greece returns from EEST (UTC+3) to EET (UTC+2) on 25 October 2026. The label above reflects the state on 17 October 2026. The WMO World Weather Information Service entry for Athens shows +0300 with daylight saving in effect.
passport_validity_rule: Greece is in the Schengen area. The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years (the page was last checked 19 August 2026); the UK FCDO and the Government of Canada state the same 3-month margin beyond the date you leave the Schengen area. Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. The Greek National Tourism Organisation (visitgreece.gr) describes the same 90-days-within-six-months limit for visa-exempt nationals and refers other nationals to the Greek embassy or consulate.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (18 October 2026; re-checked on travel-europe.europa.eu, which still says it is not in operation and no applications are collected). The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) states that ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. The Government of Canada's Greece advice, modified 5 October 2026, says applications are not yet open and to apply only through the official EU website once the system is launched. France's diplomatie.gouv.fr (April 2026) says ETIAS is expected in the last quarter of 2026 with a EUR 20 fee (free under 18 or over 70); that is an expectation, not a confirmed start date, and no confirmed date was found on any page opened for this guide, so check travel-europe.europa.eu before travelling. When it starts it will be a pre-travel authorisation, not a visa, for visa-exempt nationals. The Entry/Exit System (EES) is already live: per diplomatie.gouv.fr it has been phased in since 12 October 2025 and is fully operational from 10 April 2026, replacing passport stamping, and Canada's advice says facial image and fingerprints are collected on entry with nothing to do before you travel. The UK FCDO page (undated in the text opened) says Greek authorities indicated they would not collect fingerprints and photos from UK travellers under EES; treat that as a statement about UK travellers that may have changed. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport and the Greek embassy or consulate in your country). The FCDO says you may need to show a return or onward ticket and prove you have enough money; no Greek government page opened for this guide states an onward-ticket rule, a minimum number of blank pages, or a proof-of-funds figure, so none is stated here. mfa.gr returned errors to automated fetches, so this guide relies on EU, UK, Canadian, Australian, French and Greek tourism-board (GNTO) pages. Cash: the Government of Canada's Greece page (updated 5 October 2026) says that if you carry EUR 10,000 or more (or the equivalent) you must declare it to customs when you enter or leave the European Union; this does not apply to travel within the EU. Smartraveller (Australia, still current 18 October 2026) also says travellers on short stays must register fingerprints and a photo under EES on arrival, with nothing to do beforehand. No arrival card or health declaration is mentioned on the Canadian page.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR, including an early infant dose for babies 6-11 months)
Hepatitis A (especially for smaller cities, villages, rural areas or street food)
Rabies (discuss with a clinician depending on activities and access to post-exposure care)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: CDC's Greece page has no malaria section; the Government of Canada's advice says limited malaria transmission may occur but risk to travellers is very low
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Greece page states yellow fever vaccine is not required for entry and not recommended; everything in the recommended list is medical advice only. CDC's page was last reviewed 25 August 2026 (yellow fever section updated 23 April 2025) and carries a Level 1 notice about rising global measles cases (28 May 2025). EU travellers should carry an EHIC or equivalent, per visitgreece.gr; the UK FCDO says UK travellers need a GHIC or EHIC for medically necessary state healthcare, that it is not a substitute for travel insurance, and advises insurance covering local treatment and medical evacuation. The Government of Canada says health care is adequate but varies across the country. FCDO says to dial 112 or 166 for an ambulance. EODY (eody.gov.gr), the national public health organisation, returned an error to automated fetches, so CDC, FCDO and GNTO are used as fallbacks; no official statement on tap water or West Nile virus was opened.

money.atm_notes: visitgreece.gr's travel tips state that credit card holders may take money from the ATMs of the collaborating banks, that its currency is the euro (banknotes 5 to 500 EUR; coins 1 and 2 EUR and 1 to 50 cents), and that bank hours are Mon-Thu 8:00-14:30 and Fri 8:00-13:30, closed on public holidays. Its 'Before you travel' page advises calling your bank or card company before travelling so they know you will use the card in Greece. No official source opened gave card-acceptance levels, tipping norms or VAT-refund thresholds, so those are null.

power.adapter_note: visitgreece.gr states electric power in Greece is 230 V / 50 Hz and the plugs are type F; its 'Before you travel' page adds that North American appliances need a transformer and British appliances need an adaptor. Non-official guides say type C plugs also fit the sockets; that was not confirmed by an official source, so only type F is listed here.

emergency.notes: visitgreece.gr (Greek National Tourism Organisation) lists 112 as the European emergency number, 100 police, 166 First Aid National Center (ambulances), 199 Fire Authority, 1571 Tourist Police (24/7), 1016 SOS Doctors and 210 77 93 777 for the Poisoning Phone Center. The Government of Canada's Greece page confirms 112 and 100 and 1571 for tourist police but does not list 166 or 199; the UK FCDO says to call 112 in immediate danger and to dial 112 or 166 for an ambulance, to call 112 if you see a wildfire, and to make sure your phone can receive emergency alerts (it points to @112Greece for official updates). Some non-official websites list 171 for the tourist police; the two official pages opened (GNTO and Canada) give 1571, so 1571 is used. No official page opened gave a coast guard number, so none is listed. Confirmed on official Greek pages opened 18 October 2026: civilprotection.gov.gr/en/112 (112, free, works across the EU); Hellenic Police direct-lines page astynomia.gr/citizens-guide/direct-lines (100 for emergencies nationwide; 1571 tourist line in Greek, English, French and German; 1033 for police services in Attica, Thessaloniki, Serres, Pieria and Pella); gov.gr national emergency numbers pages titled '166 - Medical Emergency Service (EKAB) Number' and '199 - Hellenic Fire Service Number'; and the Hellenic Fire Service site header shows 199. Government of Canada (updated 5 October 2026): 112, 1571 tourist police, 100 police.

getting_around.summary: Islands: the Government of Canada's Greece advice states that ferries between mainland Greece and its islands meet European safety standards but that weather conditions and strong winds can cause cancellations or significant delays, and that the meltemi wind may bring high waves and disrupt transportation; the UK FCDO warns of regular strikes, sometimes called at short notice, that can disrupt buses, trains, ferries and air travel. No ferry operator timetable or the Ministry of Maritime Affairs' ferry pages could be opened (that ministry's passenger-rights portal and Coast Guard site returned HTTP 403 and the ministry site had an expired certificate), so no operator, route, journey time or fare is given here; check each operator's own page close to the date. Athens: OASA (the Athens urban transport organisation) runs buses and trolleybuses and sells the ATH.ENA ticket and card used across the city's transport; its Visit Athens page says Metro Line 3 connects the airport directly to Syntagma and that Airport Express buses X93, X95, X96 and X97 run on a 24-hour basis, and that you can pay with a contactless bank card or mobile wallet without pre-buying a ticket. Intercity rail: Hellenic Train runs the national passenger trains; its Athens-Thessaloniki page says the route runs daily with frequent services but states no journey time or fare, and links a timetable PDF, so no journey time is given here (third-party sites disagree). Hellenic Train sells single journeys, multi-trip cards and OASA interoperable tickets and offers online ticket purchase.

passes.covers: OASA's prices page lists the 90-minute ticket at 1.20 EUR (discounted 0.50 EUR), the 24-hour ticket at 4.10 EUR and the 5-day ticket at 8.20 EUR.
