timezone_note: Indonesia spans three zones and none of them observe daylight saving. WIB / Western Indonesia Time (UTC+7, IANA Asia/Jakarta) covers Sumatra, Java — including Jakarta and Yogyakarta — and West and Central Kalimantan. WITA / Central Indonesia Time (UTC+8, IANA Asia/Makassar) covers Bali, Lombok and the rest of Nusa Tenggara, Sulawesi and South/East/North Kalimantan. WIT / Eastern Indonesia Time (UTC+9, IANA Asia/Jayapura) covers Maluku and Papua. This guide uses WITA because Bali (Denpasar) is the single most likely arrival point for a visitor; if you are landing in Jakarta instead, set your clock an hour earlier to UTC+7. The WMO/BMKG station records confirm Denpasar at +0800 and Jakarta at +0700, both with no DST.
passport_validity_rule: Indonesia's Directorate General of Immigration requires a national passport valid for at least six months from the date of arrival. The official e-Visa portal states the passport biodata page must show "a minimum validity of 6 months from the date of your arrival to Indonesia", and the same six-month-from-arrival rule is stated for Visa on Arrival issued at the border.
entry_requirement_notes: Three things beyond the visa itself. (1) ALL INDONESIA ARRIVAL CARD — mandatory. Since 1 October 2025 every passenger arriving from abroad, regardless of nationality or visa type, must submit an arrival declaration through the All Indonesia system at allindonesia.imigrasi.go.id or the All Indonesia app. It is free, can be completed up to three days before arrival, and replaces the separate immigration, customs, health and quarantine forms (including the old electronic customs declaration). Only allindonesia.imigrasi.go.id is official. (2) BALI TOURIST LEVY — still in force. Every foreign tourist entering Bali pays a one-off IDR 150,000 levy under Bali Provincial Regulation No. 2 of 2025 (amending Regional Regulation No. 6 of 2023). Pay before or on arrival through the Bali provincial government's Love Bali portal at lovebali.baliprov.go.id, which issues a QR voucher; an exemption application route exists on the same portal. Copycat payment sites exist — use only the baliprov.go.id domain. (3) ONWARD TICKET AND FEES — Immigration states that VOA applicants must show a return ticket or a ticket onward to another country, and officers reserve the right to ask for a printed return ticket on arrival. Visa on Arrival / e-VOA costs IDR 500,000, permits a 30-day stay for tourism, and can be extended once for a further 30 days at an immigration office; it cannot be converted to another stay permit. Separately, bringing in more than IDR 100,000,000 in cash requires a customs declaration. (4) FEE STATUS — the fee stated on Immigration's own VOA page and by the UK FCDO today is IDR 500,000; a higher fee (reported as IDR 750,000 for e-VOA and IDR 1,000,000 for VOA on arrival) was proposed by the Directorate General of Immigration in August 2026 but is not confirmed as in force, so check evisa.imigrasi.go.id before paying. (5) BLANK PAGES — Indonesia's own pages do not state a figure; UK FCDO says at least two blank pages and Global Affairs Canada says at least one, so carry two.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever — certificate required only for travellers arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from a non-risk country
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccinations up to date (MMR, DTaP, polio, varicella, influenza)
Japanese encephalitis (for some activities and longer stays)
health.malaria_risk: None in Jakarta or Ubud, and none in the resort areas of Bali and Java, the Gili Islands or the Thousand Islands (Pulau Seribu). Transmission is present in all eastern provinces (Maluku, North Maluku, East Nusa Tenggara, Papua, West Papua), in rural Kalimantan, West Nusa Tenggara, Sulawesi and Sumatra, and at low levels in rural Java.
health.notes: The yellow fever certificate is the only vaccination actually checked at the border, and only if you are arriving from a yellow-fever risk country — everything else on this list is medical advice, not an entry condition. A typical Bali or Jakarta trip needs no malaria prophylaxis. Note that a 2022 Immigration article on counter Visa on Arrival still lists a full-dose COVID-19 vaccination certificate among its requirements, while the current official e-VOA document list does not mention one; if you want certainty on that point, check evisa.imigrasi.go.id shortly before you fly.

money.card_acceptance: Visa and Mastercard are the most widely accepted and work at merchants across the major cities and tourist areas including Bali, Jakarta and Yogyakarta; JCB is accepted through BNI, CIMB Niaga, Mandiri and BRI affiliations, and American Express acceptance is limited, largely via Bank Danamon. Cards are reliable in hotels, larger restaurants and larger stores but not in warungs, markets or small local businesses. Shops do not always display which cards they take, so ask before ordering.
money.cash_culture: Carry rupiah in cash, especially outside the main cities — the national tourism board recommends withdrawing cash in a major city before heading anywhere remote. ATMs dispense IDR 50,000 or IDR 100,000 notes, and those larger notes can be hard to break in rural and non-tourist areas, so deliberately keep a stock of small notes. Notes in circulation run from IDR 1,000 to IDR 100,000. Bringing in more than IDR 100,000,000 (roughly USD 6,500) in cash must be declared to customs.
money.tipping: Tipping is discretionary rather than an obligation. Hotels and restaurants inside hotels operate a regulated service charge ("uang servis") added to the bill under Ministry of Manpower Regulation No. 7 of 2016, which requires that charge to be distributed to the staff — so where you see a service charge on the bill, the staff are already receiving it and a further tip is optional. No official Indonesian source sets a tipping percentage, and this record deliberately does not invent one.
money.atm_notes: ATMs on the Cirrus, Maestro and Plus networks are widespread in major cities and tourist areas. JCB cardholders can withdraw at affiliated bank ATMs (BNI, CIMB Niaga, Mandiri, BRI) and American Express cardholders at Bank Danamon ATMs. Machines dispense either IDR 50,000 or IDR 100,000 notes. No official source for per-withdrawal fees or dynamic-currency-conversion practice was available, so none is stated here — as everywhere, decline any ATM offer to bill you in your home currency.

power.adapter_note: Indonesia uses the two-pin European plug at 230 V / 50 Hz. Travellers from continental Europe and most of Asia need no adapter; UK (type G) visitors need a simple plug adapter only. Visitors from the United States, Canada and most of South America should check that their devices are dual-voltage (phone and laptop chargers usually are) and otherwise bring a voltage converter — the official tourism board advises exactly this. Adapters are sold in local minimarkets throughout Indonesia if you forget one.

emergency.notes: 112 is Indonesia's national emergency number, reachable from mobile and satellite phones, and is the number to use if you are unsure which service you need. Ambulance and medical emergencies can also be reached on 118 as well as 119. Two other numbers are worth saving: 115 for BASARNAS search and rescue (relevant for sea, diving and mountain incidents) and 129 for natural-disaster assistance. No separate national tourist-police number is published by the tourism board. Whether an English speaker answers is not guaranteed by any official source, so having your accommodation call on your behalf is often faster.

getting_around.summary: Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 13,000 islands, so moving between regions means flying or taking a ferry. The busiest gateways are Soekarno-Hatta (Jakarta), Juanda (Surabaya), I Gusti Ngurah Rai (Bali), Sultan Hasanuddin (Makassar) and Kualanamu (Medan), with connecting flights onward to smaller islands; PELNI runs multi-port inter-island ferries and ASDP runs single-route vehicle and passenger ferries. PT Kereta Api Indonesia (KAI) is the national rail operator, running intercity trains, Greater Jakarta commuter services and airport rail links, but its network covers Java and parts of Sumatra and does not extend to Bali, so getting around that island means ride-hailing, a hired car with driver, or a scooter. In cities, Damri buses serve the airports and metered taxis, ride-hailing apps, ojek (motorbike taxi) and bemo (minivan) fill in the rest. Indonesia has no nationwide tourist rail or transit pass — KAI lists no such product — so journeys are bought point to point.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Prepaid SIMs are sold from operator booths in the arrivals halls of the main international airports — Telkomsel, Indosat/IM3, XL, Smartfren, 3/Tri and Axis all have a presence. Registration is compulsory and the booth staff do it for you: a visitor registers with their passport, while residents use a KITAS or KITAP. eSIM does exist on Indonesian networks (Telkomsel sells prepaid eSIM starter packs), but Telkomsel's own prepaid eSIM registration page asks for an Indonesian KTP and family card, so a visitor is usually better off with a physical SIM registered against a passport at the airport, or an international travel eSIM bought before departure. Pocket wifi rental is offered as an alternative, orderable online for airport pickup or mailing. Free wifi is common at major airports, hotels, Jakarta train stations, malls, cafés and tourist sites.
connectivity.typical_cost: No official price list for a ~10 GB / two-week visitor bundle could be verified from an operator or government source, so none is invented here. For scale: the national tourism board states airport SIM prices "vary for each provider starting from IDR 10,000", and Telkomsel lists its SIMPATI eSIM starter pack (3 GB, plus call and SMS allowance) from IDR 25,000 (roughly USD 1.50). Checked 28 September 2026.

timezone_note: Italy has a single time zone, Central European Time (CET, UTC+1), and moves to UTC+2 for summer time (italia.it). The Italian tourism portal says the clocks change overnight between Saturday and Sunday and the exact dates change each year. Under the EU-wide rule as recorded in the IANA tz database for Europe/Rome, summer time (CEST, UTC+2) began on 29 March 2026 and ends on 25 October 2026, when clocks return to CET (UTC+1); that date pair is the IANA/EU schedule and was not read off an Italian government page. The label above reflects the state on 2026-10-17.
passport_validity_rule: Italy applies the Schengen rule. The Italian tourism portal (italia.it) states that non-EU visitors need a passport valid for at least three months after the planned date of departure from the Schengen Area; the UK FCDO's Italy entry guidance adds that the passport must also have been issued less than 10 years before the date of arrival (passports renewed before 1 October 2018 may fail this test). The three months run from leaving the Schengen Area, not from arriving in Italy. EU and Schengen-country citizens may use a valid national ID card instead of a passport.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa-free short stays are Schengen-wide: the UK FCDO states that visitors who do not need a visa may stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period across the Schengen Area, with earlier Schengen visits in the previous 180 days counting toward the 90. ETIAS is NOT in force today (checked 2026-10-18): the official EU ETIAS site (travel-europe.europa.eu/en/etias) states "ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point" and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch; it gives no start date (the earlier "last quarter of 2026" target no longer appears on that page, so no start date should be assumed). Canada's travel advice likewise says ETIAS applications are not yet open. The UK government warns that websites selling ETIAS authorisations now are fraudulent. The separate Entry/Exit System (EES) IS operating: the Commission says it has been fully operational across all Schengen countries since 10 April 2026 (the UK government dates its start to 12 October 2025), so non-EU visitors may be asked for fingerprints and a photo at the border, free of charge, and should allow longer queues. The FCDO says that at Italian border control you may be asked to show accommodation proof, travel insurance, a return or onward ticket and enough money for the stay; this is stated as something you may need to show, not as a fixed rule with a published amount, so whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed. Cash or travellers' cheques worth 10,000 euros or more must be declared on entry or exit (FCDO); Global Affairs Canada says the same for 10,000 euros or more when entering or leaving the EU, and Smartraveller adds that this covers all forms of currency and that no declaration is needed travelling to or from another EU country. Smartraveller (12 Oct 2026) also reports temporary border checks on arrivals from Spain and at the Slovenia land border, so allow extra time. Registration: hotels and other accommodation providers register guests with the police; a visitor arriving from another Schengen country who is not staying somewhere that does so must file a declaration of presence with the local questura within 8 days (FCDO and italia.it). Italian police can stop you for an identity check at any time, so carry photo ID (FCDO). Tourist tax: many major Italian cities charge a small per-night tourist tax that varies by city and hotel star rating and is usually collected by the hotel, often in cash (FCDO). Italy's own foreign ministry pages (esteri.it, viaggiaresicuri.it) and travel-europe.europa.eu could not be read by an automated fetch, so the rules above come from the italia.it tourism portal, the European Commission's home-affairs pages and the UK FCDO as fallbacks.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
Measles (MMR), including an early dose for infants 6-11 months
Mpox (for adults expecting certain activities, per CDC)
Rabies (depending on activities and access to post-exposure care)
Tick-borne encephalitis (for extensive tick exposure in endemic areas)
health.malaria_risk: None listed - the CDC's Italy page lists no malaria risk or prevention guidance.
health.notes: Nothing is checked at the border: the CDC states Italy does not require yellow fever vaccination and does not recommend it for Italy. Other CDC-listed risks are dengue and leishmaniasis (insect and sand-fly bites) and leptospirosis from contaminated water or soil; the UK FCDO adds ticks, West Nile disease and altitude sickness in the Alps and Dolomites. Italy's tourism portal says medical assistance is guaranteed to anyone who goes to a public hospital or similar facility, that foreign nationals temporarily visiting are entitled to basic dental care, and recommends buying travel health insurance before departure. The FCDO notes that UK prescriptions are not accepted, that pharmacies are marked with a green cross, and that a GHIC or EHIC covers medically necessary state healthcare but is not a substitute for travel insurance. Call 118 for an ambulance. No official source reached here stated whether tap water is safe to drink, so this guide does not say.

money.card_acceptance: The Italian tourism portal states that in addition to cash you can pay with the most popular credit cards (Visa, Mastercard/Cirrus/Maestro, American Express, and the domestic Bancomat, Postamat and PagoBancomat systems), and that in larger centres you can pay with your smartphone through dedicated apps. It does not say how universal acceptance is among small businesses.
money.cash_culture: The tourism portal gives no view on how cash-reliant Italy is. One official note on cash: the UK FCDO says hotels often ask for the city tourist tax in cash and advises getting a receipt.
money.tipping: Italy's tourism portal states that tipping is not compulsory and there are no established rules; it says it is customary to leave about 10% of the bill if you were satisfied with the service.
money.atm_notes: The tourism portal says banks with 24/7 ATMs are spread across Italy and that you can exchange currency or withdraw cash at airports, large train stations and banks or exchange agencies. It states no fee or limit information.

power.voltage: 220 V AC as stated by italia.it
power.adapter_note: italia.it says Italian sockets follow standard CEI 23-50 and are symmetrical and non-polarised, so a plug fits either way. It names the C-type socket (2 or 3 round holes) and the L-type socket (larger pins), and says the multistandard socket accepts all types of Italian plugs and the German Schuko plug. Adapters are sold in supermarkets, dedicated shops and most hotels. Check your device's rated input voltage before plugging in; the portal gives 220 V and 50 Hz.

emergency.notes: italia.it states that the single number for emergencies in Italy is 112, free and dialled without a prefix, and lists State Police 113 (accidents, thefts, etc.), fire brigade 115 (fires, weather emergencies) and urgent medical help 118 (also relevant to mountain or cave rescue). Other numbers on the same page: sea rescue 1530, forest ranger 1515, travel information 1518, and Automobile Club d'Italia roadside assistance 803.116. The UK FCDO's Italy page lists the numbers slightly differently (118 ambulance, 115 fire, and 112 for police) and mentions the 112 Where ARE U app, which works only in some parts of Italy; both sources agree 112, 115 and 118, so 112 is the safe first call and the operator routes you. No official source consulted confirmed a dedicated tourist police line, so none is listed here. Smartraveller (opened 2026-10-18) lists 112 for emergency assistance, 113 police, 115 fire and rescue, 118 medical, and Global Affairs Canada gives 112; FCDO lists 112 for police, so 113 (State Police) is kept as the structured police value.

getting_around.summary: Rail is the backbone for visitors. italia.it says Trenitalia and Italo Treno run more than 300 daily connections between the big cities, and that Milan to Rome by high-speed train takes just over three hours; Italo's own site lists Rome-Florence 1h 30min, Milan-Florence 1h 55min, Rome-Naples 1h and Milan-Venice 2h 30min, and says its trains connect 51 major cities via 58 stations. Trenitalia's high-speed brand is Frecciarossa, alongside Frecciargento, Frecciabianca, Intercity and Regionale services. Tickets can be bought on each operator's website, via apps, at travel agencies or at station offices; check on regional tickets whether you must validate them at a station machine before boarding. In cities, italia.it says it is compulsory to buy a bus, tram or metro ticket at an authorised outlet (tobacconists, newsagents, bars) before boarding and validate it once on board; metros exist in Milan, Rome, Naples, Brescia, Turin, Catania and Genoa. No official operator page reached here gave a city transit pass price, so none is listed. Driving: the FCDO says you need a pass to drive into the historic centre of many Italian cities in a private or hire car; the boundaries are usually marked ZTL in black on a yellow background and passing the sign without a pass can lead to a fine. Italy's consulate in Toronto adds that ZTL cameras issue fines that are mailed to the owner's home country and that a rental company can pass on the driver's details. italia.it says ZTL rules vary by city, with signs at each entrance. Transport strikes are often called at short notice (FCDO).

passes.name: Trenitalia Pass
passes.covers: Trenitalia describes it on its English homepage as the offer dedicated to international visitors exploring Italy. The homepage does not state its price, validity or which trains it covers.
passes.worth_it: Not assessed: no price or coverage could be verified from an operator page. Compare against ordinary point-to-point fares on Trenitalia or Italo before buying.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: italia.it says you can use a SIM card from an Italian operator with your chosen amount of data, and recommends buying an Italian SIM for longer stays to keep costs down. It also says hotels, transport providers and many bars, restaurants and attractions offer free Wi-Fi, and that Piazza Wi-Fi Italia is a national free network with an offline hotspot map in the wifi.italia.it app. It advises checking roaming tariffs beforehand and points to europa.eu for roaming cost details. It does not mention eSIM or any ID requirement to buy a SIM.

timezone_note: Japan observes a single time zone nationwide, from Okinawa to Hokkaido, and does not use daylight saving time.
passport_validity_rule: Japan sets no minimum remaining validity beyond the trip itself: the passport only has to stay valid for the length of the stay. UK government entry guidance for Japan states "your passport must be valid for the length of your stay. No additional period of validity is required." JNTO's own visa page says only that all foreign visitors must hold a valid passport. Note that an onward airline or a transit country may still apply its own six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: Nationals of the 74 countries and regions on Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs visa-exemption list (page dated 1 September 2025) may enter for short-term stays without a visa, normally 90 days (15 days for Indonesia and Thailand, 30 for Brunei and Qatar); some listed countries (Brazil, Peru, Serbia, Thailand and others) are exempt only with an ICAO-compliant ePassport, and others need a visa. No pre-travel electronic travel authorisation is in force for Japan today. A scheme called JESTA has been announced but is not operating: Japan's Immigration Services Agency plan says it aims to introduce it in FY2028 (earlier than the original 2030), and no start date, eligible nationalities or fee have been published, so do not pay any site selling a "JESTA" or "Japan ETA". Visit Japan Web registration is not mandatory (JNTO: "Registration is not required, but advance registration makes procedures like tax-free shopping more convenient"), but every arriving passenger must make a customs declaration (Japan Customs: all passengers entering Japan are required to declare their belongings; paper forms are given on the plane or at Customs, and Visit Japan Web is the recommended electronic route). Cash or other means of payment (cheques, travellers cheques, securities) worth more than 1,000,000 yen must be declared to Customs on a separate form. Practical trap: if you plan to use a Japan Rail Pass you need the "Temporary Visitor" stamp or sticker in your passport, and the automated immigration gates do not apply one — use a staffed counter or ask a clerk to stamp it.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccinations (MMR, diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis, polio, chickenpox, influenza, shingles)
Japanese encephalitis (longer stays or extensive rural/outdoor exposure)
Mpox (for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry to Japan — CDC lists yellow fever vaccine as both "not required" and "not recommended" for Japan, and its Japan destination page carries no malaria section and no antimalarial recommendation. Everything in the recommended list above is medical advice only; nothing on it is checked at immigration.

money.card_acceptance: International credit, debit and prepaid cards are generally accepted across the country and increasingly in shops and restaurants, and work for long-distance rail such as the shinkansen and the Narita Express. Short-distance train and subway fares typically cannot be paid by card, and smaller independent businesses may still be yen-only.
money.cash_culture: Japan remains, in JNTO's own words, "still very much a cash culture" — carrying some cash is recommended for the whole trip, and many smaller establishments accept only yen. A prepaid IC card (Suica, Pasmo) covers public transport, convenience stores and a growing number of shops, and is the usual way to avoid carrying coins, though it is not accepted everywhere either.
money.tipping: Not practised and best avoided. JNTO states "In Japan, it's not common to tip for services such as those provided in bars, cafes, restaurants, taxis, and hotels" and that tipping "can cause discomfort and confusion if you do." The one traditional exception is a gratuity called kokorozuke, which is given in an envelope rather than as loose cash; a private guide or interpreter used to overseas practice may also accept a tip.
money.atm_notes: Not every Japanese ATM takes foreign cards. The two networks JNTO names as accepting them are Japan Post Bank ATMs and Seven Bank ATMs in 7-Eleven stores (the latter offer 12-language menus). JNTO also warns that ATMs often charge for withdrawals, that many are not open 24 hours, and that they can occasionally run out of cash — so do not leave a withdrawal to the last minute.

power.frequency: 50Hz (eastern Japan, including Tokyo) / 60Hz (western Japan, including Nagoya, Kyoto and Osaka)
power.adapter_note: JNTO describes Japanese outlets as taking two flat parallel prongs (the Type A pattern) and states "The voltage used throughout Japan is uniformly 100 volts, A.C." Coming from a 230V country you need a plug adapter, and voltage matters more than the plug: dual-voltage devices such as phone and laptop chargers, hair dryers and shavers work nationwide, but any single-voltage 230V appliance needs a step-down transformer. Adapters and transformers are sold in electronics districts such as Tokyo's Akihabara and at major appliance retailers.

emergency.notes: Police 110; fire and ambulance 119 (UK FCDO Getting help page for Japan). The JNTO safety page now names only 110 as the emergency number, so 119 rests on FCDO. No official source consulted lists 112 for Japan, so do not rely on it. For English-language help, the JNTO Japan Visitor Hotline on 050-3816-2787 runs 24 hours a day for emergencies such as illness and disasters, in English, Chinese, Korean and Japanese; the Tokyo Metropolitan Police English helpline is 03-3501-0110, 24 hours, 365 days a year.

getting_around.summary: Almost every visitor moves by rail. The JR network plus the shinkansen links the major cities, city subways and private lines cover everything inside them, and a prepaid IC card (Suica or Pasmo) tapped at the gate is the simplest way to pay for short hops — short-distance rail and subway fares generally will not take a foreign credit card. Buses, ferries, domestic flights and taxis fill the gaps, and a rental car is mainly worth it outside the major cities.

passes.name: Japan Rail Pass
passes.covers: A joint product of the six JR Group companies giving nationwide travel on JR lines, with Ordinary Car and Green Car versions in 7, 14 and 21-day durations. Special conditions apply to the fastest NOZOMI and MIZUHO shinkansen services, which the pass does not simply cover.
passes.worth_it: An Ordinary 7-day pass is 50,000 yen through 30 September 2026 and 53,000 yen from 1 October 2026 (14-day 80,000 rising to 84,000; 21-day 100,000 rising to 105,000). JNTO's own guidance is that the regional passes are better value if you are staying in one area, so the nationwide pass really only pays off on a multi-region, long-distance itinerary.

passes.name: Regional JR passes (JR TOKYO Wide Pass, JR EAST PASS, JR-West, JR-Central, JR Kyushu, Hokkaido, ALL SHIKOKU, Hokuriku Arch)
passes.covers: Each covers one region — for example the JR TOKYO Wide Pass covers greater Tokyo including Mt. Fuji, Nikko and the Izu Peninsula, and the Hokuriku Arch Pass links Tokyo and Osaka via Nagano, Toyama, Ishikawa and Fukui.
passes.worth_it: JNTO states that regional passes offer better value than the nationwide pass when you are exploring a single area.

passes.name: Suica / Pasmo IC card
passes.covers: Prepaid tap-to-pay for public transport nationwide, plus convenience stores and a growing number of shops and restaurants.
passes.worth_it: Not a discount pass but the practical default for city travel and short hops, and the usual alternative to carrying cash. Not accepted absolutely everywhere.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Visitors can buy a prepaid SIM. JNTO's official Mobile Tips site states the handset must be SIM-free (unlocked) and must carry Japan's technical standards conformity certification mark for wireless equipment; nano, micro and standard SIM sizes are sold. JNTO points visitors to major airports, electronics megastores such as Bic Camera and Yodobashi Camera, and travel agencies. JNTO does not state any ID, passport or registration requirement for a prepaid tourist data SIM. Rented pocket Wi-Fi is the common alternative and is available at every major airport or by online reservation for hotel delivery; SoftBank's Free Wi-Fi Passport also gives two weeks of free access to about 400,000 hotspots.
connectivity.typical_cost: No official figure for a ~10GB / 2-week plan could be verified. The only price JNTO publishes is roughly 3,000 yen for a 1GB, 30-day data plan (checked 28 September 2026).

climate.precipitation_note: Tokyo's normal monthly precipitation is 59.7 mm. JMA notes that northwesterly winter winds leave the Pacific side sunny while the Sea of Japan side gets heavy snow.
climate.crowd_note: JNTO names 27 December to 4 January (plus adjacent weekends) as a peak period to avoid; from roughly the second week the month is one of the quietest of the year.

climate.precipitation_note: 56.5 mm — the lowest monthly normal of the year in Tokyo. Heavy snow continues on the Sea of Japan side, and inland Hokkaido regularly falls to around -20C.
climate.crowd_note: Falls outside all three of JNTO's named peak periods; among the least crowded months for visitors.

climate.precipitation_note: 116.0 mm. JMA describes spring as alternating cyclones and anticyclones with large short-term temperature swings.
climate.crowd_note: Demand builds sharply in the second half of the month as cherry blossom season starts: JNTO's 2026 forecast puts first bloom at 19 March in Tokyo, 24 March in Fukuoka and 26 March in Osaka.

climate.precipitation_note: 133.7 mm, with JMA noting increasing sunshine towards late spring.
climate.crowd_note: The busiest blossom weeks in Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka fall in early April, with Tohoku and Hokkaido following from mid-April (Sapporo forecast around 19 April). Golden Week begins 29 April — JNTO names 29 April to 5 May and adjacent weekends as a period to avoid.

climate.precipitation_note: 139.7 mm. JMA notes the rainy season already starts in early May in Okinawa and mid-May in Amami, well before mainland Japan.
climate.crowd_note: Golden Week (29 April to 5 May plus adjacent weekends) is a JNTO-named peak to avoid; after it, mid and late May is one of the best-value stretches of the year. Kushiro's late-blooming cherries are forecast around 5 May.

climate.precipitation_note: 167.8 mm. The Baiu rainy season begins in the Kanto/Koshin region around 7 June on the JMA 1991-2020 average — a cloudy, rainy early-summer period caused by a stationary front.
climate.crowd_note: No JNTO-named peak period; visitor numbers are low, largely because of the rain.

climate.precipitation_note: 156.2 mm. The Kanto Baiu ends around 19 July on average (JMA), after which the North Pacific High brings intense heat — western Japan regularly exceeds 35C.
climate.crowd_note: No JNTO-named peak until mid-August, but heat and humidity make long sightseeing days hard work.

climate.precipitation_note: 154.7 mm. JMA records August as the peak of typhoon formation (5.7 per month on the 1991-2020 average) and the hottest month.
climate.crowd_note: The week centred on 15 August (Obon) is a JNTO-named peak to avoid — domestic travel and transport are heavily booked. Combined with the heat and typhoon risk, this is the hardest month to visit.

climate.precipitation_note: 224.9 mm. JMA notes September brings heavy rain from the autumnal front and from tropical cyclones, with typhoon formation still near its annual peak.
climate.crowd_note: Outside all JNTO-named peak periods. Autumn colour begins in northern Hokkaido and the high mountains from late September.

climate.precipitation_note: 234.8 mm — the highest monthly normal in Tokyo, inflated by late-season tropical cyclones, though JMA describes October itself as generally sunny under frequent anticyclones.
climate.crowd_note: Outside all JNTO-named peak periods; comfortable temperatures and the start of the autumn-colour season working south from Hokkaido.

climate.precipitation_note: 96.3 mm — dry and settled in Tokyo, though JMA notes cold northwesterly flows and rising precipitation on the Sea of Japan side.
climate.crowd_note: JNTO calls November the best month to see autumn colour in most of Japan, so famous temple gardens and mountain areas get busy — but it is not one of JNTO's three named domestic travel peaks.

climate.precipitation_note: 57.9 mm — among the driest months in Tokyo, with heavy snow starting on the Sea of Japan side.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet and clear until about 27 December, when JNTO's New Year peak period (27 December to 4 January) begins and many businesses close.

phrases.local: ありがとうございます

timezone_note: One zone nationwide. Visit Maldives (the national tourism board) states the country is '5 hours ahead of GMT', which agrees with the IANA zone Indian/Maldives at UTC+5 with no daylight saving. Note that many resorts run their own 'island time' one or two hours ahead of Malé time to give guests more daylight; that is a resort convention, not a legal time zone, and flights and ferries run on the national UTC+5 clock.
passport_validity_rule: Maldives Immigration requires a passport or travel document with at least one month's validity, and its tourist-visa page says passengers with extended validity are not allowed to enter. UK FCDO states the same: the expiry date must be at least one month after the date you arrive. Two other governments advise more: Global Affairs Canada says Canadian travellers need a passport valid at least 6 months from the date of entry, and Singapore's MFA says at least 6 months' validity on the expected date of departure from the Maldives. Those are those governments' own advisories; the Maldivian rule is one month, but airlines sometimes apply stricter checks, so a passport with 6+ months left is the safe choice.
entry_requirement_notes: A free 30-day visa on arrival is issued to tourists (30-day figure per UK FCDO; Maldives Immigration's tourist-visa page states a visa on arrival but not the length). Maldives Immigration requires confirmed return journey tickets as part of a complete itinerary, sufficient funds to cover the stay (or an approved sponsorship), and a prepaid confirmed booking at a registered facility; it warns that a complete itinerary does not guarantee entry. MANDATORY ONLINE FORM: every traveller must submit the Traveller Declaration on the IMUGA portal (imuga.immigration.gov.mv) within 96 hours before arrival. It is free of charge (IMUGA: 'completely FREE of charge'), so use only the official portal. A valid yellow fever vaccination certificate is required if arriving from, or recently transiting through, a country with yellow fever transmission risk (children under one year exempt, per Maldives Immigration). Maldives Immigration states that, effective 15 April 2025, entry is not granted on Israeli passports. Green tax: accommodation providers charge a per-person, per-night green tax; the amount depends on the type of accommodation and has changed, and the figures on official pages and in press reports do not agree, so none is stated here. Ask your resort or guesthouse what will be charged and when. Global Affairs Canada also notes a US$50 departure tax, usually included in the airfare.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever - required for travellers aged 9 months and older arriving from, or with an airport transit or layover of more than 12 hours in, a country with risk of yellow fever virus transmission (CDC). Not required for travel direct from a country with no risk.
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines (MMR, polio, tetanus/diphtheria/pertussis, influenza, varicella, shingles)
health.malaria_risk: None
health.notes: Yellow fever is the only vaccination tied to entry, and only on the arriving-from-a-risk-country basis above — everything else on the recommended list is medical advice, not a border check. CDC's Maldives destination page lists no malaria risk and recommends no malaria prophylaxis. CDC does flag dengue and chikungunya as mosquito-borne risks, so bite prevention matters more than pills here. Health care outside Malé is limited, and a resort in an outer atoll can be a long boat or seaplane journey from a hospital; medical evacuation is expensive, which is the practical argument for insurance, though the Maldives does not state an insurance requirement for entry.

money.card_acceptance: Visit Maldives, the national tourism board, states that 'all major credit cards are accepted in the country'. In practice that is strongest at resorts, Malé, and Velana International Airport; small guesthouses, cafes and ferries on inhabited local islands are the places to expect cash.
money.cash_culture: Resorts are effectively USD-denominated: rates, bills and extras are quoted and settled in US dollars, and the Foreign Currency Act 32/2024 (in force 1 January 2025) is built around that reality — it obliges resorts, integrated tourist resorts and resort hotels to exchange USD 500 per tourist per month, or 20% of gross monthly sales, into rufiyaa with a local bank (USD 25 per tourist for lower-tier tourist accommodation). The same Act requires domestic transactions generally to be conducted in Maldivian rufiyaa except where the law provides otherwise, so rufiyaa is what you need for ferries, local-island shops and taxis. Carry some rufiyaa for a local-island or ferry itinerary; a resort-only trip can be done almost entirely on a card in USD.

power.adapter_note: Visit Maldives states the supply is 240 volts. No Maldivian government or tourism-board page found states the plug type(s) or the frequency, so those are left null rather than guessed — check with your resort before you fly.

emergency.notes: Sources differ on the number to dial. The Maldives Police Service website lists 911 as its emergency number, plus the communications-centre lines +960 332 2111 and +960 332 2112, and 1478 as the Tourist Police hotline ('tourist assistance and emergency services'). Global Affairs Canada lists police 119 or +960 332 2111, medical 102, fire 118; Singapore's MFA lists police 119 / 332 2111, fire 118, medical 102; UK FCDO says to dial 102 for an ambulance. The numbers shown are the 119 / 102 / 118 set (each given by at least one foreign government, 102 by three); the Maldivian police site itself only shows 911, so try 911 if 119 does not connect. Other official hotlines previously noted from the police site: Maldives Immigration 1434, Health Protection Agency 1676. On a resort island, call the front desk or duty manager first: they coordinate the seaplane or speedboat evacuation that any real emergency will need.

getting_around.summary: There is no road network between islands and no railway — every journey is a boat or a plane. Visit Maldives describes the pattern: resort transfers are pre-arranged at booking, by speedboat for resorts near Velana International Airport and by seaplane or domestic flight for those further out, with several daily flights linking the country's domestic and international airports. Independent travel between inhabited local islands runs on the scheduled public ferry network from Malé to most of the atolls, which is cheap and slow and runs on a fixed weekly timetable rather than daily. In Malé itself, taxis serve the airport. Seaplanes fly in daylight only, so a late international arrival can mean an overnight in Malé or Hulhumalé before the onward transfer.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Visit Maldives states that prepaid SIM cards are available from two mobile service providers at the airport, usable for local and international calls and for data. No official source found states what identity document is required to register one.

climate.precipitation_note: About 114 mm. Northeast (iruvai) monsoon, the dry season, which the Maldives Meteorological Service puts at January to March.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season. Very busy and most expensive in the first ten days as the New Year period runs out, easing afterwards.

climate.precipitation_note: About 38 mm — by a wide margin the driest month of the year in Malé.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season, and the most reliable weather of the year. Book well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: About 74 mm. Still dry-season conditions, with the sea usually calm and visibility good.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season. Prices start to soften late in the month.

climate.precipitation_note: About 123 mm. Transitional month; the hottest of the year and rainfall climbing towards the wet season.
climate.crowd_note: Shoulder. Still reliably sunny early in the month, with rates dropping as the month goes on.

climate.precipitation_note: About 219 mm. The southwest (hulhangu) monsoon, the wet season, normally begins in mid-May per the Maldives Meteorological Service — squally wind and short heavy downpours rather than all-day rain.
climate.crowd_note: Low season, with the year's sharpest fall in rates.

climate.precipitation_note: About 167 mm. Wet season, with the strongest winds of the year and choppier crossings.
climate.crowd_note: Low season. Quiet resorts and low prices; expect some lost afternoons to rain.

climate.precipitation_note: About 150 mm. Wet season, but a relative dip in rainfall between the May and August peaks.
climate.crowd_note: Shoulder. European summer holidays fill some resorts despite the season, so rates are not at their lowest.

climate.precipitation_note: About 176 mm. Wet season, plankton-rich water — the strongest months for manta ray and whale shark sightings in the western atolls.
climate.crowd_note: Shoulder. Northern-hemisphere holiday demand keeps prices up mid-month.

climate.precipitation_note: About 199 mm. One of the wettest stretches of the year.
climate.crowd_note: Low season and genuinely quiet, which is the trade-off for the rain.

climate.precipitation_note: About 194 mm. Still wet-season conditions; winds easing compared with mid-monsoon.
climate.crowd_note: Low season. Good value, with weather improving late in the month.

climate.precipitation_note: About 231 mm — the wettest month in Malé on the 1981-2000 normals.
climate.crowd_note: Low season until the very end of the month, when rates begin climbing towards Christmas.

climate.precipitation_note: About 217 mm, but falling fast through the month as the northeast monsoon sets in; the second half is usually much drier than the first.
climate.crowd_note: Peak from roughly 20 December. Christmas and New Year are the most expensive nights of the year and sell out months ahead.

timezone_note: The Ley de los Husos Horarios (in force 30 October 2022) sets four standard zones: Zona Centro (90 deg W, UTC-6) covering most of the country including Mexico City, Guadalajara, Oaxaca and Merida; Zona Pacifico (105 deg W, UTC-7) for Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, Sonora and Nayarit except Bahia de Banderas; Zona Noroeste (120 deg W, UTC-8) for Baja California; and Zona Sureste (75 deg W, UTC-5) for Quintana Roo, which is where Cancun, Playa del Carmen, Tulum and Cozumel sit. Daylight saving was abolished nationwide by that law; the only exception is a seasonal time in listed northern-border municipalities of Coahuila, Nuevo Leon, Tamaulipas, Chihuahua and the whole of Baja California, running from 02:00 on the second Sunday in March to 02:00 on the first Sunday in November.
passport_validity_rule: Mexico requires a passport or travel document that is valid for the whole period of your stay, with pages free for entry and exit stamps. No Mexican authority states a minimum validity beyond the stay - there is no six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: The paper FMM tourist card is gone for air arrivals. INM no longer issues a physical migration form to anyone entering Mexico by air: the Federal Migration Agent at the filter stamps the passport and records the estimated departure date, and the traveller can download the Forma Migratoria Multiple Digital (FMMd) once, within the days granted, by scanning the QR code at the checkpoint or via the INM services portal (inm.gob.mx/spublic/portal/inmex.html). At land border crossings the form still exists as the FMM Electronica: you complete it on the INM website, print it, and hand it over at the crossing point for the stamp. The stay is up to 180 days, but the exact number of days is at the immigration officer's discretion at the moment of entry - it is not automatically 180, and the number is what the officer records against the stamp. Mexican consulates state that officers may additionally ask a tourist for a hotel reservation and a return ticket, and the visitor condition requires economic solvency; these are discretionary checks rather than a blanket published requirement, so carry proof of onward travel and accommodation even though no rule mandates it. A visa is not needed for stays up to 180 days for nationals of the listed visa-exempt countries; separately, holders of a valid visa or permanent residence in the USA, Canada, Japan, the UK or any Schengen country may enter without a Mexican visa regardless of nationality (the tourism ministry's page says the same for permanent residents of Chile, Colombia and Peru). Brazilian passport holders are not visa-exempt: since 5 February 2026 they can obtain an electronic visa online (visaelectronica.sre.gob.mx) for a single entry by air only, as a visitor without permission for paid work; entry by land or sea still needs a consular visa (SRE press release 021/2026). Cash and monetary instruments worth more than USD 10,000 (or the equivalent) must be declared to customs on entering or leaving Mexico; carrying the money is not an offence, failing to declare it is, with a fine of 20% to 40% of the excess and possible prison above USD 30,000 (ANAM).

recommended_vaccinations: Rabies (only for travellers with likely animal exposure)
Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTP, polio, varicella, influenza, COVID-19)
health.malaria_risk: Limited and localised - CDC reports transmission only in Campeche, Chiapas and southern Chihuahua, all P. vivax. No malaria along the US-Mexico border and none in the main resort and city destinations.
health.notes: Nothing is checked at the border: CDC lists no yellow fever entry requirement for Mexico, and Mexico's tourism ministry states no vaccinations are compulsory for most visitors, only that routine immunisations should be up to date. Chemoprophylaxis is advised by CDC only for the three malaria areas; elsewhere insect-bite precautions are enough. CDC also flags dengue, Zika, chikungunya and Chagas as insect-borne risks, a cyclosporiasis increase in travellers returning from Cancun and the Riviera Maya, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever in northern border states. Mexico City sits at about 2,300 m, so allow for altitude. Public and private hospitals are obliged to treat visitors regardless of nationality, and the tourism ministry recommends international travel insurance.

money.card_acceptance: No Mexican authority publishes a card-acceptance map, so treat card coverage as unverified outside established businesses and plan to carry pesos. What is official: Profeco requires businesses to state clearly which payment methods they accept and to take banknotes of any denomination, and it bans minimum-consumption conditions in restaurants and bars.
money.cash_culture: Mexico's tourism ministry says most visitors find it cheapest and most convenient simply to withdraw pesos from an ATM with an international card, with banks and casas de cambio in airports, cities and resort areas as the alternative. Paying in US dollars is explicitly discouraged - some tourist-area businesses take it, but at poor rates. The ministry also advises visitors not to carry large amounts of cash.
money.tipping: Expected, and by custom 10-15% of the bill in restaurants, bars and food stalls, plus loose change for porters, taxi drivers and cleaning staff. Legally it is always voluntary: Profeco states a tip is a voluntary gratuity that cannot be added to the bill without the customer's consent, no business may demand it or set the amount, and consumers can complain if they are made to pay one. Bargaining is normal in markets and on large purchases but not in fixed-price shops.
money.atm_notes: Using another bank's ATM carries a Mexican-side fee on top of anything your home bank charges. CONDUSEF's published range for a cash withdrawal at an ATM other than your card's issuer runs from about 8.62 pesos plus VAT at the cheapest bank to 40 pesos plus VAT at the most expensive, and fees are generally higher at machines in supermarkets, shopping centres, airports, bus terminals, convenience stores, pharmacies and petrol stations than at bank branches. By rule the commission must be shown on screen before you confirm, so read that screen and cancel if it is not worth it. CONDUSEF also advises checking the card reader for tampering, shielding the keypad, avoiding machines in poorly-chosen locations and keeping receipts.

power.adapter_note: Mexican official standards specify a 127 V single-phase supply at 60 Hz. Profeco's quality study of Mexican sockets and plugs shows the domestic socket as the North American duplex type - two flat parallel slots plus a round earth hole - and defines a clavija as an insulating body with two flat metal blades, with three-pin earthed plugs also sold. A traveller from a 230 V country needs both a physical adapter and a device that accepts 100-240 V; anything single-voltage 230 V will need a transformer, not just an adapter. Travellers from the USA and Canada need no adapter at all.

emergency.notes: 911 is the single national emergency number, dialable free from any landline or mobile anywhere in Mexico, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year; the call is routed by the Emergency Call Attention Centres to police, ambulance, fire or civil protection as needed. Whether the legacy 066 number or the European 112 still connect could not be verified from an official source, so dial 911. Separately, 078 is the national tourist assistance line run by the Secretaria de Turismo: its operators speak several languages and it handles tourist information, safety advice, contact with embassies and consulates, transport and accommodation questions, and can refer you to official bodies. It is an assistance line, not a police force. Major destinations also have visitor assistance units and Centro de Asistencia y Proteccion al Turista (CAPTA) offices.

getting_around.summary: Mexico is large and most long hops are done by plane or by long-distance coach - the tourism ministry rates the intercity bus network as one of the most extensive in Latin America and notes that the service level surprises many first-time visitors. Rail is limited but growing: the government-run Tren Maya links 34 stations across Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatan and Quintana Roo, including Palenque, Campeche, Merida, Izamal, Chichen Itza, Cancun, Playa del Carmen, Tulum and Chetumal, with tickets sold through its own reservation site. Within cities, Mexico City and Monterrey have metros, several cities have BRT corridors (Metrobus, Macrobus, Mexibus), and ride-hailing apps operate in most major cities and resorts; the ministry advises using authorised taxi desks inside airports rather than hailing on the street. Foreign driving licences are valid for car hire, federal motorways are tolled, and 'Hoy No Circula' plate-based driving restrictions apply in Mexico City, Puebla and Toluca.

passes.name: Tarjeta de Movilidad Integrada (Mexico City)
passes.covers: Mexico City's rechargeable transport smart card; the tourism ministry lists these city cards as accepted on the metro, city buses, Metrobus and other local transport services.
passes.worth_it: Get one on arrival if you plan to use city transport at all - it is the cashless way to pay across the network rather than a discount product. It is a city card only, with no value outside Mexico City.

passes.name: Mi Movilidad (Guadalajara)
passes.covers: Guadalajara's equivalent rechargeable transport card, accepted across local metro, bus and BRT services.
passes.worth_it: Only worth it if you are spending time in Guadalajara; each metropolitan area runs its own card and they are not interchangeable.

passes.name: Feria (Monterrey)
passes.covers: Monterrey's rechargeable transport card for the metro and local bus network.
passes.worth_it: Same logic as the other city cards - a local convenience, not a national pass.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: A prepaid Mexican SIM is cheap and easy to buy, and the tourism ministry recommends it over international roaming; your handset must be unlocked. Telcel, AT&T and Movistar all have national coverage, strong in cities and resort areas and patchy in remote rural areas. Free Wi-Fi is widely available in hotels, cafes, restaurants, airports, shopping centres and some public squares. Important recent change: guidelines published in the Diario Oficial on 9 December 2025 require every mobile line to be linked to an identified user before it works normally, and unlinked lines are disabled except for emergency calls once the transition deadline passes. Foreign nationals register with a passport (or a temporary CURP for foreigners), and providers record name, country of origin and passport number; biometrics, photographs and copies of ID are explicitly not stored. Expect to show your passport when buying or activating a SIM.

climate.precipitation_note: Deep in the dry season - about 12 mm over roughly 3 rainy days in Mexico City. Clear skies, cold mornings at altitude.
climate.crowd_note: Busy through Dia de Reyes on 6 January, then noticeably quieter. Pacific and Caribbean beach resorts are in their high season.

climate.precipitation_note: The driest month of the year in Mexico City - about 6 mm across 2 rainy days.
climate.crowd_note: Reliable weather and no major national holidays; among the easiest months to travel.

climate.precipitation_note: Still dry, about 12 mm. Warming fast, and haze can build over the central highlands late in the dry season.
climate.crowd_note: Spring equinox draws large crowds to archaeological sites such as Chichen Itza and Teotihuacan. Semana Santa can fall in late March, which fills domestic destinations.

climate.precipitation_note: The hottest month in Mexico City by average maximum, and still largely dry at about 24 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Semana Santa is the biggest domestic travel week of the year - beaches, colonial towns and coach routes all fill and prices rise.

climate.precipitation_note: The tourism ministry calls May the hottest month nationally, especially inland and in the north. Rain begins to return - about 59 mm over 11 rainy days in Mexico City. Eastern Pacific hurricane season opens 15 May.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet between Semana Santa and the summer holidays, but hot.

climate.precipitation_note: The wet season arrives properly: about 133 mm over 16 rainy days in Mexico City, typically as afternoon storms rather than all-day rain. Atlantic hurricane season opens 1 June.
climate.crowd_note: Low season inland; rain rarely stops sightseeing but afternoons need planning around.

climate.precipitation_note: About 174 mm over 22 rainy days in Mexico City - rain on most days, again mostly late in the afternoon.
climate.crowd_note: Mexican and North American school holidays fill beaches. Oaxaca's Guelaguetza, one of the country's great indigenous festivals, is in July and books out the city.

climate.precipitation_note: The wettest month in Mexico City at about 176 mm. Atlantic hurricane activity picks up sharply from mid-August on the Gulf and Caribbean coasts.
climate.crowd_note: Peak summer holidays continue. Guadalajara's international mariachi festival runs in August.

climate.precipitation_note: Still very wet at about 158 mm, and this is the statistical peak of the Atlantic hurricane season (10 September) - the highest-risk month for the Caribbean and Gulf coasts.
climate.crowd_note: Independence celebrations on 15-16 September are a nationwide highlight but also the busiest domestic weekend of the autumn.

climate.precipitation_note: Rain tapers off to about 71 mm over 10 days. Hurricane risk persists on both coasts until 30 November but eases through the month.
climate.crowd_note: Guanajuato's Festival Internacional Cervantino runs in October, and Day of the Dead celebrations begin around 28 October - book Oaxaca, Mexico City and Patzcuaro well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry again at about 17 mm over 4 days, with clear, mild days and cool nights on the highlands. Arguably the best all-round month.
climate.crowd_note: Day of the Dead on 1-2 November is the single most oversubscribed few days of the Mexican calendar; after the first week the country empties out and the weather stays excellent.

climate.precipitation_note: The driest stretch of the year - about 5 mm. Cold mornings in Mexico City and the central highlands.
climate.crowd_note: Pilgrimages to the Basilica de Guadalupe on 12 December, then posadas and Christmas holidays from mid-month; beach resorts and flights are at their most expensive.

timezone_note: A change is in the air here and the official position is unsettled, so treat this as the one detail to confirm on arrival. From October 2018 Morocco ran on GMT+1 all year under decree 2.18.855, dropping back to GMT for the whole of Ramadan each year — most recently from 03:00 on 15 February 2026 to 02:00 on 22 March 2026, announced by the Ministry of Digital Transition and Administrative Reform. On 25 June 2026 the Head of Government announced a decision to abandon GMT+1 and return to GMT 'starting the end of this summer' (official portal maroc.ma), and Moroccan press reports the switch took effect on 20 September 2026 — but no government page confirms that date, and the IANA time zone database, which is what actually sets the clock on your phone and on this page, still places Morocco at UTC+1. We show UTC+1 for that reason rather than following the press reports. The live clock above is computed from the IANA database, so it will follow the real change automatically once it is recorded there.
passport_validity_rule: Official sources disagree, and NextStamp does not pick one silently. The value it checks against is six months from the date of arrival, because three governments state a six-month rule: Germany's Auswärtiges Amt (travel documents must be valid at least six months at entry), Brazil's embassy in Rabat (at least six months from the date of arrival) and Global Affairs Canada (at least six months beyond the date you expect to leave Morocco, the strictest wording, counted from departure, so a long stay needs more). The UK FCDO instead says the passport must expire at least three months after arrival, and the Moroccan National Tourist Office (visitmorocco.com) says only that a passport must cover the duration of the stay for organised trips. Morocco's consular site (consulat.ma) blocks automated requests and no first-hand Moroccan page gave a month count. Many airlines also apply a six-month rule at check-in. Safest plan: a passport valid six months past arrival, and six months past departure if you travel on a Canadian passport or stay long.
entry_requirement_notes: Tourist stays of up to 90 days are visa-free for exempt nationalities (the UK FCDO, Germany's Auswärtiges Amt, Global Affairs Canada and Brazil's embassy in Rabat each say so for their own citizens). The Moroccan National Tourist Office says the maximum tourist stay is 90 days for all nationalities and that an extension of a further 90 days can be requested at the nearest police station; Global Affairs Canada says to contact the foreigners' section of the local police station at least 15 days before the 90 days end, and that overstaying can mean being held until seen by a prosecutor and fined. Nationalities that are not exempt apply for an e-Visa or AEVM electronic travel authorisation through Morocco's official portal acces-maroc.ma (its 'Do I need a visa' checker on the home page asks nationality, residence, passport type and any other valid visa), or at a Moroccan embassy or consulate. Currency: Moroccan customs (douane.gov.ma) requires a declaration at the entry customs office when the foreign currency or payment instruments you bring in equal or exceed 100,000 dirham; keep the stamped copy, which is what justifies the funds when you leave and is valid for a single stay of up to six months for non-residents. The UK FCDO and Germany's Auswärtiges Amt give the same 100,000 dirham threshold. The dirham is a closed currency: Global Affairs Canada and Brazil's embassy say it is illegal to take dirhams out of Morocco and unused dirhams can be converted at the airport on departure with proof of the original purchase, while Germany's Auswärtiges Amt says cash dirham in or out is capped at 2,000. Passports: a damaged passport can be refused (FCDO, Germany), border officials should stamp it on entry and travellers have had trouble leaving without a stamp (FCDO), and a polio vaccination certificate can be required if arriving from a polio-affected country. Private boats must arrive at a recognised port of entry, and a vehicle brought in must leave with you (Global Affairs Canada). Global Affairs Canada (updated 26 May 2026) adds that some countries have imposed Ebola-related entry restrictions and health screening on people who recently visited an affected country; NextStamp did not find a Moroccan measure of this kind, so check with your airline before departure. NextStamp found no first-hand statement on an onward-ticket requirement or on blank passport pages, so those are left unconfirmed.

required_vaccinations: Polio — certificate required only if arriving from a polio-affected country (UK FCDO)
health.notes: CDC lists no vaccinations as required for entry to Morocco and says yellow fever vaccine is neither recommended nor required. The only certificate found is the conditional polio one: the UK FCDO and Germany's Auswärtiges Amt say proof of polio vaccination can be required of people arriving from a polio-affected country, and Brazil's embassy in Rabat says no vaccination certificate of any kind is needed from its citizens. Everything in the recommended list is advice, not a border check. CDC notes that rabid dogs are commonly found in Morocco, and the UK FCDO adds that stray dogs can be aggressive and that altitude sickness is a risk in parts of the country. CDC's Morocco destination page has no malaria prevention section, and NextStamp could not open the malaria tab of the UK's TravelHealthPro Morocco page, so no malaria risk level is stated rather than guessing one. For an ambulance the UK FCDO says dial 150, while Morocco's Ministry of Health lists 15 for SAMU (see emergency notes).

money.card_acceptance: The Moroccan National Tourist Office states that Visa and Mastercard are accepted by most hotels and by some restaurants, shops and petrol stations — i.e. cards work in the formal tourist economy but not everywhere.
money.atm_notes: The Moroccan National Tourist Office says ATMs are widespread throughout Morocco, and that bureaux de change operate at airports, in hotels, in banks and in cities, with a passport required for exchange transactions. No official source was found for card fees or dynamic-currency-conversion practice, so none is stated.

emergency.notes: Morocco's Ministry of Health lists 19 for police and 15 for SAMU (ambulance) and the fire service, plus 022 25 25 25 for SAMU Maroc nationally. Brazil's embassy in Rabat gives the same police and fire numbers (19 for police in large cities, 15 for fire) and adds 177 for police in rural areas. The UK FCDO's Getting help page lists a different set: ambulance 150, fire 150, police 190 and Gendarmerie (military police) 177. If one number does not connect, try the other. NextStamp found no official Moroccan confirmation that 112 reaches emergency services, and no official listing for a tourist police line, so neither is stated here.

getting_around.summary: ONCF, the national rail operator, runs what the tourist office calls Africa's second-largest rail network, linking Marrakech to Oujda and most major cities — though not Agadir, Nador or many smaller towns. The Al Boraq high-speed service currently serves four stations: Tangier, Kenitra, Rabat and Casablanca; tickets are sold at stations, on oncf.ma and through the ONCF Voyages app. Supratours coaches pick up where the railway stops. Within cities, petits taxis are colour-coded by city — red in Casablanca and Agadir, blue in Rabat, Tangier and Asilah, orange in Marrakech.
