phrases_language: French (Morocco's de facto language of business, tourism, signage and menus alongside Arabic and Amazigh; a visitor gets further with French than with any other non-Arabic language, and it needs no romanization. Moroccan Arabic — Darija — is what people speak among themselves.)

timezone_note: Peru uses a single time zone nationwide and does not observe daylight saving time, so the offset is UTC-5 year round (IANA zone America/Lima).
passport_validity_rule: PROMPERU (the official tourism board) states that entry requires a legitimately issued passport with a minimum validity of six months from the date of entry into the country. The UK FCDO states the same rule for British nationals: the passport expiry date must be at least 6 months after the date of arrival.
entry_requirement_notes: Official sources state the permitted stay differently and none could be reconciled today. PROMPERU (peru.travel) says the maximum stay granted is 90 days and cannot be extended; Global Affairs Canada says no tourist visa is needed for a stay of less than 90 days per 365-day period; the UK FCDO says visitors normally get up to 90 days in any 180-day period, with officials able to grant a maximum of 183 days in 365 as a visitor. Peru's Foreign Ministry visa table and Migraciones (migraciones.gob.pe, gob.pe) could not be opened today (the government portal blocks automated browsers), so whether a 90-day stay can be extended once was not confirmed. Plan around 90 days and check the permitted stay recorded on your own entry record on the Migraciones website. Arrivals at international airports are registered digitally through the Tarjeta Andina de Migracion (TAM) and passports are not stamped (FCDO, Global Affairs Canada); if you enter overland you must get an entry stamp yourself, and an overstay is a penalty payable on exit. Declare anything dutiable or prohibited; Global Affairs Canada states that carrying more than US$10,000 (or equivalent) must be declared on arrival and departure. Stays for business, study or work require the relevant visa from a Peruvian consulate before travel. Peru's Ministry of Health (DGE) also asks travellers returning from Ebola (Bundibugyo virus) outbreak zones to notify CDC Peru in advance and self-monitor for 21 days. Whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed: no Peruvian authority page that could be opened states it either way, and Global Affairs Canada says only that customs officials may ask to see a return or onward ticket, proof of accommodation and sufficient funds, which is a possibility, not a stated requirement. Carry an onward ticket anyway; airlines also apply this check at departure.

recommended_vaccinations: Typhoid (if visiting areas with poor sanitation or staying over a month)
Yellow fever (for travel below 2,300 m in the listed eastern jungle regions, including parts of Cusco and Puno; not recommended for Lima, Cusco city, the Inca Trail or Machu Picchu)
Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap, varicella, polio, influenza, COVID-19)
health.malaria_risk: No transmission in Lima Province, Cusco city, Machu Picchu, the Sacred Valley, Lake Titicaca or anywhere above 2,500 m. Transmission occurs below 2,500 m east of the Andes (including Iquitos and Puerto Maldonado), where chemoprophylaxis is recommended; rare cases occur in Tumbes and Piura.
health.notes: No yellow fever vaccination is required for entry: the US CDC states Peru does not require proof of yellow fever vaccination for entry, and Global Affairs Canada says the same. Peru's own Ministry of Health (DGE) says authorities recommend prior vaccination and that a vaccination certificate may be requested at some forest-area entry points considered endemic; no official page found limits a requirement to travellers arriving from risk countries, so that wording is not asserted. If you are going to the Amazon, carry a certificate to be safe. The real health risk for a typical Peru itinerary is altitude, not disease. The CDC Yellow Book records Cusco city at 3,339 m (about 11,000 ft) and Lake Titicaca at 3,812 m (about 12,500 ft), and states that travellers going above 2,500 m (8,200 ft) are at risk of altitude illness - acute mountain sickness, high-altitude pulmonary edema and high-altitude cerebral edema. It specifically flags the Lima-to-Cusco flight, which gains roughly 3,350 m in about an hour, as an ascent rate that raises the risk, and notes that acute mountain sickness affects close to half of travellers during their first 48 hours in Cusco, though it is usually mild. CDC guidance is gradual ascent and, for travellers at risk, acetazolamide prophylaxis prescribed in advance - so this is a conversation to have with a doctor before booking, not after landing. Practical consequence for planning: do not schedule the Inca Trail or a high pass in the first day or two after flying into Cusco.

emergency.notes: Police 105, fire 116 and SAMU ambulance 106 are the numbers published by the Presidencia del Consejo de Ministros on the Peruvian state platform (gob.pe/547-telefonos-de-emergencia, read earlier and not reopenable today); the same page lists highway police 110 and Defensa Civil 115. Global Affairs Canada (travel.gc.ca/destinations/peru, updated 15 October 2026) agrees on police 105 and fire 116, but lists 116 for medical assistance as well and gives a tourist police WhatsApp line, +51 980 122 335, which is the tourist-police number shown (it is a WhatsApp number, not a voice short code). Where the two disagree on the ambulance, the state platform's 106 is kept; if 106 does not connect, try 105 or 116. SAMU on 106 is listed for Lima and a named set of regions (Amazonas, Ancash, Ayacucho, Huancavelica, Huanuco, Junin, La Libertad, Loreto, Madre de Dios, Piura, Lima Region, Tacna, Tumbes, Ucayali, Lambayeque and Pasco); Cusco is not on that list, so in Cusco or Puno expect to reach an ambulance through the police on 105 or directly through a clinic. No single general emergency number is published, so none is shown; whether 911 or 112 connects is not confirmed by any official source found.

getting_around.summary: Distances are long and the Andes make roads slow, so most visitors fly between Lima, Cusco and Arequipa and then travel by road or rail locally; the Lima-Cusco hop is the one most itineraries are built around, and it is also the altitude jump that needs a rest day at the other end. In Cusco and the Sacred Valley, movement is by road (colectivo, bus or hired transport) plus the rail line to Aguas Calientes/Machupicchu Pueblo, which is the only way in other than walking. The part of a Peru trip that genuinely cannot be improvised is Machu Picchu itself: entry is capacity-capped by ministerial resolution, tickets are sold only by the state, and the popular dates go early.

passes.name: Llaqta de Machupicchu entry ticket (boleto de ingreso)
passes.covers: Timed entry to the Machu Picchu citadel on a specific date and circuit. Sold exclusively by Peru's Ministry of Culture through tuboleto.cultura.pe - the ministry's 2026 capacity resolution states sales are only through that portal, so any other seller is a reseller.
passes.worth_it: Not optional - you cannot enter without one. Entry is capped by ministerial resolution at 5,600 visitors per day on the specific high-season dates listed in the resolution and 4,500 per day for the rest of the year. The Ministry of Culture opened the whole 2026 season for advance reservation on 17 November 2025 (Machu Picchu reservations from midday), moving the opening forward from December to November specifically to avoid saturation on the busiest dates - so the realistic advice is to book as soon as the following year's window opens, and certainly several months out for June-August, rather than weeks out. Reserve on the portal and then pay on the same platform within the published payment schedule or the reservation lapses.

passes.name: Red de Caminos Inka permit (Inca Trail)
passes.covers: Trekking permit for the Inca Trail network into Machu Picchu, sold through the same official platform, tuboleto.cultura.pe, and only through a licensed operator.
passes.worth_it: Permit numbers are limited and the whole year opens for reservation on one day - for 2026 that was 17 November 2025, with Inca Trail reservations opening at 08:00, four hours before the Machu Picchu citadel tickets. Treat the trail as something you book the moment the window opens, up to roughly a year ahead, not something you add to a trip that is already dated. Hard constraint to plan around: the Ministry of Culture closes the entire Inca Trail network for the whole of February every year for maintenance and conservation, reopening 1 March, so a February trip cannot include it. Closures for heavy rain outside February have also happened.

climate.precipitation_note: Wettest month of the year in Cusco, 145 mm. Afternoon downpours are the norm and trail and road conditions suffer.
climate.crowd_note: Low season apart from a short New Year bump; the citadel is at its 4,500-a-day cap rather than 5,600.

climate.precipitation_note: Still deep in the wet season, 134 mm, with the heaviest sustained rain of the year around Cusco.
climate.crowd_note: Quietest month, but the entire Inca Trail network is closed 1-28 February for maintenance, so a trek-based itinerary is impossible.

climate.precipitation_note: Rain easing but still substantial at 107 mm; the landscape is at its greenest.
climate.crowd_note: Inca Trail reopens 1 March and is far less contested than mid-year.

climate.precipitation_note: Sharp drop to 43 mm as the wet season ends; clear spells return.
climate.crowd_note: Green scenery with dry-season skies arriving and far fewer people than June-August - arguably the best value month.

climate.precipitation_note: Effectively dry at 9 mm. Nights are getting cold at altitude.
climate.crowd_note: Dry-season conditions before the July-August crush.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest stretch of the year, under 2 mm, with warm days and near-freezing nights in Cusco.
climate.crowd_note: High season. Inti Raymi on 24 June fills Cusco; permits and hotels for that week go furthest ahead of anything else.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry, 4 mm, with the coldest nights of the year at altitude.
climate.crowd_note: Busiest month alongside August; expect the 5,600-a-day high-season cap and sold-out dates.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry at 9 mm; windy and dusty in the highlands.
climate.crowd_note: Peak of the peak. Book entry and permits many months ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: First light rains return, 22 mm, with mostly settled weather.
climate.crowd_note: Crowds thin noticeably after the northern-hemisphere holidays while conditions stay good.

climate.precipitation_note: Warmest days of the year in Cusco with rain building to 39 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Comfortable shoulder month; afternoon showers become likely.

climate.precipitation_note: Wet season arriving in earnest, 72 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet, and the month the following year's Machu Picchu and Inca Trail reservations open.

climate.precipitation_note: Back into heavy rain at 123 mm.
climate.crowd_note: Wet, but Christmas and New Year bring a short local and holiday-travel surge.

timezone_note: A single time zone applies to the whole country, including Palawan and Mindanao, and there is no daylight saving time.
passport_validity_rule: The Philippine government's official e-visa portal states that visa-free temporary visitors' passports must be "valid for at least six (6) months beyond the applicant's date of departure" from the Philippines. The UK FCDO's Philippines page words it as an expiry date at least 6 months after the date you arrive. The stricter of the two readings, six months beyond your planned departure date, is the one recorded here.
entry_requirement_notes: Four things beyond the passport rule. (1) Onward travel: visa-free visitors "must also possess return tickets to their country of origin or outward-bound tickets to their next country of destination", per the official e-visa portal; the UK FCDO's Philippines page says most visitors are expected to have proof of return or onward travel and that officials and airlines may ask to see it. (2) eTravel: registration at etravel.gov.ph is required for all arriving foreign and Filipino passengers and you show the QR code to the airline before boarding. It is free and, per the official eTravel FAQ, may be done within 72 hours (3 days) before arrival; the UK FCDO says the same ("within the 72 hours before your arrival"). A green QR code goes straight to immigration, a red one means a Bureau of Quarantine check first. Diplomats, foreign dignitaries and their delegations, 9(e) visa holders and diplomatic/official/service passport holders are exempt. A Bureau of Immigration advisory page on mandatory eTravel registration is published only as an image that could not be read, so no earlier-than-72-hours rule is recorded. (3) Visitors must have no derogatory record with the Bureau of Immigration. (4) Cash: per the UK FCDO, you cannot take in more than 50,000 Philippine pesos, and foreign currency over US$10,000 must be declared. Stay lengths, per the official e-visa portal: most visa-free nationals get an initial 30 days; Brazil and Israel get 59 days; Hong Kong SAR passport holders get 14 days. Indian passport holders: since 8 June 2025, 14 days (non-extendible, non-convertible, tourism and business) with a confirmed hotel booking and proof of financial capacity; Indians holding a valid American, Japanese, Australian, Canadian, Schengen, Singapore or United Kingdom visa get 30 days for tourism on a valid passport plus a return or onward ticket. Older Philippine consulate pages still describe a 14-day (extendible to 21) rule for Indians holding such visas; the e-visa portal is the more current source and is followed here, so check your own nationality on the e-visa policy page. Apart from the Indian 14-day route above, no proof-of-funds or mandatory travel-insurance requirement was found on any official Philippine source. The Philippine Embassy in Tokyo's visa-free page could not be opened (blocked to automated access), so its wording was not checked directly.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever (only if arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from a non-risk country)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP, polio, varicella, influenza)
Japanese encephalitis (stays of a month or more, or extended rural/outdoor exposure)
Rabies (for travellers with likely animal contact)
health.malaria_risk: Present in the province of Palawan and the Mindanao island group. Metro Manila and other urban centres are malaria-free. CDC advises prescription antimalarials for travel to risk areas.
health.notes: Only the yellow fever certificate is an entry condition, and only for arrivals from a yellow-fever risk country (CDC: required from age 9 months, including layovers over 12 hours in such countries; not required for direct travel from the US). The UK FCDO adds that proof of polio vaccination may be needed if arriving from certain countries with a transmission risk. Everything else on the recommended list is advisory and is not checked at the border. Dengue is a year-round mosquito-borne risk and the UK FCDO notes heightened dengue risk during the June-to-October rainy season, so insect-bite avoidance matters more than any vaccine for a typical short visit.

emergency.notes: 911 is the Philippines' national emergency hotline, covering police, fire and medical response. The UK FCDO's Philippines health advice tells travellers to "Call 911 and ask for an ambulance". The Department of the Interior and Local Government has been consolidating more than thirty separate local emergency numbers into this single nationwide 911 line. The Philippines' own emergency-hotline pages (e911.gov.ph, gov.ph/the-government/hotlines, officialgazette.gov.ph/emergency-hotlines) all return HTTP 403 to automated fetches, so the number here is cited to the UK FCDO's page about the Philippines rather than to a first-hand Philippine source. Whether 112 also connects, and whether English is reliably answered outside Metro Manila, could not be verified from an official source.

climate.precipitation_note: Deep in the dry season: 19mm normal for Manila. PAGASA classes December to February as the cool dry season, and January as the coolest month nationally (mean 25.5C).
climate.crowd_note: Busiest stretch of the year for foreign visitors; book Palawan and Boracay well ahead. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Driest month in Manila's normals at 7.9mm. Still within PAGASA's cool dry season.
climate.crowd_note: Reliable weather and high demand; prices stay at dry-season levels. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 11.1mm in Manila. PAGASA's hot dry season runs March to May, so heat starts building.
climate.crowd_note: Good sea conditions with the heat still manageable. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Manila's hottest average high (33.5C in the normals) with only 21.4mm of rain.
climate.crowd_note: Holy Week is the busiest domestic travel week of the year; beaches and inter-island ferries fill up. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Rainfall jumps to 165.2mm as the dry season ends. PAGASA records May as the warmest month nationally (mean 28.3C).
climate.crowd_note: Hot and increasingly wet; the transition month, with rates starting to soften. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: PAGASA's rainy season begins: 265.0mm in Manila as the southwest monsoon sets in.
climate.crowd_note: Quieter and cheaper, but afternoon downpours and the first tropical cyclones disrupt island-hopping. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 419.6mm in Manila. PAGASA puts the peak of the typhoon season at July through October, when nearly 70% of typhoons develop.
climate.crowd_note: Low season; ferry cancellations and flight disruption are common. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: Wettest month in Manila's normals at 486.1mm, inside PAGASA's July-to-October typhoon peak. The Philippines averages about 20 tropical cyclones a year in its area of responsibility, 8 or 9 of which cross the country.
climate.crowd_note: The month most likely to have a trip rearranged by weather; Metro Manila flooding closes roads. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 330.3mm in Manila, still inside the typhoon peak.
climate.crowd_note: Cheapest fares of the year, but the least dependable for a fixed island itinerary. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 270.9mm in Manila. The last month of PAGASA's typhoon peak; rainfall starts easing late in the month.
climate.crowd_note: Improving toward month end, but still worth building slack into flight connections. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 129.3mm in Manila. PAGASA's rainy season formally runs to the end of November, but conditions improve markedly; late-season cyclones still occur.
climate.crowd_note: A good-value window before December rates rise. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

climate.precipitation_note: 75.4mm in Manila as PAGASA's dry season begins; the cool dry season runs December to February.
climate.crowd_note: Dry, comfortable weather but a heavy domestic travel period around Christmas and New Year. (Editorial judgement, not a sourced figure.)

timezone_note: Primary zone is Europe/Lisbon, which covers mainland Portugal; Madeira (Atlantic/Madeira) keeps the same clock as the mainland, while the Azores (Atlantic/Azores) run one hour behind it (UTC-1 in winter, UTC+0 in summer). The Azores and Madeira are not separate entries in this guide; the zone differences are from the IANA database, not from a page opened for this guide. Summer time follows the EU rule of the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October, so on 17 October 2026 mainland Portugal is on WEST (UTC+1) and clocks go back to WET (UTC+0) on Sunday 25 October 2026 (the last Sunday of October that year). A web search listed the Observatorio Astronomico de Lisboa (oal.ul.pt) as giving 25 October 2026 for the change, but its pages could not be opened (expired TLS certificate), so the date rests on the last-Sunday rule rather than on a page cited here.
passport_validity_rule: Portugal is in the Schengen area. The EU's Your Europe portal states that for a short stay the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the last 10 years (counted from the day you enter). UK FCDO's Portugal entry page gives the same two conditions. Portugal's own visa portal (vistos.mne.gov.pt), for visa applicants, asks for a travel document valid over 3 months after the date of exit. Short stays are limited to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen area. This applies to the mainland, Madeira and the Azores.
entry_requirement_notes: ETIAS is NOT in force today (17 October 2026), as far as any official page opened for this guide shows. The European Commission's ETIAS page (dated 6 October 2025) states that ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' and that the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. A later Commission news item (28 April 2026) says ETIAS 'is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026' with the exact date to be communicated later, and the French foreign ministry (April 2026) says it is 'not yet operational'. No page opened for this guide announces an actual start date, so do not treat any date as fact; check travel-europe.europa.eu before you travel. When it starts it will be a pre-travel authorisation (not a visa) for visa-exempt nationals: the Commission gives a fee of EUR 20 (people under 18 or over 70 exempt from the fee) and validity of 3 years or until the passport expires. What is already live is the Entry/Exit System (EES): the Commission says it has been fully operational across all Schengen countries since 10 April 2026; per UK FCDO it replaces manual passport stamping, you may be asked to register fingerprints and a photo at the border, and the digital record is valid for 3 years. Whether you need a Schengen visa depends on nationality (see the visa rules for your passport and vistos.mne.gov.pt). Official pages say border officers may ask for proof of enough money and an onward or return ticket (FCDO), and Portugal's visa portal requires a return reservation and bank statements from visa applicants, but no page opened for this guide states that visa-exempt visitors must hold an onward ticket as a fixed condition or gives a proof-of-funds figure, and the consulates quote differing figures, so an onward ticket, blank pages and a funds figure are not stated here. FCDO's entry page gives no separate entry rules for Madeira or the Azores. Cash: Portugal's customs authority (info-aduaneiro.portaldasfinancas.gov.pt, page titled 'Viaja com 10.000 euros ou mais em dinheiro? Nao se esqueca de o declarar!') and Global Affairs Canada say that carrying EUR 10,000 or more in cash (or equivalent) into or out of the EU must be declared to customs; this does not apply to travel within the EU. Global Affairs Canada (updated 11 August 2026) also says ETIAS applications are 'not yet open' and that customs officials may ask to see a return or onward ticket and proof of sufficient funds, which fits that: a request, not a fixed condition. The ETIAS site (travel-europe.europa.eu/en/etias, opened 18 October 2026) still says ETIAS 'is currently not in operation'; the Commission's EES page says EES 'became fully operational on 10 April 2026'.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
Hepatitis A (especially for smaller cities, villages, rural areas or street food)
Rabies (pre-exposure vaccination to be decided with a healthcare provider)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's Portugal page
health.notes: No vaccination is a condition of entry: CDC's Portugal page states yellow fever vaccine is not recommended and not required for entry (page section last updated 23 April 2025; the page was last reviewed 25 August 2026). The recommended list is medical advice only. The page has no malaria section, carries only a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025) and has no notices specific to Madeira or the Azores. It also names leptospirosis, leishmaniasis (sand fly bites), hantavirus and tuberculosis under non-vaccine-preventable risks and says road crashes are a major risk. Emergency care is via 112. For non-urgent medical advice, UK FCDO's health page lists SNS 24 on +351 808 24 24 24 on the mainland (press 9 for English), +351 800 24 24 20 for Madeira and Porto Santo, and +351 808 24 60 24 for the Azores, and says a GHIC or EHIC covers medically necessary state healthcare but is not an alternative to travel insurance. CDC and FCDO are used as fallbacks because no page from Portugal's health ministry (sns.gov.pt / dgs.pt) was opened for this guide.

emergency.notes: UK FCDO's Portugal pages (a fallback; no Portuguese government emergency page could be opened) list one number, 112, for ambulance, fire and police, and say the police are the PSP (Policia de Seguranca Publica) in cities and the GNR (Guarda Nacional Republicana) in smaller towns and rural areas. Police, ambulance and fire are therefore all shown as 112. For non-emergency medical advice FCDO lists SNS 24 on 808 24 24 24 (mainland; press 9 for English), 800 24 24 20 (Madeira and Porto Santo) and 808 24 60 24 (Azores). No dedicated tourist police line and no separate direct ambulance or fire number was found on an official page, so none is listed here. Global Affairs Canada (travel.gc.ca/destinations/portugal) independently says 'Dial 112 for emergency assistance' and the European Commission (digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/112) says 112 reaches ambulance, fire brigade or police and is available everywhere in the EU free of charge.

getting_around.summary: Long-distance travel on the mainland is led by CP (Comboios de Portugal). Per CP's own pages, the Alfa Pendular is its fastest service (maximum speed 220 km/h, introduced 1999; 301 seats, free Wi-Fi, a cafeteria and bar carriage) with Braga to Faro and Lisbon to Porto given as typical journeys, and Intercidades is a separate intercity service connecting the main cities (Minho to the Algarve, Lisbon to Porto, the Alentejo and the Centre). CP advertises up to 65% off when you buy Alfa Pendular or Intercidades tickets in advance. No official journey time or fare for any route was opened for this record, so none is given: check the CP timetable and fares on cp.pt. Lisbon and Porto each run their own operator fares (see the passes below). Carris Metropolitana (the regional bus network around Lisbon), the Madeira and Azores bus and ferry networks, and domestic flights were not researched.

passes.name: Lisbon Carris/Metro single ticket and 24-hour tickets
passes.covers: Metro de Lisboa's 2026 fare sheet (effective 1 January 2026) lists a Carris/Metro single ticket at 1.90 EUR (one journey on the whole Carris/Metro network within 1 hour of first validation, not valid for consecutive Metro rides) and a 24-hour ticket for unlimited travel on Carris and Metro at 7.25 EUR, with variants adding Transtejo (Cacilhas) at 10.35 EUR and CP at 11.40 EUR. The sheet does not say which CP lines the 11.40 EUR ticket covers.
passes.worth_it: A 24-hour ticket at 7.25 EUR equals roughly four single tickets, so it pays off on a day of four or more separate journeys. The sheet also lists a navegante occasional card at 0.50 EUR to hold the ticket; confirm the current figures with Metro de Lisboa or Carris before buying.

passes.name: Porto Andante Tour and Andante 24 (Z2)
passes.covers: Metro do Porto's tariff in force from 1 January 2026 lists Andante Tour 1 at 7.75 EUR (24 consecutive hours from first validation) and Andante Tour 3 at 16.55 EUR (72 consecutive hours), and an Andante 24 ticket for zone Z2 at 5.35 EUR (24 hours in the zones bought). The Andante site says the Tour card works across the Andante intermodal network but not on the Funicular dos Guindais or the STCP tram, and cannot be topped up.
passes.worth_it: The Tour passes are for visitors using metro, bus and train widely, while the Andante 24 (Z2) is cheaper if you stay inside the zones you bought. Which zone your trips need was not checked, and the Metro do Porto page gave an Andante Azul (occasional) card at 0.60 EUR and a Z2 single at 1.40 EUR; check andante.pt for the zone map.

passes.name: CP long-distance tickets (Alfa Pendular, Intercidades)
passes.covers: Point-to-point tickets for CP's Alfa Pendular and Intercidades trains, sold on cp.pt; no national rail pass was found on an official page.
passes.worth_it: Not a pass: book each journey. CP advertises up to 65% off for advance purchase, so for fixed travel dates buy early; the discount terms were not read in full.

timezone_note: Serbia has a single time zone and observes EU-style daylight saving. Per the IANA tz database for Europe/Belgrade, summer time (CEST, UTC+2) began 29 March 2026 and ends 25 October 2026, when clocks return to CET (UTC+1). Checked against the IANA database on 2026-09-28; the label above reflects the state on that date.
passport_validity_rule: Serbia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs states the passport must be valid at least 90 days after the intended date of departure from the Republic of Serbia, contain at least two consecutive blank pages, and have been issued within the past 10 years. This is a 90-days-beyond-departure rule, not a six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: Visa position depends on passport. Serbia's MFA (visa-regime pages, opened 2026-10-17) lists ordinary passports of, for example, the USA, UK, Singapore and Brazil as visa-free for up to 90 days in a six-month period counted from the date of first entry. India is different: the MFA page for India says diplomatic and official passports need no visa for up to 90 days, but ordinary passports require a visa. Under a 2014 Government decision, however, holders of national passports with a valid Schengen, UK or EU member state visa, or a visa of the United States, and holders of foreign passports with a residence permit in the Schengen area, the EU or the US, may enter and stay up to 90 days in a six-month period within the validity of that visa or permit without a Serbian visa (a residence permit issued as a separate card must be shown with the passport). The MFA page does not name a UK residence permit. Since 23 April 2025 Serbia also issues electronic visas, the Digital Travel Authorization, but only to nationals of countries enabled on welcometoserbia.gov.rs and only if low-risk and reciprocity conditions are met; otherwise a sticker visa applies. The pages opened did not list which nationalities are enabled, so Indian eligibility is not confirmed here: check welcometoserbia.gov.rs or the nearest Serbian mission before booking. Foreigner registration (the 'white card') is still in force: the stay must be registered with the police within 24 hours of arrival or of accommodation being provided. Hotels and other paid accommodation providers register guests; for visitors staying in a private home the host is legally responsible for registering them within 24 hours (MFA registration page and the police page). Permanent residents have eight days. Whether registration can also be done online was not confirmed from the official pages opened today, so do not assume it. Serbia's MFA also states entry may be refused without sufficient funds, defined as 50 EUR per day of stay shown by cash or a bank statement; health insurance covering at least 20,000 EUR of medical costs is recommended, not mandatory; and border officers may ask to see a return flight ticket and proof of a paid hotel booking, though Serbia does not state an onward ticket as a condition of entry. UK FCDO advice (2026-10-17) agrees: visa-free up to 90 days in any 6 months, passport valid at least 90 days after departure, register with local police within 24 hours.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
Mpox (for travellers expecting certain activities such as new sexual partners or large public events)
Tick-borne encephalitis (for extensive outdoor or tick exposure)
Rabies (depending on planned activities and access to post-exposure treatment)
health.malaria_risk: None
health.notes: Nothing is checked at the Serbian border: the CDC states yellow fever vaccination is not required for entry to Serbia, and the vaccines above are advisory only. CDC lists no malaria risk for Serbia. Tick-borne encephalitis is the one Serbia-specific item, relevant for hiking and rural outdoor time rather than city visits. The National Tourism Organisation of Serbia states that public mains water is safe to drink, and that all tourists have the right to emergency medical care during their stay.

emergency.notes: Police 192 and ambulance 194 are confirmed by the National Tourism Organisation of Serbia. Fire 193 and the pan-European 112 come from the UK FCDO's Serbia travel advice, used as a fallback because Serbia's own tourism and interior pages reached here did not list them; treat 193 and 112 as FCDO-sourced rather than first-hand Serbian citations. The tourism board also lists 1987 for AMSS roadside assistance. No official source consulted confirmed a dedicated tourist police line, so none is listed here.

getting_around.summary: Serbia is compact and mostly covered by road: the government's own visitor portal describes roughly 1,000 km of motorway, putting Belgrade about an hour from Novi Sad and under two hours from most of the north and south. The headline rail service is the modernised 'Soko' high-speed train, which the same portal states runs Belgrade to Novi Sad in about 35 minutes with free Wi-Fi; tickets and timetables come from Srbijavoz, the national passenger rail operator. Within Belgrade, GSP runs more than 150 bus, tram and trolleybus lines plus over 20 night lines.

climate.crowd_note: Lowest visitor numbers of the year outside the New Year period; Orthodox Christmas falls on 7 January.

timezone_note: South Africa uses a single time zone, Africa/Johannesburg (UTC+2), all year. The South African Tourism UK-market page 'Know before you go' gives the time as GMT+1 when the UK and Ireland are on summer time and GMT+2 when they are on winter time, which is consistent with a fixed UTC+2 and no clock change in South Africa.
passport_validity_rule: Passport must be valid for at least 30 days after the date you intend to leave South Africa, and must have at least two blank (unused) pages. The South African mission in Ottawa (DIRCO) states: 'The passport must be valid for a period of at least 30 days after the planned departure from South Africa' and 'Two unused blank visa pages are required when a person reports to a port of entry. Non-compliance will result in refusal of admission to South Africa.' The UK FCDO's South Africa entry page gives the same rule (at least 30 days after you leave, two or more blank pages). Home Affairs' travel-documents page states 'Passports must be valid for at least 30 days after the intended departure date' and 'at least two blank pages for entry stamps. These pages must be facing', but that wording sits in its section on South African passports and does not itself say it applies to foreign visitors, so the mission and FCDO pages are the support for visitors. Stored as 1 month beyond exit; the rule is precisely 30 days, so a passport with 30 days left on departure day is acceptable.
entry_requirement_notes: VISA: Home Affairs' 'Exempt Countries' schedule (issued 9 December 2025, marked 'subject to change without notice') lists 90 days visa-free for ordinary-passport holders of the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, Germany, Singapore and Brazil; for India the page text as read showed 90 days only for what appeared to be diplomatic, official and service passports and no ordinary-passport entry could be confirmed, so Indian ordinary-passport holders should check the visa rules and the DIRCO or VFS pages. The UK FCDO page adds that you can visit without a visa for up to 90 days for business or tourism. CHILDREN (two official sources disagree on wording): Home Affairs' 'Travel requirements for children' page (marked revised November 2019, following the first amendment to the Immigration Regulations that took effect 1 December 2018) asks for a 'birth certificate / equivalent document', defined as an extract from the Birth Register containing the child's and parent(s)' particulars, and says consent from the parent(s) cited on the birth certificate is needed when a parent is not travelling with the child, with the consent letter not older than 6 months. It does not use the word 'unabridged'. The South African Consulate-General in Toronto's page for children under 18 (no date given) still says parents 'must produce an unabridged-birth certificate' and, for one parent travelling, an affidavit from the other parent, a court order or a death certificate. Home Affairs' page lists exemptions, including children in direct transit at an international airport and children whose passport names the parent(s); it does not state whether the rules are currently enforced as written, so carry the full birth certificate showing both parents plus consent documents. A 2015 Home Affairs tourist advisory PDF also says 'unabridged' but pre-dates the 2018 amendment and is not relied on. Official pages opened for this guide did not state an onward-ticket requirement or proof-of-funds figure, so whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed. ELECTRICITY SUPPLY: Eskom's media statement of 8 July 2026 reported more than 413 consecutive days without loadshedding, and separately a 'load reduction' measure still affecting some areas, mainly in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, with five provinces (Western Cape, Northern Cape, Free State, North West, Mpumalanga) free of it; Eskom itself calls the two 'fundamentally different challenges'. That is the position on 8 July 2026, not a forecast; no newer Eskom page was opened. TRAVELLER DECLARATION (in force): SARS's notice 'Required Online Traveller Declarations from 1 July 2026' says all travellers entering or leaving South Africa through air, land, sea and rail ports must submit a declaration before travelling, through the SARS Customs Online Traveller Declaration portal, the SATMS app or Scan-to-Declare QR codes; its FAQ says to submit no more than 24 hours before departure (for journeys with stops, the last leg to South Africa), that it includes foreign travellers, that each traveller including children and infants needs one (a parent or guardian can complete it), and that air or sea transit passengers who stay in the transit area are excluded. SARS says travellers will not be denied entry solely for not having completed it in advance, and can be helped at the port, but a false or missing declaration can mean delays, detention, forfeiture or penalties. The UK FCDO page also tells visitors to submit an online traveller declaration. CURRENCY (sources disagree): SARS's Travellers page (updated 19 August 2026) and FAQ give R100 000 as the threshold above which written South African Reserve Bank permission is needed, and say declaring currency below that is voluntary; the UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada pages still say to declare more than R25 000 or USD 10 000. SARS is the issuing authority, so R100 000 is treated as the better-supported figure; the older figures appear on foreign advisories. ETA: the Electronic Travel Authorisation was launched on 12 August 2026 (SAnews, Minister Schreiber's launch speech on gov.za), initially for China, India, Indonesia and Mexico, at OR Tambo, Cape Town, King Shaka and Lanseria airports, with land and sea ports to follow. The Minister said it 'will progressively become compulsory' for short-stay visits from countries that require visas and voluntary for visa-exempt travellers; the pages opened do not say it is yet compulsory for any nationality or give a fee. Indian citizens need a visa to visit (Department of Tourism, September 2025), so for India the ETA is the online route, not a visa-free entry; check eta.dha.gov.za or the nearest mission before booking. USA, UK, Canada, Australia, Germany, Singapore and Brazil passport holders do not need an ETA for up to 90 days.

health.malaria_risk: Malaria is a notifiable condition in South Africa with three endemic provinces: KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga and Limpopo (Department of Health). The NICD says transmission generally occurs in low-altitude areas of northern KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo and Mpumalanga, with the high-transmission season generally September to May. CDC lists Kruger National Park and uMkhanyakude (KwaZulu-Natal), Mopani and Vhembe (Limpopo) and Ehlanzeni (Mpumalanga) districts as areas where prophylaxis is recommended. Cape Town, Johannesburg and the Garden Route are not among the areas named.
health.notes: ENTRY: The National Department of Health's 'Health Protocols for Travellers Arriving in South Africa' (on health.gov.za) says all travellers over 1 year old arriving from a yellow fever risk country must produce a valid International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis, that those without may be refused entry or quarantined for up to 6 days or until the certificate becomes valid, and that a signed waiver letter from a travel health practitioner is needed for medical exemption (those travellers are placed under quarantine surveillance). The protocol points to the WHO list of countries with risk of yellow fever transmission rather than naming them, so check that list. CDC's page says the vaccine is not required for travellers coming direct from the US, and that yellow fever vaccination is not recommended for South Africa itself. Travellers carrying medicine for personal use are required to have authorisation from SAHPRA (same protocol, section 5). All arrivals can be subject to entry screening including temperature checks. MALARIA: the Department of Health advises consulting a travel clinic or doctor before travel to decide whether prophylaxis is needed, and taking steps to avoid mosquito bites outdoors in the evening in endemic areas; CDC recommends atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine or tafenoquine for the districts above and lists mosquito avoidance only for other transmission areas (King Cetshwayo, Zululand, Capricorn, Greater Sekhukhune, Waterberg). CDC's malaria and yellow fever sections were updated 23 April 2025 and the page was last reviewed 25 August 2026; the NICD article is dated 3 November 2025. CDC also carries a rabies alert about Cape fur seals (South Africa and Namibia): do not approach or touch seals. All of this is medical information, not advice.

money.tipping: South African Tourism's UK-market page says 'South Africa is similar to the UK, with 10-15% customary in restaurants and for tour guides.' That is a UK-edition tourism-board page with no date, so treat the range as guidance rather than a rule.

emergency.notes: The Western Cape Government lists Police Flying Squad 10111, Ambulance 10177 and 'Cell Phone Emergency' 112 (MTN, Vodacom, Cell C, Telkom), and also states 'Currently, there's no single emergency number in South Africa'; it says for fire and rescue to 'see your district municipality for emergency contact numbers' (page undated). The national Department of Tourism's safety page lists police 10111, 112 'from a cellphone' and 10177 for ambulance/fire. Because the two official pages differ on fire, no fire number is shown rather than assuming 10177 covers it; ambulance 10177 is supported by both. No dedicated tourist police number was found, so none is listed here. The Department of Tourism page gives tourism complaints on 012 444 6000 or 0860 686 747, which is not an emergency line. RE-CHECK 18 October 2026: the Department of Tourism safety page lists 'Police (SAPS) 10111', 'Police from cellphone: 112' and 'Ambulance/ Fire: 10177'; the Western Cape page again lists no fire number ('Please see your district municipality') and says there is no single emergency number; Global Affairs Canada lists 'firefighters: 10111 or 10112 from a cellular telephone' and 'medical assistance: 10177'; the UK FCDO lists police 10111 and 'emergency services on 112 (mobile only)'. Three official pages give three different answers for fire, so no fire number is shown. Police 10111, ambulance 10177 and 112 from a mobile are each supported by at least two of these pages.

timezone_note: South Korea uses a single time zone nationwide, Korea Standard Time (Asia/Seoul in the IANA database), and does not currently observe daylight saving time. The Korean government pages used for this guide give times in KST (for example the K-ETA exemption runs to 31 December 2026 KST and the e-Arrival card window is counted in KST).
passport_validity_rule: Korea sets no minimum remaining validity beyond the trip itself: the passport only has to stay valid throughout the stay. The Embassy of Korea in Singapore (mofa.go.kr) answers the question directly: you may enter with a passport that has less than 6 months of remaining validity "as long as your passport remains valid throughout your stay." Government of Canada advice says the passport "must be valid beyond the date of expected departure from South Korea" and UK FCDO says it must have an expiry date after the date you leave (for stays up to 90 days; FCDO adds 6 months from arrival for long-term visas). Two catches: a K-ETA lasts 3 years or until the passport expires, whichever is sooner, so a passport that expires soon shortens the K-ETA; and your airline or a transit country may still apply its own six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: CHECKED 17 and 18 October 2026. (1) K-ETA (Korea Electronic Travel Authorization): IN FORCE as the general rule for visa-free visitors, but TEMPORARILY WAIVED for 22 nationalities/regions until 31 December 2026 (KST). Korea's Ministry of Justice extended the waiver for one year, 1 January to 31 December 2026, per Korean MOFA notices dated 29 December 2025 and 5 January 2026. A Korean MOFA notice dated 18 March 2026 (Embassy in Estonia) also names Estonia among the countries covered, and Global Affairs Canada ("exempt ... until December 31, 2026") and UK FCDO ("temporarily exempt ... until December 31, 2026") confirm the end date for Canadians and Britons. The KTO (VisitKorea) page lists the exempt nationalities (Estonia is not on it): Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Macau; United States (including Guam), Canada; United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, Netherlands, Spain, Poland, Sweden, Finland, Norway, Belgium, Denmark, Austria; Australia, New Zealand. Of the eight passports NextStamp covers, UK, USA, Canada, Australia, Germany and Singapore are on that list; India and Brazil are not and need an approved K-ETA before boarding (if they are visa-exempt at all; check visa.go.kr). Nothing opened for this guide says the waiver continues past 31 December 2026, so a trip that starts on or after 1 January 2027 should assume a K-ETA is needed and check k-eta.go.kr (its notice list shows an item dated 2026-03-20 titled as a temporary-exemption extension notice whose text could not be opened here). Facts for those who do need or want one: fee KRW 10,000, non-refundable even if refused; usually assessed within 72 hours but can take longer and there is no express service; valid 3 years or until passport expiry, whichever is sooner; must be approved before boarding; approval does not guarantee entry (the immigration officer decides). An exempt traveller can still apply voluntarily, which also spares them the arrival card. Beware look-alike sites; apply only at k-eta.go.kr or the official app. Transit passengers who do not clear immigration at Incheon do not need one. (2) e-Arrival card: IN FORCE. Government of Canada states all travellers must submit an entry declaration, online up to 3 days before arrival (e-arrivalcard.go.kr, free, counted in KST) or on paper on arrival; UK FCDO says paper forms are still available. A 2025 KTO article said the paper card was planned to end after December 2025, which the 2026 FCDO and GAC pages contradict, so expect the online form to be the faster route. K-ETA holders do not have to submit it. Beware fake e-Arrival sites (Korea Immigration Service notice of 9 March 2026). (3) Q-CODE: NOT a blanket registration. It is required of travellers who have visited or transited an area on KDCA's Quarantine Inspection Required lists. The KDCA list for Q4 2026 (as of 1 October 2026) has two tiers: for 'strict' areas (including India, Brazil, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, and the US states of New Mexico, Michigan and Washington) everyone arriving from or via them must submit a Q-CODE or health declaration form; for the wider 'quarantine inspection required' list (which includes, for example, the rest of the US, Canada, Australia, Japan, Singapore, Germany and England) it is mandatory only if you have symptoms. Registration opens up to 7 days before arrival (GAC, KTO), the fine for non-compliance is up to KRW 10 million, and the list is revised quarterly, so re-check kdca.go.kr before travel. (4) Stay length is set by nationality: UK FCDO says up to 90 days for tourism or short business; Government of Canada says Canadians need no visa for up to 180 days; KTO and Korean MOFA direct travellers to visa.go.kr for their nationality. UK FCDO states you must hold an onward or return ticket; the Korean and Canadian pages opened for this guide did not mention it, so the onward-ticket rule rests on FCDO alone. No blank-page requirement was found on any official page, so none is listed here. UK FCDO says you must declare anything prohibited or subject to tax or duty; Korea Customs Service says bringing in up to USD 10,000 (foreign currency, KRW notes or cheques) needs no declaration, and anything above that must be reported on the Traveler Declaration Form (tick the currency item and hand it to a customs officer); a Certificate of Foreign Currency Declaration cannot be issued once you have passed immigration, and failing to report can mean up to one year in prison or a fine of up to KRW 100 million. Korea Immigration contact centre: 1345 (+82-2-1345 from abroad).

Separate from vaccination, the Q-CODE health registration rules in entry_requirement_notes can apply depending on where you have travelled recently.

power.adapter_note: The Korea Tourism Organization states the standard is 220 volts at 60 Hz and that outlets take two round holes. It does not name a plug-type letter, so none is recorded here. Without a multi-voltage adapter you can borrow or buy one at a hotel front desk, and KTO lists airports, retail stores, duty-free shops and convenience stores as sources.

emergency.notes: The Korea Tourism Organization lists 112 for police and 119 for fire and medical emergencies; the Government of Canada's South Korea page gives the same (112 police, 119 medical and fire). KTO says if you do not speak Korean, say "English please" or "Interpreter please" when the call connects. KTO also lists +82-1339 for infectious-disease emergencies; for a life-threatening emergency use 119. The 1330 Korea Travel Hotline (+82-2-1330 from abroad) is run by the Korea Tourism Organization for non-life-threatening help such as transport questions and interpretation, 24 hours a day, with phone support in Korean, English, Japanese, Chinese, Russian, Vietnamese, Thai and Malay (some languages have shorter hours). No tourist-police number appears on the KTO page, so none is listed here, and no source opened confirms that 112 works as a general international emergency number in Korea, so no general emergency number is shown. UK FCDO (getting-help page) lists Ambulance 119, Fire 119, Police 112 and the Danuri Call Centre 1577 1366 (24/7 interpretation); Global Affairs Canada gives police 112, medical 119, fire 119.

getting_around.summary: The Korea Tourism Organization describes the KTX as a high-speed train running at up to 330 km/h from Seoul, Yongsan and Cheongnyangni stations to Busan, Pohang, Mokpo, Yeosu, Gangneung, Andong and other cities; the Seoul to Busan Gyeongbu Line is 447.1 km and the busiest route. SRT is a separate high-speed service (up to 300 km/h) from Suseo Station towards Busan or Mokpo. Tickets can be bought at ticket offices, on the KORAIL website or KORAIL+ app, at kiosks, and through NAVER Train Booking or KakaoT; sales open one month before departure at 07:00 and close 20 minutes before departure. KORAIL's English customer centre is +82-1599-7777 (08:00-20:00). KTO gives no Seoul to Busan journey time, so none is stated here. In cities, a rechargeable transport card (T-money, among others) pays for subways and buses. KTO pages were last updated in August 2026.

passes.name: Korail Pass (KORAIL Pass)
passes.covers: KTO: a train pass exclusively for international travellers, sold as 2-, 3-, 4- or 5-day flexible passes usable within ten days. It gives unlimited use of standard cabins during the pass period, up to two seat reservations a day, unlimited standing tickets, and first-class booking at 50% of the original first-class fare. It does not cover SRT, subways or temporary tourist trains. KTO says it is booked through korail.com (English, Japanese, Chinese).
passes.worth_it: No current prices were found on a page that could be opened, and older price tables conflict with the pass structure now described (KORAIL changed pass types and age categories from 11 December 2025, per a search result not opened in full), so no figure is given and no verdict on value is offered. Check the price against your planned KTX journeys on korail.com before buying.

passes.name: T-money card
passes.covers: KTO: a rechargeable prepaid card costing 3,000 to 5,000 won, sold at convenience stores nationwide (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven and others) and at information centres in Seoul subway stations on Lines 1 to 8. It works on public transport and at affiliated shops showing the Tmoney logo, and also at expressway toll gates. Reloading is at subway ticket machines, up to 500,000 won. KTO notes a transit-fare transfer discount when using a transportation card.
passes.worth_it: Not a discount pass but the practical default for city buses and subways. Refunds of more than 50,000 won are only possible at Tmoney Town at Seoul Station; smaller balances can be refunded at convenience stores, so top up modestly. KTO also lists a foreigner-only Mpass (fixed-period unlimited-ride card, bought with Korean won cash only) and says its separate Climate Card became limited to use within Seoul from 1 October 2026.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: KTO states visitors can rent a Wi-Fi egg or smartphone and buy SIM cards at the roaming centres at Incheon, Gimpo, Gimhae and Jeju airports (fees are on each provider's site). Physical USIMs are also sold at convenience stores such as CU, GS25, 7-Eleven and Emart24, though stock varies by branch. An eSIM can be bought online and activated by scanning a QR code; check your phone is eSIM-compatible. Free public Wi-Fi is available at most public locations including airports and subway and train stations (wififree.kr).

timezone_note: Mainland Spain and the Balearic Islands use Europe/Madrid: CET (UTC+1) in winter and CEST (UTC+2) in summer. The Canary Islands are on Atlantic/Canary, one hour behind the mainland (WET, UTC+0 in winter; WEST, UTC+1 in summer), which spain.info confirms in its practical-tips page ('UTC +1, except in the Canary Islands, where UTC +0 (one hour behind) is used'; clocks change twice a year). Offsets and the 2026 clock-change dates were checked against the IANA tz database (via Python zoneinfo) on 2026-10-17: summer time began 29 March 2026 and ends 25 October 2026, when mainland clocks return to CET (UTC+1). The label above reflects the state on 2026-10-17.
passport_validity_rule: Spain applies the Schengen rule. The EU's Your Europe portal states the passport should be valid for at least 3 months after the date you intend to leave the EU and must have been issued within the previous 10 years on the day you enter. Spain's consulate in Washington gives the same condition: valid until at least three months after the planned date of departure from the Schengen territory. This is a 3-months-beyond-departure rule, not a six-month rule.
entry_requirement_notes: Spain follows the Schengen short-stay rules: up to 90 days in any 180-day period for visa-exempt nationals (Your Europe), and tourists of some nationalities need a visit visa. Spain's consulate in Washington lists a round-trip or return ticket as required 'in all cases', and spain.info says a tourist must prove the availability of economic resources for the planned stay and for the return or transfer to another country. Funds: the Spanish consulate in Washington gives 122 EUR per person per day in 2026 with at least 1,099 EUR for stays of 9 days or more; the Spanish embassy in Canberra gives 122.10 EUR per day with a 1,098.90 EUR minimum. The two differ by rounding; the Canberra figure is the more precise one and the amounts are re-set each year, so carry proof of funds (cash, card, bank statement) and check the figure for your travel year. ETIAS: the European Commission's ETIAS page says ETIAS 'is currently not in operation and no applications for travel authorisations are collected at this point' (page last updated 6 October 2025), and a Commission news item of 28 April 2026 says it is scheduled to start in the last quarter of 2026 with the exact date to be announced later in the year. Spain's Washington consulate likewise says it is expected to become operational in the last quarter of 2026 and that no action is required from travellers yet. No start date had been confirmed in any source opened on 2026-10-17, so ETIAS is NOT in force today; re-check before travel. EES: the Commission's 28 April 2026 news item states the Entry/Exit System has been fully operational across all Schengen countries since 10 April 2026; non-EU travellers are registered (including biometrics) on entry and exit instead of having passports stamped. EU, EEA and Swiss citizens may enter with a national identity card or passport. These rules apply to mainland Spain, the Balearic and Canary Islands; no source opened here gave separate rules for Ceuta or Melilla, so none are stated. Border checks: Global Affairs Canada and the UK FCDO both say officers may ask for a return or onward ticket and proof of sufficient funds (the Spanish consulate in Washington lists a return ticket as required in all cases). Both also say the passport needs 3 months' validity beyond departure from Schengen (FCDO adds: issued less than 10 years before arrival). Global Affairs Canada (checked 2026-10-18) says ETIAS applications are not yet open; the Ottawa embassy page gives CAD 197.40 per day and CAD 1,776.60 minimum for 2026, consistent with the Canberra EUR figures.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers under 60; those 60 and older may get it)
Mpox (for adults expecting certain activities such as new sexual partners)
Rabies (depending on activities and access to post-exposure care)
health.notes: Nothing is checked at the Spanish border: the CDC states yellow fever vaccination is not required for entry and does not recommend it for Spain. The CDC Spain page does not list a malaria risk, so no risk is stated rather than asserting 'none'. The CDC notes dengue and leishmaniasis (spread by mosquitoes and sand flies) and advises avoiding bites. On care for visitors, spain.info states emergency treatment is guaranteed for everyone in hospitals and some health centres, care at private centres is always paid for, free care for illness or accident under the European Health Card applies to citizens of the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, and it recommends always travelling with international medical insurance. Medicines are bought at pharmacies, identified by green crosses.

money.card_acceptance: spain.info states that bank cards, especially Visa and MasterCard, are accepted in most shops, restaurants, hotels and museums, that cash is also accepted, and that withdrawal or currency-exchange fees are often charged. For local buses, spain.info's airport FAQ adds that fares are usually paid on boarding and cash is usually the only payment allowed, with change often limited to 20 EUR.
money.atm_notes: spain.info says withdrawal or currency-exchange fees are often charged; it names no specific ATM network and no official source consulted gave fee levels.

emergency.notes: Opened 2026-10-18. 112 is the single emergency number for police, ambulance and fire (UK FCDO 'Dial 112 and ask for an ambulance'; Global Affairs Canada 'Dial 112'; DGT table 'Centro de emergencias 112'; spain.info). 091 is the Policia Nacional emergency line (policia.es tourist safety leaflet: 'the National Police emergency telephone number'; DGT table). 062 is the Guardia Civil (guardiacivil.es: 'En el número 062, la Guardia Civil te atendera directamente, las 24 horas'; DGT table); 092 is local police (DGT table). Ambulance and fire are given as 112 because that is what official foreign-ministry pages state; 061 is a regional health-emergency line (for example Galicia, per Xunta de Galicia) and 080/085 fire lines are local, so none is stated as a national number. The Policia Nacional's tourist telephone complaints line (not an emergency line) is 902 102 112. No dedicated tourist-police emergency line was confirmed.

getting_around.summary: Spain's tourism board describes high-speed AVE trains connecting major destinations such as Barcelona, Seville or Valencia with Madrid in three hours or less; its table gives Madrid to Barcelona 2 h 30 min, Madrid to Seville 2 h 30 min, Madrid to Valencia 1 h 40 min and Madrid to Zaragoza 1 h 35 min. Long-distance and AVE trains are run by Renfe, which also operates Cercanias commuter networks around major cities. In Madrid, Renfe's Cercanias page says one-way fares can be paid at the turnstiles with a contactless bank card or phone and that tickets must be validated at the departure and arrival stations. For city buses and the metro, spain.info's airport FAQ says metro and train journeys are paid for at the station (usually from ticket machines), while bus fares are usually paid on boarding, often in cash only.

passes.name: Renfe Spain Rail Pass
passes.covers: Renfe's pass for people with residence outside Spain: you choose 4, 6, 8 or 10 trips and Standard or Comfort seats (Premium is not available). It covers Long Distance trains including AVE, and regional Media Distancia and Avant trains with seat reservation. The pass is personal and non-transferable.
passes.worth_it: Renfe's page states no price, so whether it beats point-to-point tickets cannot be judged from the official source. Each journey must still be validated by booking a ticket for that specific route (online under 'My passes', at ticket offices, travel agencies or by phone), you have up to 6 months from purchase to make the first trip, and the pass is valid for one month after the first trip.

passes.name: Madrid unlimited-travel transport pass (30-day and annual)
passes.covers: Renfe's Cercanias Madrid page says the pass allows any number of trips by bus, metro and Cercanias during its validity; options include 30-day and annual passes, loaded onto a Public Transport Card that can be topped up at station self-service machines.
passes.worth_it: Renfe's page gives no price and does not say whether visitors can obtain one, so it is listed for awareness only; single one-way tickets and contactless turnstile payment are the stated alternatives for a short stay.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: spain.info states that visitors using non-EU phone numbers may pay extra for calls and mobile data, depending on their provider, and suggests buying a prepaid SIM card with a data package suited to your needs. It adds that travellers from the EU use their phones at the same roaming rates as at home. No official source opened here covers eSIM availability or any ID or registration requirement for a prepaid SIM.
