timezone_label: Sri Lanka Standard Time (UTC+5:30, no DST)
timezone_note: One zone for the whole island, offset by 30 minutes from whole hours and with no daylight saving. Half an hour ahead of Nepal-style offsets is a common mix-up; it is the same clock as India.
passport_validity_rule: The Department of Immigration and Emigration states as a general condition of entry that you must hold "a passport valid for a minimum period of six months from the date you arrive in Sri Lanka". The UK FCDO states the same rule for British travellers: the passport's expiry date must be at least 6 months after the day you arrive.
entry_requirement_notes: The Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) is a MANDATORY ADVANCE authorisation, not a visa on arrival. The Department of Immigration and Emigration states that "all foreign nationals, including nationals of the above-mentioned 40 countries ... are required to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) prior to arrival in Sri Lanka" (immigration.gov.lk/pages_e.php?id=60, and the same wording on eta.gov.lk). With effect from 25.05.2026 the tourist ETA is issued FREE OF CHARGE to nationals of 40 countries (including the USA, UK, Canada, Australia, India, China, Japan, Germany and France), plus Maldives, Seychelles and Singapore; the fee waiver does not remove the requirement to apply before travelling, and ETA fees paid before 25.05.2026 are non-refundable. The free tourist ETA is valid for 30 days from first arrival with double entry permitted (90 days for Maldivian nationals); longer stays require a paid extension through the immigration portal. Two further conditions are stated by immigration.gov.lk: a visit-visa holder must hold "a written assurance (ticket) to return to the country of domicile or a visa to the next country of destination", and Immigration must be "satisfied that you have adequate funds for your maintenance whilst in Sri Lanka and for the payment of your return passage" — no figure is published for what counts as adequate, so none is stated here. No blank-passport-page minimum is published by Sri Lankan immigration. The free-ETA list (as published on immigration.gov.lk and eta.gov.lk, checked 2026-10-17) does not include Brazil: Brazilian passport holders are among "all other foreign nationals" who must still obtain an ETA before arrival under the general ETA rules. Neither official page states a fee amount for those nationalities, so none is stated here; check the fee on eta.gov.lk before paying, and pay only through that site. Singapore is not among the 40 but gets a free ETA under a reciprocal arrangement, as do Maldives and Seychelles.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever — certificate required for travellers aged 9 months and over arriving from, or having transited, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for direct travel from a non-risk country
recommended_vaccinations: Japanese encephalitis (for longer stays or rural/outdoor itineraries)
Routine vaccines including MMR and COVID-19
health.malaria_risk: None — WHO certified Sri Lanka malaria-free on 5 September 2016 and the WHO Sri Lanka country office reaffirmed ten years of sustained elimination in April 2026.
health.notes: Yellow fever is the only vaccination actually checked at the border, and only for arrivals from a transmission-risk country; everything in the recommended list is advice, not an entry condition. Sourcing conflict worth naming: WHO's certification and its 2026 follow-up are unambiguous that there is no local malaria transmission, while the CDC destination page still carries generic 'malaria is a risk in some parts of Sri Lanka, fill your prescription before you leave' boilerplate. The WHO certification is the better-supported position and is what the malaria entry above reflects; a traveller who sees the CDC wording should know it is not a Sri Lanka-specific finding. Vigilance against re-introduction (imported cases) is a WHO theme, but that is a public-health programme concern, not a traveller prophylaxis recommendation.

money.card_acceptance: Sri Lanka Tourism states that most hotels, restaurants and shopping centres accept credit cards, and warns that some establishments illegally try to add a surcharge for paying by card. Outside those settings — small eateries, tuk-tuks, markets, rural areas — assume cards are not accepted.
money.atm_notes: Sri Lanka Tourism says it is easy to withdraw money island-wide at ATMs using international credit or debit cards. The UK FCDO is more cautious and is worth heeding: ATMs exist in major towns but not all of them accept international cards, most major banks allow Visa and Mastercard cash withdrawals, and bank card fraud is common — use ATMs inside a bank or hotel where possible and check the machine for signs of tampering. Bank hours are 0900–1300 Monday to Friday, with some city branches open until 1500 or on Saturday mornings.

power.adapter_note: Sri Lanka Tourism publishes the supply as "230–240 volts, 50 cycles AC" and advises bringing a stabiliser for laptops, but does not publish which socket types are in use, and no other Sri Lankan government source states them — so plug_types is left null rather than guessed. A traveller from a 230V country needs no voltage converter; the socket shape is the only open question and is worth checking with the accommodation.

emergency.notes: No Sri Lankan government source publishes a single consolidated emergency-number list that could be found, so the police and fire numbers here come from the UK FCDO's Sri Lanka travel advice — a foreign government's page used as a fallback, not a first-hand Sri Lankan citation. FCDO lists police as "118/119" (119 is given here as the primary; 118 is worth trying if it does not connect), fire and rescue as 111, ambulance as "011 2691111 or 1990", and tourist police as 011 2421052. Sri Lanka Tourism's own travel-tips page independently confirms 1990 for the ambulance service (the state-funded 1990 Suwa Seriya service) but gives a DIFFERENT tourist police number, +94 11 2382209, and adds a 1912 tourism hotline — both sets are reproduced here rather than one being picked silently. Whether 112 reaches an emergency operator in Sri Lanka was not confirmed by any official source, so no general emergency number is shown. No official source was found confirming whether English is answered.

getting_around.summary: Sri Lanka Railways runs the intercity network and is the way most visitors cover long distances; seats can be reserved in advance through its seat-reservation system and the Pravesha smart-ticketing platform rather than only bought at the counter, and it markets scenic services such as the Ella Odyssey and Dunhinda Odyssey to tourists. Road transport (buses, hired cars with driver, tuk-tuks) covers everything the railway does not, but no official Sri Lankan source setting out fares, coverage or booking for those was found, so nothing is asserted about them here.

climate.precipitation_note: Northeast monsoon. The west and south coasts are in their dry half — Colombo averages only 58mm over about 5 rain days, one of its two driest months. The opposite is true on the other side of the island: the northeast monsoon is soaking the east and north, so Trincomalee, Batticaloa and Arugam Bay are wet and the eastern sea is rough.
climate.crowd_note: High season on the southwest and south coasts; the first week is still busy with the New Year tail. Editorial judgement, not a sourced measurement.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest month on the southwest coast — Colombo averages 73mm over about 5 rain days — as the northeast monsoon weakens. The east coast is still on the wrong side of that monsoon, though it is easing there too.
climate.crowd_note: Peak of the southwest-coast season; beach towns and whale-watching out of Mirissa are at their busiest. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: First inter-monsoon begins: rain arrives island-wide as afternoon and evening thunderstorms rather than as monsoon rain, and Colombo's total climbs to 128mm. This is the brief window when neither coast is monsoon-hit — the east is drying out while the southwest is still mostly fine.
climate.crowd_note: Still high season in the south and west but thinning after February. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: First inter-monsoon at full strength: 246mm in Colombo over about 14 days, almost all of it convective afternoon storms that clear. Hottest month of the year by daytime maximum. Both coasts are workable, which is unusual.
climate.crowd_note: Sinhala and Tamil New Year falls in April and domestic travel surges around it; transport and coastal accommodation get tight. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: The switch. Southwest monsoon onset makes this Colombo's second-wettest month (392mm, about 16 rain days) and hits the southwest coast and the hill country hardest — Sri Lanka Tourism describes it as heavy rainfall on the southwest coast and hills. Simultaneously the east and north dry out, and Trincomalee, Arugam Bay and Jaffna enter their good season.
climate.crowd_note: Southwest beach season ends; east-coast season begins. Low prices on the west, rising on the east. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Southwest monsoon established. Colombo's total drops sharply from May (185mm) but rain falls on about 16 days, so it is persistent rather than heavy, and the hills stay wet. The east coast is dry and settled — this is when Arugam Bay's surf season is running.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet on the southwest coast, building on the east. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest month of the southwest monsoon in Colombo (122mm) — the monsoon's rain is concentrated on the hills and the far southwest rather than the city. The east and north are at their driest and sunniest of the year.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season on the east coast and through the cultural triangle; European summer holidays add to it. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: As July: 120mm in Colombo, the southwest monsoon still running but at its least intrusive on the west-coast lowlands, and the east coast dry. The best single month to be on the eastern side of the island.
climate.crowd_note: Busiest month on the east coast and the second high season nationally. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: The southwest monsoon's tail, and Colombo's rainfall jumps back to 245mm over about 15 days. The east coast is still fair but its season is closing as the second inter-monsoon approaches.
climate.crowd_note: Thinning on both coasts; a genuine gap between the two high seasons. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Second inter-monsoon — the one time of year both coasts are wet at once. 365mm in Colombo over about 17 rain days, the highest rain-day count of the year, with heavy thunderstorms and squalls island-wide. Neither coast offers a reliable escape from the other.
climate.crowd_note: Lowest visitor numbers of the year and the widest choice of closed restaurants and hotels. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Wettest month in Colombo (414mm) as the second inter-monsoon runs into the onset of the northeast monsoon. Rain is widespread; the east and north are moving into their wet season just as the southwest starts to clear late in the month.
climate.crowd_note: Still low, though the southwest coast starts reopening towards the end of the month. Editorial judgement.

climate.precipitation_note: Northeast monsoon takes hold and the pattern flips back: Colombo drops to 175mm and the southwest and south coasts move into clear skies and calm seas, which Sri Lanka Tourism calls peak season there. The east coast is now the wet side.
climate.crowd_note: Southwest-coast high season restarts; Christmas and New Year are the most heavily booked fortnight of the year. Editorial judgement.

timezone_note: The Tourism Authority of Thailand states the country's time zone as GMT+7; Thailand uses a single time zone nationwide and does not observe daylight saving.
passport_validity_rule: A passport must be valid for at least six months and have at least one blank page. The UK FCDO states the expiry date must fall at least six months after the date you arrive and that you need at least 1 blank page; Global Affairs Canada says valid at least 6 months upon entry. The Royal Thai Embassy's page for the 30-day visa exemption words it as valid for at least six months 'upon returning to the country of residence' - counting from arrival is the stricter, better-supported reading, so plan on it.
entry_requirement_notes: Since 15 September 2026 the visa exemption for nationals of 60 countries and territories (including the US, UK, Canada, Australia, Japan, India, Switzerland, New Zealand, Germany, Singapore and all 27 EU member states; Brazil is not on the list) allows a stay of up to 30 days for tourism only - it replaces the previous 60-day scheme and does not cover business or work. The Royal Thai Embassy says the stay can be extended by up to 30 days solely at the discretion of the immigration officer. Entry via a land border checkpoint under this exemption is generally limited to two times per calendar year (Malaysian, Bruneian, Indonesian and Singaporean nationals are exempt from that limit). Seychelles and Mauritius get 15 days; Azerbaijan, Belarus and Serbia are covered by Visa on Arrival. Proof of funds: the Royal Thai Embassy states travellers must possess adequate cash of 20,000 THB per person or 40,000 THB per family; the UK FCDO quotes a lower 10,000 THB per person / 20,000 THB per family - carry the higher amount to be safe. Onward travel: the Thai MFA's visa Q&A (a page last updated in 2022) lists a round-trip air ticket among requirements, while the UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada say you may be asked for evidence of onward or return travel and can be refused entry without it - carry a confirmed onward or return booking. Separately, all foreign nationals must complete the free Thailand Digital Arrival Card (TDAC) online at tdac.immigration.go.th within 3 days before arrival; it is not a visa. Royal Thai Embassy guidance exempts only travellers transiting without passing through immigration control and Border Pass holders. If you arrive from, or have an airport layover of more than 12 hours in, a yellow fever risk country, a vaccination certificate is required.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever (only if arriving from, or after a layover of more than 12 hours in, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, for travellers aged 9 months or older; not required for direct travel from the US, and Thailand itself has no yellow fever risk)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap, polio, influenza, chickenpox, shingles)
Japanese encephalitis (depending on duration and activities)
health.malaria_risk: Limited and localised. The CDC reports most cases in the provinces bordering Myanmar, Cambodia and Malaysia (rare cases in Buri Ram), especially rural forest and forest-fringe areas, where atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline or tafenoquine is advised. Rare to few cases occur elsewhere, including Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai and the islands of Koh Pha Ngan, Koh Samui and Phuket. The CDC reports no transmission on the Krabi Province islands (Koh Lanta, Koh Phi Phi, Koh Yao Noi, Koh Yao Yai) or in Pattaya City. In other transmission areas (including Buri Ram) insect-bite prevention alone is recommended rather than medication.
health.notes: Nothing on this list is checked at the Thai border for an ordinary arrival — the only vaccination that can be demanded on entry is yellow fever, and only if you are arriving from a risk country. Everything else is medical advice, not an entry condition. Dengue, Zika and rabies are present; air pollution in Bangkok and Chiang Mai can be high, worsened by seasonal smoke haze. The UK FCDO warns that all Thai hospitals require a guarantee of payment before treating patients, so adequate health insurance is effectively essential.

money.atm_notes: Card and ATM fraud occurs. The UK FCDO reports incidents of ATM skimming and advises using an ATM inside a bank and always protecting your PIN. The Government of Canada advises using ATMs in well-lit public areas or inside a bank or business, avoiding card readers with irregular or unusual features, covering the keypad when entering your PIN, keeping your card in sight when it is handled by others, and monitoring statements for unauthorised transactions.

power.adapter_note: The Tourism Authority of Thailand states electricity runs at 220 volts with sockets compatible with European-style Type C or Type F plugs. A traveller from a 230V country (UK, EU, Australia, India) therefore needs no voltage converter — only a plug adapter if their plug shape differs. Travellers from 100-120V countries (US, Canada, Japan) need equipment rated for 220V or a converter; most modern phone and laptop chargers are dual-voltage, but check the label.

emergency.notes: Visitors should generally call the Tourist Police on 1155 first — the Tourism Authority of Thailand describes it as a 24-hour support line for travellers, and TAT also promotes a Thailand Tourist Police app. Whether 112 also connects to Thai emergency services could not be verified from an official source, and no official source was found stating which lines are answered in English.

getting_around.summary: The Tourism Authority of Thailand points visitors to tuk-tuks, songthaews and taxis, plus the BTS Skytrain and MRT metro in Bangkok, with domestic flights and long-distance trains and buses linking regions. Renting a car or motorbike is common but carries real risk: the UK FCDO reports a high number of road traffic accidents, particularly involving motorcycles, and warns that motorcycles and scooters hired in tourist areas are often unregistered and cannot legally be used on a public road. TAT advises checking road rules, licence requirements and insurance before driving, and notes that major airports now use biometric processing.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Visitors can buy a prepaid tourist SIM or eSIM on arrival. True (Thailand's largest operator, which absorbed dtac) sells Tourist SIM and Tourist eSIM products at True and dtac service centres nationwide, at airport counters open 24/7, and through its online store. A valid passport is required to register, in compliance with NBTC regulations, with a maximum of three SIMs per person per brand.
connectivity.typical_cost: 449 THB for an 8-day unlimited-data 'Tourist INFINITE' SIM from True, as listed on 28 September 2026; 15-day and 30-day versions are also sold but their prices were not published on the page, and a 10-day data-only variant exists. A USD equivalent is not given here because no exchange rate was verified against an official source.

climate.precipitation_note: The driest month in Bangkok — about 9 mm of rain on average. These are Bangkok (central Thailand) normals; regional variation across the country is significant.
climate.crowd_note: Core of the cool dry season and the busiest stretch for foreign visitors; book accommodation and domestic flights well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: Still very dry, around 30 mm on average, with heat beginning to build.
climate.crowd_note: High season continues with comfortable conditions; northern Thailand can see agricultural burning haze late in the month.

climate.precipitation_note: About 29 mm — still dry, but daytime heat is noticeably stronger.
climate.crowd_note: High-season crowds start to thin as the heat rises.

climate.precipitation_note: The hottest month of the year in Bangkok, with about 65 mm of pre-monsoon rain.
climate.crowd_note: Songkran, the Thai New Year, falls in mid-April — TAT scheduled Bangkok celebrations across 9–15 April in 2026, with the main traditional dates 13–15 April. Expect heavy domestic travel, higher prices and some business closures around those dates.

climate.precipitation_note: The southwest monsoon arrives — rainfall jumps to roughly 220 mm, typically as heavy afternoon downpours rather than all-day rain.
climate.crowd_note: Low season begins; rates fall and sites are quieter.

climate.precipitation_note: Around 149 mm — a relative lull within the rainy season.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet and good value; humidity is high throughout.

climate.precipitation_note: About 155 mm, spread through the month.
climate.crowd_note: A secondary bump from European and regional summer holidays, but well short of the winter peak.

climate.precipitation_note: Around 197 mm as the monsoon strengthens again.
climate.crowd_note: Still moderately busy with summer-holiday travellers; expect wet afternoons.

climate.precipitation_note: The wettest month in Bangkok by a clear margin — about 344 mm. Flooding is possible in parts of the country.
climate.crowd_note: The quietest month for visitors, with the lowest prices, but the highest chance of washed-out days.

climate.precipitation_note: Still wet at roughly 242 mm, though the monsoon typically eases through the second half of the month.
climate.crowd_note: Quiet and inexpensive; conditions usually improve markedly toward month end.

climate.precipitation_note: Rainfall drops sharply to about 48 mm as the dry season sets in.
climate.crowd_note: High season restarts — arguably the best balance of dry weather and pre-Christmas crowd levels.

climate.precipitation_note: Very dry, around 10 mm, and the coolest month of the year in Bangkok.
climate.crowd_note: Peak of the season; the Christmas and New Year fortnight is the busiest and most expensive of the year.

timezone_note: Türkiye uses a single time zone nationwide and has stayed on UTC+3 year-round since 2016 — clocks are not put forward or back for daylight saving, so the gap to European countries widens by an hour in their winter. Turkish diplomatic missions describe the country's time as GMT+3.
passport_validity_rule: Under Law no. 6458 on Foreigners and International Protection, a traveller's passport or travel document must be valid for at least 60 days beyond the 'duration of stay' granted by their visa, e-Visa, visa exemption or residence permit — not merely 60 days beyond the date of entry. Türkiye's Ministry of Foreign Affairs gives the worked example that a 90-day duration of stay requires 90 + 60 = 150 days of passport validity at the moment of entry, and a 30-day stay requires 90 days. The same ministry separately advises travellers to hold a passport valid for at least 6 months from arrival. NextStamp checks this as five months beyond your entry date (about 152 days): Türkiye ties the 60 days to the duration of stay you are *granted*, not to the day you actually leave, so measuring from departure would under-state the requirement on a short trip. Five months from entry matches how both the UK Foreign Office and Global Affairs Canada state it to their citizens, and clears the 150-day figure in the ministry's own worked example.
entry_requirement_notes: Most tourist visitors either enter visa-free or use the e-Visa obtained online at www.evisa.gov.tr; the e-Visa is valid only when the purpose of travel is tourism or commerce, and work, study or other purposes require a visa from a Turkish embassy or consulate. Many nationalities (for example British citizens) may visit for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Passengers arriving by cruise ship may enter without a visa for a maximum of 72 hours. Documentary filming, research and archaeological work require special advance permission from the Turkish authorities. No Turkish government source found states a proof-of-funds, accommodation-booking, travel-insurance or onward-ticket requirement for ordinary tourist entry, and there is no mandatory online arrival form. The 1-blank-page figure is as stated by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office for entry to Türkiye; Türkiye's own sites do not publish a blank-page rule. Currency: the UK FCDO and Global Affairs Canada both say there is no limit on bringing foreign currency or Turkish lira into Türkiye; on leaving, you cannot take out Turkish lira worth more than US$5,000, and other currency above US$5,000 must be declared to Turkish Customs (Canada adds that funds above that need proof they came from authorised banks).

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccinations up to date (MMR, DTaP/Tdap/Td, polio, chickenpox, influenza, shingles)
Rabies (only for travellers with likely animal exposure through work or activities)
health.malaria_risk: Not clear-cut from official sources. CDC's Türkiye destination page states 'Malaria is a risk in some parts of Türkiye (Turkey)' but lists no antimalarial medicine in its Vaccines and Medicines table, and Türkiye does not appear on WHO's list of countries and territories certified malaria-free. Ask a travel clinic about your specific route rather than assuming either way.
health.notes: Nothing health-related is checked at the Turkish border for ordinary tourist arrivals — CDC states yellow fever vaccine is neither recommended nor required for entry to Türkiye, and the vaccines above are advisory only. Travel insurance covering local treatment and medical evacuation is strongly advised by several governments. Practical warning from the UK FCDO: foreign prescriptions are not accepted by Turkish pharmacies, and some medicines that are ordinary elsewhere are controlled in Türkiye — check with a Turkish embassy before travelling with prescription medication.

money.atm_notes: No official Turkish source was found covering ATM fees or dynamic-currency-conversion practice. The Government of Canada's travel advice for Türkiye advises using ATMs located inside a bank or business or in well-lit public areas, and covering the keypad with one hand when entering a PIN.

emergency.notes: Türkiye's Ministry of the Interior consolidated its separate emergency lines — 110 fire, 112 medical, 155 police, 156 gendarmerie, 122 AFAD disaster, 177 forest fire and 158 coast guard — into the single number 112, which was extended to all 81 provinces as of June 2021. 112 is the number the UK and Canadian governments both tell their citizens to dial in Türkiye (the UK FCDO says 'Dial 112 and ask for an ambulance'). No official source states whether calls are answered in English, so do not assume they will be; the gendarmerie (jandarma) rather than the police covers rural areas and much of the coast.

getting_around.summary: Türkiye's official tourism board describes high-speed trains, domestic flights, intercity buses and city subways as the practical ways to cross the country, calling the intercity bus network 'one of the most affordable ways to travel across Türkiye', with comfortable seats, online reservations and reasonable fares. Rail is run by TCDD (Turkish State Railways) and connects all major cities, with high-speed (YHT) lines running Ankara–İstanbul and Ankara–Konya. Within İstanbul, a single contactless card covers the municipal transport network.

passes.name: İstanbulkart
passes.covers: İstanbul's municipal public transport, including the Metro İstanbul rail network; it is the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality's transport and payment card, issued by Belbim.
passes.worth_it: Effectively required rather than optional — it is how you pay for city transport. Buy and top it up at the Biletmatik ticket-vending machines in metro stations on arrival.

passes.name: MuseumPass Türkiye
passes.covers: More than 350 museums and archaeological sites belonging to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, one entry per site.
passes.worth_it: Worth it only if you will visit several ticketed state museums and sites within its 15-day window, which starts at your first museum visit. Regional versions (MuseumPass İstanbul, Museum Pass Cappadocia) exist for shorter or single-region trips. It is not valid for Night Museology entries.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Turkish mobile lines are tied to the holder's identity document, and a device registered by a foreign visitor can only be used with GSM lines registered to that passport holder. The bigger trap is the handset, not the SIM: BTK (the Information Technologies and Communications Authority) allows a phone brought in from abroad to be used on a Turkish network for 120 days counted from your date of entry into the country, after which the device is cut off from Turkish networks unless its IMEI is registered — a paid registration made through the e-Devlet portal. A single short holiday is unaffected; long stays and repeat visits on the same passport are where people get caught.

climate.precipitation_note: One of the two wettest months in İstanbul (about 89 mm on the long-run average); cold, grey and occasionally snowy.
climate.crowd_note: Quietest time of year for the classic sights, with the shortest queues and the lowest room rates. Coastal resort towns are largely shut.

climate.precipitation_note: Still wet (about 71 mm) and still cold; snow in İstanbul and across the Anatolian plateau is normal.
climate.crowd_note: Low season continues. Cappadocia is atmospheric under snow but balloon flights are cancelled more often in winter weather.

climate.precipitation_note: Drying out slowly (about 62 mm); changeable, with cold snaps still likely.
climate.crowd_note: Shoulder season — cheap and uncrowded, but the weather is a gamble and some coastal hotels have not reopened.

climate.precipitation_note: Noticeably drier (about 48 mm) and mild; among the most comfortable months for walking cities and ruins.
climate.crowd_note: Excellent weather brings the first real crowds, and İstanbul's tulip displays draw visitors. Book ahead but expect shorter queues than midsummer.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry and warm (about 33 mm); reliable sunshine without summer heat.
climate.crowd_note: Arguably the best all-round month: the coast is warm enough to swim, inland sites are not yet punishing, and crowds are below the July–August ceiling.

climate.precipitation_note: Dry (about 28 mm) and hot; the Mediterranean and Aegean coasts are considerably hotter than İstanbul.
climate.crowd_note: Peak season is under way. Coastal resorts fill quickly and prices climb.

climate.precipitation_note: Driest stretch of the year (about 22 mm). İstanbul is hot and humid; inland and southern-coast temperatures run well above the İstanbul figures.
climate.crowd_note: Highest crowds and highest prices, overlapping with European school holidays. Sightseeing at Ephesus, Pamukkale or Cappadocia is best done at opening time.

climate.precipitation_note: Still very dry (about 24 mm) and as hot as July, with high humidity in İstanbul.
climate.crowd_note: The busiest month alongside July. Great for the coast, hard work for hot inland archaeology.

climate.precipitation_note: Warm and mostly dry (about 40 mm) as the summer heat eases.
climate.crowd_note: The other strong month: sea temperatures are still warm, the heat is manageable, and the family-holiday crowds thin after the first weeks.

climate.precipitation_note: Rain returns (about 66 mm) but days are still mild and pleasant.
climate.crowd_note: Good-value shoulder season. Coastal resorts begin winding down towards the end of the month; cities stay comfortable.

climate.precipitation_note: Wet (about 78 mm) and cooling fast.
climate.crowd_note: Low season. Cheap and quiet for İstanbul and Cappadocia; the coast is essentially closed for swimming.

climate.precipitation_note: The wettest month in İstanbul (about 99 mm), cold and often grey.
climate.crowd_note: Low season apart from a short New Year bump in İstanbul. Expect the shortest daylight hours of the year for sightseeing.

timezone_note: One time zone for all seven emirates. The UAE government fact sheet states "The UAE is 4 hours ahead of GMT" and Experience Abu Dhabi gives "+4 hours in front of UTC"; neither mentions daylight saving, which the UAE does not observe.
passport_validity_rule: The UAE government portal states plainly: "Passports must be valid for at least 6 months from the date of entry into the UAE." UK FCDO guidance for the UAE says the same for visitors — your passport's expiry date must be at least 6 months after the date you arrive — and adds that the requirement drops to 3 months for holders of a UAE residence permit.
entry_requirement_notes: MEDICATION IS THE THING THAT CATCHES PEOPLE OUT. UK FCDO guidance for the UAE states: "You will need approval from the UAE authorities to bring in medication that the UAE classes as narcotic, psychotropic, controlled or semi-controlled" and "You must get approval in advance from the UAE Ministry of Health to bring medication." On quantity: "You can bring up to 3 months' supply of medication as a visitor, reduced to one month's supply if the medication is included in the list requiring approval", and applications are "normally processed within 5 working days". The approving body is the UAE Ministry of Health and Prevention (MoHAP), which runs an e-permit service, "Issue of Permit to Import Medicines for Personal Use", and publishes the controlled/semi-controlled lists; mohap.gov.ae refused every automated request made during this research, so the rule above is cited to the FCDO rather than to MoHAP directly — check mohap.gov.ae yourself before travelling, and carry the original prescription and a doctor's letter regardless. Recreational and controlled drugs are a banned import outright (u.ae customs guidance lists "controlled/recreational drugs and narcotic substances" among prohibited goods) and the UAE enforces this severely. CASH: the UAE government customs page (u.ae) says travellers entering or leaving with "more than AED 60,000 in cash" (or the equivalent in other currencies, financial instruments, precious metals or stones) must declare it to ICP, online or through the Afseh app; Global Affairs Canada words it as "AED 60 000 or more", so declare if you are at or near the figure. VISA: many nationalities get a visitor visa on arrival free of charge, but the permitted stay differs by passport (FCDO: British citizens up to 90 days in any 180-day period) and u.ae warns that "Lists of countries eligible for visa on arrival may vary from time to time" - check your own nationality before booking. INDIAN PASSPORTS are different: ICP (announcement of 25 June 2026) says the 14-day entry visa costs AED 100 (extendable once during the stay) and the 60-day visa AED 250 (single entry, non-extendable), for ordinary-passport holders who hold a valid visa, residence permit or US Green Card from the US, EU or UK, or a valid residence permit from Japan, South Korea, Australia, Canada, Singapore or New Zealand. ICP's 60-day service page lists an issuance fee of AED 250 plus a smart-services fee of AED 100 (AED 350 in total), so budget for that; the entry visa must be used within 30 days of issue, and overstay is fined AED 50 per day. The same ICP announcement extends the 60-day category to nationals of Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, the Philippines, Kenya and South Africa who hold such a visa or residence permit. PROOF OF ONWARD TRAVEL: neither u.ae nor FCDO states an onward-ticket, hotel-booking or proof-of-funds rule for visitors arriving visa-free, but ICP's "Issuance of a Visa" service page lists a return travel ticket and valid UAE health insurance among its requirements for visit visas applied for in advance, so carry a return or onward booking. Passport: GAC adds that temporary passports and emergency travel documents are not accepted for entry. Security advisories (e.g. FCDO's July 2026 regional-tensions update) do not change these entry rules.

required_vaccinations: Yellow fever (only for travellers aged 9 months and older arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; not required for travel direct from the USA or Europe)
recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccinations (MMR, diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis, polio, chickenpox, influenza, shingles)
Rabies (only for travellers with likely animal exposure)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None
health.notes: Yellow fever is the only vaccine tied to entry, and only conditionally: CDC lists it as not required for travellers arriving direct from the United States, and required for travellers aged 9 months and older arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Everything in the recommended list is medical advice only and is not checked at immigration. CDC's UAE destination page carries no malaria section and recommends no antimalarial drugs for the UAE. Global Affairs Canada (14 October 2026) says the same: proof of vaccination is required if you arrive from, or transit through an airport in, a country where yellow fever occurs; CDC (page reviewed 25 August 2026) counts layovers over 12 hours in such a country. Both say yellow fever vaccination is not recommended for the UAE itself.

money.card_acceptance: Experience Abu Dhabi (the emirate's official tourism board) states that "Credit and debit cards are widely accepted" and that "Most shops, hotels and restaurants in Abu Dhabi accept major credit and debit cards (Visa, MasterCard, American Express, etc.)", while advising you to "check before you order or purchase anything if there is no visible sign of card acceptance". Souks and smaller independent shops are the usual gap.
money.cash_culture: Cards cover most of a normal trip, but the tourism board's own advice is that "Carrying cash with you is recommended, as smaller shops or souks may not have access to a card machine", and that in souks and smaller shops "currency in smaller bank notes would be preferred". A few hundred dirhams in small notes is enough for most visitors; the dirham is pegged at USD 1 = AED 3.6725.
money.tipping: Not expected, but common. Experience Abu Dhabi: "Tipping is not expected but is commonly practised in the emirate. Gratuities to hotel and restaurant staff are at your discretion." Check the bill first — many fine-dining and high-end restaurants add a service charge of around 10% plus a 6% tourism levy, and menus say when those are already included. Where they are not included, the tourism board suggests 10-15%.
money.atm_notes: ATMs are everywhere — "in all shopping malls, major supermarkets, most petrol stations and the airport" — and accept American Express, Cirrus, Global Access, MasterCard, Plus System and VISA. Most are part of a central network, so a card from another bank works "for a nominal charge". For changing cash, the tourism board says bureaux de change "often offer better rates than the banks", while hotels exchange "at standard (non-competitive) rates"; a passport is required to exchange currency or travellers' cheques anywhere.

power.adapter_note: Sockets are the UK-style three-pin 13A pattern (Type G), so British and Irish plugs fit without an adapter and everyone else needs one. Two figures circulate in official UAE material: Ministry of Foreign Affairs country pages describe the domestic supply as 220 volts, while DEWA (Dubai's electricity utility) specifies its network as 230/400V at 50Hz. Either way anything rated 220-240V works unmodified; US 110V-only equipment needs a transformer, not just a plug adapter.

emergency.notes: The UAE government portal lists Police 999, Ambulance 998 and Civil Defence (fire) 997, callable from anywhere in the UAE, plus 991 for the electricity authority. For tourists specifically, u.ae lists two Dubai Tourism Police numbers: +971 50 453 8107 (the number shown above) and +971 4 609 6239; Abu Dhabi Tourism Police is on +971 2 800 2626 or +971 2 512 7777. English is widely spoken in the UAE, including by the emergency services, but no official page we could reach states a guaranteed language of response. We could NOT confirm from any official UAE source that 112 routes to UAE emergency services — dial 999/998/997 rather than assuming it does. Non-emergency government help is on 171 (Tawasul). Global Affairs Canada (14 October 2026) also lists only 999 / 998 / 997 and no 112; the 112 question stays unconfirmed.

getting_around.summary: Most visitors split their time between Dubai and Abu Dhabi, which are linked by motorway and intercity bus. Dubai has a metro, a tram, public buses and traditional abras across the creek, all paid for with an RTA nol card rather than cash. Abu Dhabi has no metro: taxis are, in the tourism board's words, "reasonably priced and the most popular way to get around the city", alongside public buses, car hire and a free Visit Abu Dhabi shuttle bus available to visitors who book a hotel or buy attraction tickets in the emirate. Metered taxis and ride-hailing are cheap and plentiful in both cities and English is widely spoken by drivers.

passes.name: nol Silver card (Dubai)
passes.covers: All Dubai public transport modes — metro, tram, bus, water transport — plus some non-transport services such as parking
passes.worth_it: The default choice for a visitor staying more than a day or two: AED 25 including AED 19 of travel credit, valid for 5 years, and it is the only practical way to pay on Dubai's metro, tram and buses.

passes.name: nol Red Ticket (Dubai)
passes.covers: A single transport mode, on a disposable paper ticket
passes.worth_it: AED 2, valid 90 days or 10 trips. Only worth it if you expect to make one or two journeys; switching modes needs a new ticket, so the Silver card is better value for almost anyone staying a full day.

passes.name: nol Travel card (Dubai)
passes.covers: All Dubai transport services, bundled with tourist offers and discounts
passes.worth_it: AED 100 including AED 19 of credit — RTA markets it at tourists, but you are paying roughly AED 75 above the Silver card for the discount booklet, so only worth it if you will actually use the offers.

connectivity.local_sim_notes: Visitors can buy a local SIM on a passport — TDRA's mobile-consumer registration policy allows visitors to register using a passport (or a GCC national ID) rather than an Emirates ID, for a limited period and up to two SIMs per service provider. e& (Etisalat) sells a prepaid Visitor Line at its business centres, outlets and partners on presentation of a valid passport and visa, in packs valid 28 days, with a maximum of two Visitor Line SIMs per passport. e& also offers a self-activated eSIM for visitors, activated by scanning a QR code and completing a facial-recognition step as soon as you clear immigration, which comes with 10GB of complimentary data valid for one day; du sells tourist prepaid plans as eSIMs too. Airport arrivals halls in Dubai and Abu Dhabi have operator desks.

climate.precipitation_note: About 11mm over roughly 2 rain days — one of the wetter months in an extremely dry year. (Figures throughout are the National Center of Meteorology's Dubai normals as published by WMO, base period 1974-1991.)
climate.crowd_note: High season. Experience Abu Dhabi calls November to April "the most pleasant time to visit", and hotel rates and beach-club demand reflect it — book well ahead.

climate.precipitation_note: Statistically the wettest month: about 36mm over roughly 4 rain days. Still sunny most days, but downpours are short and heavy and roads flood quickly.
climate.crowd_note: High season and very comfortable. Ramadan can fall in this month — its dates move about 11 days earlier each year, so check the current year before booking; during it, eating, drinking and smoking in public in daylight are restricted, some restaurants close or shorten daytime hours, and traffic is heavy just before sunset.

climate.precipitation_note: About 22mm over roughly 4 rain days, tailing off through the month.
climate.crowd_note: Arguably the best month: warm enough to swim, cool enough to walk. Still inside the November-April high season, and Ramadan or Eid al-Fitr may fall here depending on the year.

climate.precipitation_note: About 8mm over roughly 2 rain days; the last of the winter rain.
climate.crowd_note: The end of the pleasant season. Midday is already hot for sightseeing on foot, but evenings are excellent and rates start softening as the peak winds down.

climate.precipitation_note: Essentially dry — under 1mm on average.
climate.crowd_note: Outside the tourism board's recommended window. Rooms and flights get noticeably cheaper, but outdoor sightseeing is limited to early morning and evening.

climate.precipitation_note: No measurable rainfall in the normals.
climate.crowd_note: Deep summer. Everything worth doing is indoors and air-conditioned; nights stay above 26C, so even evenings are uncomfortable. Cheapest hotel rates of the year.

climate.precipitation_note: No measurable rainfall in the normals.
climate.crowd_note: The hottest month on record normals, with high Gulf humidity on top. Malls, museums and indoor attractions only; low rates, low crowds.

climate.precipitation_note: No measurable rainfall in the normals.
climate.crowd_note: As punishing as July and more humid. Many residents are away; hotels discount hard and shopping promotions run through the summer.

climate.precipitation_note: No measurable rainfall in the normals.
climate.crowd_note: Still summer in practice — the heat does not really break until October. Sea temperatures are at their warmest and least refreshing.

climate.precipitation_note: No measurable rainfall in the normals.
climate.crowd_note: The turn of the season: hot but bearable by late October, outdoor terraces and beach clubs reopening, and rates still below the winter peak.

climate.precipitation_note: Around 2mm; effectively dry.
climate.crowd_note: The official start of the pleasant season per Experience Abu Dhabi. Warm days, cool evenings, and the outdoor events calendar restarts — demand and prices climb through the month.

climate.precipitation_note: About 14mm over roughly 2 rain days.
climate.crowd_note: Peak of the peak: ideal weather and heavy Christmas and New Year demand. Expect the year's highest hotel rates and book restaurants and desert trips well in advance.

timezone_label: BST (UTC+1, summer time in effect); GMT (UTC+0) from 25 October 2026
timezone_note: The whole United Kingdom is on one clock. GOV.UK states that the clocks go back one hour at 2am on Sunday 25 October 2026 (the last Sunday in October), ending British Summer Time, and go forward one hour at 1am on Sunday 28 March 2027. VisitBritain describes the same pattern: Greenwich Mean Time in winter, British Summer Time (clocks forward one hour) in summer. The IANA zone Europe/London agrees. Today (17 October 2026) the UK is therefore on BST, UTC+1.
passport_validity_rule: GOV.UK's Standard Visitor eligibility page says: 'You must have a passport or travel document to enter the UK. It should be valid for the whole of your stay.' The UK therefore has no fixed six-month rule; the stated test is validity for the length of the stay, which the app encodes as duration-of-stay with no extra months. Two practical points: an Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) is linked to the one passport used in the application and ends when that passport expires (ETA 4.1 and 4.3 of the Immigration Rules), so a passport with little life left gives a short ETA; and airlines can apply their own stricter checks at boarding. Sourcing note: the 'whole of your stay' wording is from the Standard Visitor (visa) pages; the ETA pages opened for this guide set no separate minimum remaining validity for ETA holders.
entry_requirement_notes: The ETA is in force today (17 October 2026). GOV.UK's news release of 24 February 2026 says that from 25 February 2026 non-visa nationals are barred from entering the UK without an Electronic Travel Authorisation, and that airlines will prevent passengers boarding without an ETA, eVisa or other valid documentation. Who needs one: GOV.UK says 'Most visitors need an ETA or a visa', depending on nationality and purpose, and that you usually need an ETA rather than a visa if you are from Europe, the USA, Australia, Canada or certain other countries. Whether YOUR nationality can get an ETA is read from the live GOV.UK eligibility page ('Check if you can get an ETA', last updated 9 April 2026 when read for this guide) and the 'Check if you need an ETA or visa' tool at gov.uk/check-uk-visa, not from memory: the list changes (for example Nicaragua and St Lucia were removed on 5 March 2026, Botswana on 14 October 2025), and nationalities not on it must apply for a visa instead. At the time of reading, that page listed the EU states other than Ireland, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein, the USA, Canada, Australia, Japan, Singapore, Brazil, Mexico and the Gulf states among others; nationality shown on the passport is what counts. Cost and validity per GOV.UK: 20 GBP per person, non-refundable, applied for online or in the UK ETA app; it lasts 2 years or until the passport expires, whichever is sooner; unlimited trips while valid; each traveller needs one, including babies and children; a decision usually comes by email within a day but can take up to 3 working days, so apply before booking non-refundable travel. Only apply on GOV.UK or the official app; GOV.UK warns other sites may charge more. The ETA covers visits of up to 6 months per visit and now also covers Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man (since 9 April 2026); it does not guarantee entry. Who does not need one (GOV.UK): British and Irish citizens (dual British or Irish citizens cannot get one), people with a UK visa or permission to live, work or study in the UK or the Crown Dependencies, people living in Ireland who travel from Ireland, Guernsey, Jersey or the Isle of Man, and airside transit passengers who do not pass border control; transit through border control does need an ETA. Visa nationals (about 115 countries and territories on the Immigration Rules visa national list) must get a visa before travel. For visitors, GOV.UK's eligibility page says you must be able to pay for your return or onward journey, support yourself during the trip and leave at the end of your visit; it does not state that a booked ticket must be shown, so whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed and no blank-page count was found. Cross-checks opened 2026-10-18: Global Affairs Canada's UK page (travel.gc.ca, updated 26 May 2026) confirms strict ETA enforcement from 25 February 2026, that 'Your passport must be valid for at least the expected duration of your stay' (transport companies may apply stricter rules), and that you must travel on the passport used for the ETA. Fee discrepancy between two GOV.UK pages: the ETA guide (gov.uk/eta and gov.uk/eta/apply) states 'An ETA costs 20 GBP' and 'It costs 20 GBP to apply online or through the UK ETA app', while the 24 February 2026 news release still says 16 GBP; the guide pages are the current fee page, so 20 GBP is used here, but confirm the fee on the application screen before paying. Onward ticket: Global Affairs Canada says UK Border officials 'may ask you to show them a return or onward ticket' and proof of funds, but no UK government page opened states that a ticket is required, so whether an onward ticket is required is not confirmed; carrying proof of onward travel is sensible.

recommended_vaccinations: Routine vaccines up to date (chickenpox, DTaP/Tdap/Td, influenza, MMR, polio, shingles)
Measles (all international travellers fully vaccinated with MMR)
Polio (unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated travellers complete a series; adults with a childhood series may take one lifetime booster)
Hepatitis A (for street food or rural areas)
Rabies (depending on activities and access to post-exposure care)
Mpox (only for travellers with specific higher-risk exposures)
health.malaria_risk: None listed on CDC's United Kingdom page
health.notes: No vaccination is required to enter the UK: CDC's United Kingdom page states yellow fever vaccine is not required for entry. The recommendations above are CDC medical advice, not entry conditions. CDC is used as a fallback because no UKHSA or NHS page listing vaccines for visitors was opened for this guide; CDC's page was last reviewed 25 August 2026 and carries a Level 2 notice on global polio (updated 23 September 2026, saying poliovirus has been identified in the UK in the past year) and a Level 1 global measles notice (28 May 2025). Healthcare: the NHS website says A&E services are free to everyone, but that visitors who are not ordinarily resident and need NHS hospital treatment are charged 150% of the national NHS rate, and that eye tests, dental treatment and prescriptions are charged even for visitors; for stays under 6 months it advises making sure you are covered by personal medical insurance. That NHS page was last reviewed in April 2023, so check nhs.uk for current rules. For urgent but non-life-threatening problems, NHS 111 gives advice; 999 is for life-threatening emergencies. Cross-check: UKHSA's TravelHealthPro (NaTHNaC) United Kingdom page, opened 2026-10-18, states 'There are no certificate requirements under International Health Regulations' and carries no malaria or yellow fever guidance; Global Affairs Canada's UK page also says yellow fever proof is not required for entry. The NHS visitor page (nhs.uk) opened 2026-10-18 still carries 'Page last reviewed: 25 April 2023', so the 150% charging figure should be confirmed on nhs.uk before relying on it.

money.card_acceptance: VisitBritain states that credit, debit, contact and contactless payment cards are widely used throughout Britain, that Visa and Mastercard are the most common, and that American Express and Diners Club are only sometimes accepted. It also says some small shops, markets and cafes may not accept card or digital payments. VisitBritain's separate travel-tips page says most places accept contactless payments but it is a safe bet to have some cash on hand when arriving. Neither page carries a date.
money.cash_culture: VisitBritain: some small shops, markets and cafes may not take cards, so a little cash is useful. London buses do not take cash (VisitBritain); you touch in with a contactless card or Oyster.
money.tipping: VisitBritain states 'Tipping is not expected in Britain like it is in some other countries.' In taxis it is customary to round the fare up to the nearest pound; in restaurants an optional service charge may be added to the bill, and if none is added a tip is a thank-you for good service; hotel porters who take luggage to your room are customarily tipped about 2 GBP. (The page's restaurant percentage is not reproduced here because the fetched text omitted its unit.)

power.adapter_note: VisitBritain states that the voltage in Britain is 220/240 AC, 50Hz, that plugs (type G) have three rectangular pins, and that visitors will probably need an adaptor for electrical equipment. The page carries no date, and the IEC World Plugs listing was not opened to cross-check.

emergency.notes: GOV.UK states: '999 and 112 is the national emergency response service in the UK' and '112 is the pan-European equivalent to 999 and can be used in the UK'; the page lists police, ambulance, fire and coastguard as the services reached (page last updated 1 April 2025). So 999 is the number to dial and 112 also works; the number shown is 999. There is no separate number per service. Non-emergency: VisitBritain gives 101 for police matters that need no immediate response and 111 as the national non-emergency medical number (NHS 111 handles urgent but non-life-threatening problems). The NHS says 999 is for life-threatening emergencies such as serious road traffic accidents, strokes and heart attacks. Not confirmed from an official page opened for this guide, so omitted: free-of-charge status, the Emergency SMS service for deaf callers, and any tourist-police line. Cross-check: Global Affairs Canada's UK page (opened 2026-10-18) says 'Dial 999 for emergency assistance' and lists no per-service numbers; it does not mention 112. The 112 statement rests on the GOV.UK page alone, which was reopened 2026-10-18 and still reads '112 is the pan-European equivalent to 999 and can be used in the UK'.

getting_around.summary: Britain's long-distance network is National Rail: VisitBritain says it has more than 2,500 stations with different train companies serving different areas, and recommends the National Rail Journey Planner. National Rail says Advance tickets (fixed to one train and date) can usually be bought up to 12 weeks ahead, are non-refundable unless your train is delayed or cancelled and you choose not to travel, and can be amended up to the time of departure for a 10 GBP fee plus any fare difference; VisitBritain adds that booking early can lower fares and that two singles are sometimes cheaper than a return. No fare for any specific journey is given here because fares vary by route, date and time. In London, TfL's pay-as-you-go system covers the Underground, buses, trams, DLR and most National Rail services within London: National Rail says contactless works on National Rail, Underground, DLR, buses and trams within London, Oyster is accepted on the same plus London Overground, most Elizabeth line services and most National Rail in Zones 1 to 9, and daily and weekly capping applies to both. National Rail also notes that railcard and child discounts do not apply to contactless but do apply to Oyster (with named exceptions). VisitBritain says London buses do not take cash and that Tube services run from about 5:30am until midnight with some lines running overnight at weekends. Regional notes: VisitBritain says large areas such as the West Midlands and Greater Manchester have cards valid on all public transport in their region, that trams run in Edinburgh, Birmingham, Sheffield, Manchester, Nottingham and Blackpool, and that the Glasgow Subway and Tyne and Wear Metro serve those cities; it gives no Wales-specific transport detail. Note that most of the figures above come from pages undated or last updated in 2026; confirm before travel.

passes.name: Contactless or Oyster pay as you go (London)
passes.covers: Pay-as-you-go travel on the Underground, DLR, London buses and trams and National Rail services in London (contactless), and the same plus London Overground, most Elizabeth line services and most National Rail in Zones 1 to 9 (Oyster), per National Rail. Oyster holds up to 90 GBP of pay-as-you-go credit; daily and weekly capping applies to both.
passes.worth_it: Capping means you pay no more than the cap for a day's travel, and National Rail notes that capping can cost less than a One Day Travelcard. No fare or cap figure for contactless was opened from tfl.gov.uk (it returned 403 to automated fetches), so none is stated for it here. Railcard and child discounts do not apply to contactless.

passes.name: Visitor Oyster card
passes.covers: A TfL pay-as-you-go card for visitors; VisitBritain says it works on buses, the Tube, trams and most rail services within zones 1 to 6.
passes.worth_it: TfL's Visitor Shop states each card includes a non-refundable 10.50 GBP card fee, the smallest card costs 20.50 GBP (10.50 GBP fee plus 10 GBP credit), unused cards can be returned for a refund within 1 month of purchase, and a day of unlimited travel in zones 1 to 2 is 'currently capped at 8.90 GBP' (page undated, copyright TfL 2026). The Visitor Shop page did not say whether contactless costs the same or less; the card mainly helps if you do not want to use an overseas bank card for each journey.

passes.name: BritRail Pass
passes.covers: VisitBritain describes it as a tourist-only pass with unlimited journeys on National Rail services across England, Scotland and Wales, excluding non-National Rail services such as Eurostar and the London Underground; a paper pass must be activated before use.
passes.worth_it: No price or validity options appear on the VisitBritain page, so whether it beats point-to-point or Advance tickets for your route could not be checked from an official source; compare against National Rail fares for your actual journeys.

phrases_language: English. The UK has no foreign language to learn: English is what you will be spoken to in. These sixteen entries are everyday British vocabulary that visitors from other English-speaking countries and non-native speakers actually run into (queue, loo, lift, chips and so on), not a foreign language. The 'English' column gives the standard international wording and the other column the usual British equivalent. They are editorial, compiled for this guide, not from a cited official source; no government body publishes a list of British usage. Welsh, Scottish Gaelic and Irish are also official or recognised languages in parts of the UK, but none was researched here and all visitors can use English throughout.

timezone_note: America/New_York is the Eastern zone — the one most visitors land in — but the country is not on one clock. The mainland spans four zones (Eastern America/New_York, Central America/Chicago, Mountain America/Denver, Pacific America/Los_Angeles), plus Alaska (America/Anchorage) and Hawaii (Pacific/Honolulu): six zones, and nine hours between Eastern and Hawaii in summer. Per NIST, daylight saving time runs 8 March to 1 November in 2026, beginning and ending at 2:00 a.m. local time (second Sunday of March to first Sunday of November); the IANA tz database agrees, putting America/New_York on EDT (UTC-4) today and switching it to EST (UTC-5) at 02:00 on 1 November 2026. NIST states DST is not observed in Hawaii, American Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, or the state of Arizona (except the Navajo Nation, which does observe it) — so Arizona is on America/Phoenix (UTC-7 year-round) and is an hour off its neighbours for half the year. Book domestic connections against the local zone, not a single national offset.
passport_validity_rule: U.S. Customs and Border Protection requires visitors to hold a passport valid for six months beyond the intended period of stay in the United States. Citizens of the countries on CBP's published exemption list (the 'six-month club') are exempt from that rule and need only a passport valid for their intended period of stay — the list is long and includes most of Europe, the UK, Canada, Australia, Japan, South Korea, India, Brazil, Mexico and Singapore. CBP's Carrier Liaison Program publishes the current list; the edition current for this guide is dated 18 December 2025 and supersedes all earlier Carrier Liaison Program bulletins.
entry_requirement_notes: Entry is either visa-free under the Visa Waiver Program with an approved ESTA, or on a visa — and which one applies depends on nationality, not on the trip. CBP states the VWP covers citizens of 42 participating countries for tourism or business stays of up to 90 days; everyone else needs a visa from a U.S. embassy or consulate. VWP travellers must hold an e-Passport (CBP FAQ). ESTA must be approved before travel (air, sea or land), and CBP states an approval is typically valid for two years or until the passport expires, whichever comes first. ESTA fee, in force today: DHS's fiscal year 2027 inflation notice (Federal Register, 1 October 2026) sets it at $40.62 per travel authorization ($17 + $10.62 + $13), and CBP began assessing that amount on 16 October 2026; it was $40.27 before that date. If the application is denied only the $10.62 cost-recovery component is charged. The same notice leaves the HR-1 Form I-94 fee at $24 and sets the EVUS enrollment fee at $31.75 (EVUS applies only to People's Republic of China nationals holding certain U.S. visas, not to other travellers). Visa integrity fee: HR-1 created a $250 fee on nonimmigrant visas, but the only official text found says DHS would implement it in a future publication, and no implementation notice was found; collection was not confirmed as in force today (travel.state.gov sits behind a human-verification check and was not read), so check the State Department fee page if you need a visa. Entry restriction in force today: a CDC order (continued on 11 October 2026 for 30 days) bars entry of foreign nationals who were in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda or South Sudan within the previous 21 days. Global Affairs Canada also notes a U.S. proclamation, in force since 1 January 2026, restricting entry for certain nationalities, and that officers may search electronic devices. Apply for ESTA only through CBP's official ESTA channels (esta.cbp.dhs.gov); third-party sites charge a markup. Onward ticket: 8 CFR 217.2(c)(1) requires VWP applicants arriving by air or sea to hold, at the time of arrival, a round-trip ticket carrying them out of the United States to a foreign port or place (a ticket terminating in contiguous territory or an adjacent island counts only if the traveller is a resident there). The same regulation says a round-trip ticket is NOT required of VWP applicants arriving at a land border port of entry, who must instead show the CBP officer evidence of financial solvency and a domicile abroad they intend to return to. CBP is explicit that an approved ESTA does not guarantee entry: admissibility is decided by the CBP officer on arrival. Cash: anyone entering or leaving with more than $10,000 in currency or monetary instruments (combined for family or group travellers) must report it to CBP, on FinCEN Form 105; carrying more is legal, failing to report is not.

health.notes: No vaccination is required to enter the United States as a short-term visitor. The one that was — proof of COVID-19 vaccination for non-citizen, non-immigrant air passengers — ended at 12:01 a.m. EDT on 12 May 2023, when the underlying presidential proclamation was revoked; the State Department's notice records that change. Not stated here: CDC's Travelers' Health destination pages exist for travellers leaving the United States, not arriving in it, so there is no official CDC recommended-vaccination list or malaria-risk statement for the USA as a destination to cite here. (Separate, stricter vaccination requirements apply to immigrant visa applicants and adjustment of status, not to tourists.) Separate from vaccination: a CDC order currently suspends entry of foreign nationals who were physically present in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda or South Sudan in the past 21 days (Ebola); the order was last continued on 11 October 2026 for 30 days. Global Affairs Canada's U.S. advice (updated 15 October 2026) confirms proof of vaccination, including yellow fever, is not required for entry.

emergency.notes: 911 is the single number for police, fire and emergency medical services anywhere in the United States — there is no separate number per service. The call reaches a local Public Safety Answering Point, which dispatches the right agency. Do not plan on 112: FCC consumer guidance states that 112 is an international/EU number and does not work in the United States, and that 911 is what you dial here. Sourcing caveat, stated plainly: fcc.gov returns 403 to automated retrieval, so the 112 point was read from search results quoting the FCC's own page rather than fetched first-hand; the safe instruction either way is dial 911.

getting_around.summary: There is no single national transport pass and distances are continental — most visitors fly between regions and get around locally by car or rental car. Amtrak is the national intercity passenger rail operator; its USA Rail Pass covers 10 segments over 30 days to more than 500 destinations in Coach class for $499, with the pass usable within 120 days of purchase and the 30-day clock starting on the first segment. Amtrak's separate California Rail Pass is no longer sold to new customers as of 26 August 2026, though passes already bought are still honoured. For anyone visiting federal parkland, the America the Beautiful annual pass is the one broadly worthwhile national pass. Practical framing (not from a cited source): outside the Northeast Corridor, rail is a scenic option rather than a fast one, and much of the West is difficult to reach without a car.

passes.name: America the Beautiful — National Parks and Federal Recreational Lands Annual Pass
passes.covers: Entrance fees and standard amenity (day-use) fees at federal recreation sites run by the National Park Service, U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, U.S. Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management, Bureau of Reclamation and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. Covers either one private vehicle fee or four per-person fees, depending on how the site charges. Valid one year from purchase.
passes.worth_it: $80 for U.S. residents, $250 for non-residents (NPS pricing as published, page last updated 5 January 2026). Only worth it if you will enter several fee-charging federal sites within the year — entrance fees vary site by site, so check the specific parks on your route before buying. Senior options are cheaper: $20 annual, $80 lifetime.

passes.name: Amtrak USA Rail Pass
passes.covers: 10 rides (segments) over 30 days, Coach class, to a choice of more than 500 destinations on the Amtrak network.
passes.worth_it: $499, which Amtrak frames as under $50 per segment — so it pays only if you actually use long, expensive legs rather than short hops. The pass is valid for 120 days from purchase, but once you start the first segment you have 30 days to finish the rest. Reservations are still required per segment.
